papers.title: Development and Functional Testing of a Web Based Dengue Weather Alert Prototype with WhatsApp Notifications in Palu, Indonesia
papers.abstract: Background: Weather information may support dengue preparedness, although software functionality alone cannot establish forecasting accuracy. Objectives: This study developed a web based weather alert prototype integrating meteorological data and WhatsApp notifications for dengue preparedness in Palu, Indonesia. Methods: Research and development followed the Analysis, Design, and Development phases of the ADDIE model from January 14 to February 4, 2026. CodeIgniter 4 and MySQL supported coordinate based weather retrieval through OpenWeather, data storage, user registration, and automated notifications. Results: The prototype covered 46 urban villages across eight districts. Nine functional testing categories were reported as successful, including website accessibility, geographic data, weather integration, storage, notifications, decision logic, registration, profile management, and interface responsiveness. However, detailed test inputs, execution counts, and notification delivery receipts were unavailable. The 22 day development period could not independently establish a complete 30 day rainfall dataset without historical records. Weather thresholds remained literature informed assumptions without local predictive validation. Conclusions: The prototype demonstrated preliminary software integration capabilities. Reproducible functional testing, rainfall data verification, governance safeguards, and independent epidemiological validation are required before operational implementation for dengue preparedness.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在开发基于网络的登革热天气警报系统,以支持印度尼西亚巴鲁的登革热防备工作,因为天气信息可以支持登革热防备工作,尽管仅靠软件功能无法确定预测准确性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及开发一个集成气象数据和 WhatsApp 通知的基于网络的天气警报原型,覆盖印度尼西亚巴鲁八个区的 46 个城中村,时间为 2026 年 1 月 14 日至 2 月 4 日。
elements_zh.methods: 该原型是使用 ADDIE 模型开发的,CodeIgniter 4 和 MySQL 通过 OpenWeather 支持基于坐标的天气检索、数据存储、用户注册和自动通知。
elements_zh.main_results: 据报告,九个功能测试类别是成功的,包括网站可访问性、地理数据、天气集成、存储、通知、决策逻辑、注册、配置文件管理和界面响应能力。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该原型展示了初步的软件集成功能,暗示了通过基于天气的警报来预防登革热的潜在工具。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,该原型可以通过整合天气数据和 WhatsApp 通知来支持登革热防备,可能有助于公共卫生干预的早期预警系统。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究缺乏详细的测试输入、执行计数和通知送达收据,并且22天的开发周期无法在没有历史记录的情况下独立建立完整的30天降雨数据集。证据是中等的。

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:天气信息可以支持登革热防备,尽管软件功能本身无法确定预测准确性。目标:本研究开发了一个基于网络的天气警报原型,集成了气象数据和 WhatsApp 通知,用于印度尼西亚巴鲁的登革热防备。方法:研究和开发遵循 2026 年 1 月 14 日至 2 月 4 日 ADDIE 模型的分析、设计和开发阶段。CodeIgniter 4 和 MySQL 通过 OpenWeather、数据存储、用户注册和自动通知支持基于坐标的天气检索。结果:原型覆盖8个区46个城中村。据报告,九个功能测试类别是成功的,包括网站可访问性、地理数据、天气集成、存储、通知、决策逻辑、注册、配置文件管理和界面响应能力。然而,详细的测试输入、执行计数和通知传送收据不可用。22天的开发周期在没有历史记录的情况下无法独立建立完整的30天降雨数据集。天气阈值仍然是基于文献的假设,没有当地的预测验证。结论:原型展示了初步的软件集成能力。在实施登革热防备操作之前,需要进行可重复的功能测试、降雨数据验证、治理保障措施和独立的流行病学验证。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在开发基于网络的登革热天气警报系统,以支持印度尼西亚巴鲁的登革热防备工作,因为天气信息可以支持登革热防备工作,尽管仅靠软件功能无法确定预测准确性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及开发一个集成气象数据和 WhatsApp 通知的基于网络的天气警报原型,覆盖印度尼西亚巴鲁八个区的 46 个城中村,时间为 2026 年 1 月 14 日至 2 月 4 日。
analysis_zh.methods: 该原型是使用 ADDIE 模型开发的,CodeIgniter 4 和 MySQL 通过 OpenWeather 支持基于坐标的天气检索、数据存储、用户注册和自动通知。
analysis_zh.main_results: 据报告,九个功能测试类别是成功的,包括网站可访问性、地理数据、天气集成、存储、通知、决策逻辑、注册、配置文件管理和界面响应能力。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该原型展示了初步的软件集成功能,暗示了通过基于天气的警报来预防登革热的潜在工具。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,该原型可以通过整合天气数据和 WhatsApp 通知来支持登革热防备,可能有助于公共卫生干预的早期预警系统。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究缺乏详细的测试输入、执行计数和通知送达收据,并且22天的开发周期无法在没有历史记录的情况下独立建立完整的30天降雨数据集。证据是中等的。

papers.full_text: AbstractVector-borne diseases (VBD) caused by arboviruses represent a major public health threat in tropical regions. According to WHO’s Global Vector Control Response, more than 80% of the global population live in areas at risk for VBD. For instance, Aedes aegypti is the primary vector of dengue virus (DENV) and chikungunya virus (CHIKV), and its widespread distribution, particularly in Brazil, contributes to the occurrence of outbreaks. During these outbreaks, mosquitoes may acquire either monoinfections or coinfections, which can occur either simultaneously or sequentially, potentially influencing transmission dynamics. In this study, we investigated the effects of simultaneous coinfection with CHIKV and two DENV serotypes (DENV-1 and DENV-2) on the vector competence of Ae. aegypti and described the characteristics of infection and transmission phenotypes following different orders of sequential arbovirus acquisition. Simultaneous coinfection resulted in serotype-dependent outcomes. At 7 days post-infection (dpi), DENV-1 infection rates and viral loads were significantly reduced compared with monoinfections, whereas DENV-2 showed increased viral loads in saliva. At 14 dpi, CHIKV infection rates were significantly reduced in both the CHIKV+DENV-1 (CD1) and CHIKV+DENV-2 (CD2) groups, whereas CHIKV viral loads were reduced only in the CD2 group. In the sequential coinfection experiments, DENV-2 exhibited lower replication levels than DENV-1 in both sequential infection scenarios, regardless of whether DENV was acquired before or after CHIKV. Likewise, DENV-2 showed lower transmission efficiency than DENV-1, and murine transmission assays confirmed reduced viral loads for DENV-2. Overall, our findings demonstrate that CHIKV–DENV coinfection in Ae. aegypti is associated with distinct infection and transmission outcomes depending on the DENV serotype and the infection scenario. In sequentially exposed mosquitoes, distinct phenotypes were observed according to the order of arbovirus acquisition. These results highlight the complexity of arboviral coinfections within this shared vector and emphasize the importance of considering different coinfection scenarios when evaluating vector competence and transmission risk in endemic settings.Keywords: Aedes aegypti, arbovirus coinfection, chikungunya virus, dengue virus serotypes, sequential infection, simultaneous infection, vector competence 2.Materials and methods2.1. Ae. aegypti colony A well-established Brazilian colony of Ae. aegypti (strain BH), maintained at the Laboratory of Medical Entomology, Fiocruz-Minas, Brazil, was used in this study. Mosquito eggs were collected using ovitraps in the city of Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil, in 2019. Mosquitoes were reared and maintained under standard insectary conditions at 27 °C, with 80% relative humidity, and a (16-h light/8-h dark photoperiod).2.2.DENV-1, DENV-2 and CHIKVThe arboviruses CHIKV (GenBank: MH823668) (Vasconcellos et al., 2019), DENV-1, (GenBank: KP188540) and DENV-2 (GenBank: KP188569; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/KP188569) were maintained and propagated in C6/36 cells cultured in Leibovitz’s L-15 medium supplemented with 2% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS), 5 μg/mL amphotericin B, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (White, 1987). Virus titration was performed in Vero cells using a plaque assay (LaBarre and Lowy, 2001).2.3.Experimental infections in Ae. aegypti2.3.1.Monoinfection and simultaneous coinfectionThree- to five-day-old female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes were divided into five experimental groups (n = 200 per group) and infected by membrane feeding (Secundino et al., 2017). The infectious blood meal was prepared by mixing mouse blood and virus suspension at a 2:1 (v/v) ratio. The final blood meal contained 1 × 105 PFU/mL of virus. For the simultaneous coinfection groups, CHIKV and DENV were each present at the same final infectious titer (1 × 105 PFU/mL per virus).The following experimental groups of infected Ae. aegypti were established: (i) DENV-1 (D1); (ii) DENV-2 (D2); (iii) CHIKV (C); (iv) CHIKV+DENV-1 (CD1); and (v) CHIKV+DENV-2 (CD2). After feeding, engorged females were maintained on 10% glucose ad libitum for 21 days post-infection (dpi).2.3.2.Sequential coinfectionThree- to five-day-old female Ae. aegypti mosquitoes were divided into four experimental groups (n = 300 per group) and infected by membrane feeding as described above. The sequential coinfection assay was designed to simulate potential sequential arbovirus exposure scenarios in nature and characterize infection and transmission outcomes according to the order of virus acquisition. For the first infection, one group received DENV-1, another received DENV-2, and two groups received CHIKV. Seven days later, mosquitoes were exposed to a second blood meal containing the corresponding second virus as follows: (i) DENV-1 followed by CHIKV (D1C); (ii) DENV-2 followed by CHIKV (D2C); (iii) CHIKV followed by DENV-1 (CD1); and (iv) CHIKV followed by DENV-2 (CD2). After the second blood meal, engorged females were maintained on 10% glucose ad libitum for 14 days post-coinfection (dpci).2.3.3.Blood collection for mosquito infection assaysFor the mosquito infection assays described in this section, fresh blood was obtained from BALB/c mice by cardiac puncture. Animals were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of ketamine (200 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg). Blood was collected immediately after surgical anesthesia had been confirmed. Following blood collection, mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal administration of sodium thiopental (150 mg/kg), administered as an overdose (three times the anesthetic dose).2.4.RNA extraction and virus quantificationFor the monoinfection groups (DENV-1, DENV-2, and CHIKV) and the simultaneous coinfection groups (CD1 and CD2): 30 mosquitoes per group were randomly selected at 7, 14, and 21 dpi. For the sequential coinfection groups (CD1, CD2, D1C, and D2C), 30 mosquitoes were also randomly selected at 7 and 14 dpci. The selected mosquitoes were individually transferred into separate microtubes. Viral RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and stored at −70 °C. Viral RNA quantification was performed using quantitative RT-qPCR (7500 Fast Real-Time PCR, Applied Biosystems) using the TaqMan Fast Virus 1-Step kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Virus detection was based on specific TaqMan probes and primers, as previously described by Edwards et al. (2007) and Leparc-Goffart et al. (2009).2.5.Saliva collection and transmission efficiency (TE)TE was assessed at 14 dpi for all monoinfection and simultaneous coinfection groups and at 14 dpci for the sequential coinfection groups. At each time point, 10 mosquitoes from each experimental group were randomly selected for saliva collection. In one independent experiment, fewer than 10 mosquitoes were available for saliva analysis due to mortality following infection. Mosquitoes were cold anesthetized, and their legs and wings were removed. The proboscis of each mosquito was inserted into a filter tip containing 6 μL of a 1:1 mixture of sucrose solution and fetal bovine serum for 30 min. Saliva samples were collected into 1.5 mL tubes containing 100 μL of L-15 medium and stored at −70 °C until processing (do Nascimento et al., 2022). Saliva samples were analyzed using RT-qPCR to determine viral RNA loads. Viral load (VL), expressed as the number of viral RNA copies detected in each saliva sample, was used as a measure of infection intensity. Transmission efficiency (TE) was calculated as the proportion of mosquitoes with detectable viral RNA in their saliva relative to the total number of mosquitoes tested.2.6.Transmission by bite of coinfected Ae. aegyptiConcurrently with the forced salivation assay, a mosquito bite transmission assay was performed to confirm the presence of infectious virus in saliva and evaluate successful transmission to a vertebrate host during blood feeding. This assay was designed to assess virus transmission to the vertebrate host rather than infection status in individual mosquitoes. To increase the chances of successful blood feeding and virus transmission, ten female mosquitoes were used per mouse. Transmission by bite was evaluated at 14 dpci in the sequential coinfection groups (CD1, CD2, D1C, and D2C). For each experimental group, ten female Ae. aegypti mosquitoes were divided into two pools of five females. Each pool was transferred to a 3-dram plastic vial (4.8 cm in height × 1.8 cm in diameter) covered with 0.25-mm nylon mesh. One vial was placed against each ear of an anesthetized BALB/c mouse, and mosquitoes were allowed to feed for 1 h (Secundino et al., 2017).BALB/c mice were anesthetized with ketamine (200 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg). After adequate anesthesia was confirmed, animals were positioned in a custom restraint device with both ears exposed for mosquito feeding. At the end of the feeding period, mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal administration of sodium thiopental (150 mg/kg). Death was confirmed by the absence of respiratory movements and cardiac activity before tissue collection. A 4-mm punch biopsy was then collected from the mosquito-exposed area of each ear, and the right and left ear samples were transferred individually to microtubes for RNA extraction and RT-qPCR, as previously described.2.7.Statistical analysisThree independent biological experiments were performed under identical experimental conditions for both the monoinfection and the simultaneous and sequential coinfection assays. Inter-experiment variability was assessed using the Kruskal–Wallis test. As no significant differences were detected among the independent biological experiments (p > 0.05), data were pooled for the final statistical analyses. Data distribution normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Because viral load data did not follow a Gaussian distribution, comparisons between groups were performed using the Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test. Differences in infection rates (IR) and transmission efficiency (TE) were evaluated using the two-tailed χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test. Correlations among arbovirus cDNA copy numbers were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation test. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 7.00 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2026.1891568/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 3.Results3.1.Impact of simultaneous coinfection on the vector competence of Ae. aegypti for DENV and CHIKVTo assess the effects of simultaneous coinfection on vector competence, we compared monoinfected and simultaneously coinfected mosquitoes using infection rates (IR), viral loads in mosquito bodies at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, and transmission efficiency (TE) and saliva viral loads at 14 dpi. To further characterize the infection status of mosquitoes within the simultaneous coinfection groups, individual mosquitoes were classified according to the detection of DENV and CHIKV as positive for both viruses, positive only for DENV, positive only for CHIKV, or negative for both. Dual infection was the predominant outcome in both coinfection groups at most time points evaluated. At 21 dpi, dual positivity remained high in the DENV-1/CHIKV group (96.7%), whereas in the DENV-2/CHIKV group, 53.3% of mosquitoes were positive for both viruses and 46.7% were positive only for CHIKV. A small percentage of mosquitoes were positive for only one virus, whereas only one mosquito (from the DENV-2/CHIKV group at 14 dpi) was negative for both viruses (Supplementary Table 1).In the DENV-1 monoinfected group (D1), the IR was 100%, 97%, and 100% at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, whereas in the CHIKV+DENV-1 simultaneous coinfection group (CD1), IR was 87%, 90%, and 100% at the corresponding time points. At 7 dpi, the DENV-1 IR was significantly lower in the CD1 group than in the monoinfection group (p = 0.038), whereas no significant differences were observed at 14 or 21 dpi (Figures 1A–C). Median viral loads in the D1 group were 7.14 × 106, 1.25 × 107, and 3.75 × 107 viral cDNA copies at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, compared with 1.17 × 104, 2.58 × 104, and 6.75 × 103 copies in the CD1 group. A significantly lower viral load was observed in the CD1 group at 7 dpi (p = 0.0017), whereas no significant differences were detected at 14 or 21 dpi (Figures 1A–C). At 14 dpi, TE was 70% in the D1 group and 65% in the CD1 group, with median saliva viral loads of 3.29 × 102 and 7.44 × 103 copies, respectively. No significant difference in TE was observed between the two groups (Figure 1D).Figure 1Viral loads of Ae. aegypti-BH following monoinfection or simultaneous coinfection with DENV-1, DENV-2, and CHIKV at 7, 14, and 21 days post-infection (dpi). Viral loads are shown by experimental group, tissue, and time point. (A–D) DENV-1 viral load. (E–H) DENV-2 viral load. (I–L) CHIKV viral load. Each color represents a different infection condition: blue, DENV-1 monoinfection; green, DENV-2 monoinfection; red, CHIKV monoinfection; purple, DENV-1 + CHIKV coinfection; and brown, DENV-2 + CHIKV coinfection. Pie charts below each group show the infection rate of mosquitoes for each condition, while those corresponding to saliva indicate transmission efficiency. Data represent three independent biological experiments pooled for statistical analysis. Each dot represents an individual mosquito, and horizontal lines indicate the median. Statistical significance is indicated by one (*) or two (**) asterisks corresponding to p ≤ 0.05 and p ≤ 0.01, respectively.Scientific figure with scatter plots and pie charts organized into four columns labeled 7 dpi, 14 dpi, 21 dpi, and Saliva, and three rows for DENV-1, DENV-2, and CHIKV. Each panel presents viral RNA copies for different groups and time points, with statistical significance indicated by asterisks. Pie charts below plots show infection or transmission efficiency percentages, with color coding to differentiate groups.In the DENV-2 monoinfection group (D2), IR was 93%, 87%, and 50% at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, whereas in the CHIKV+DENV-2 simultaneous coinfection group (CD2), IR was 80%, 90%, and 53% at the corresponding time points. No significant differences in IR were observed between the groups (Figures 1E–G). Median viral loads in the D2 group were 1.51 × 103, 4.69 × 102, and 1.08 × 101 cDNA copies at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, compared with 1.05 × 103, 1.16 × 103, and 1.21 × 102 cDNA copies in the CD2 group. No significant differences in viral loads were detected at any time point (Figures 1E–G). At 14 dpi, transmission efficiency (TE) was 35% (7/20 saliva-positive mosquitoes) in the D2 group and 55% in the CD2 group. Although TE did not differ significantly between groups, the median saliva viral load was significantly higher in the CD2 group (5.81 × 102 cDNA copies) than in the monoinfection group (p = 0.0390) (Figure 1H).In the CHIKV monoinfected group (C), IR was 100% at 7 and 14 dpi, and 93% at 21 dpi. Median viral loads were 1.93 × 104, 4.77 × 103, and 1.19 × 104 cDNA copies at the corresponding time points (Figures 1I–K). At 14 dpi, TE was 80%, with a median saliva viral load of 1.54 × 103 cDNA copies (Figure 1L).In the DENV-1 + CHIKV simultaneous coinfection group (CD1), CHIKV IR was 97% at 7 dpi, 87% at 14 dpi, and 97% at 21 dpi, with median viral loads of 2.90 × 103, 5.43 × 102, and 6.86 × 103 cDNA copies, respectively. Compared with the monoinfected group, CHIKV IR was significantly lower at 14 dpi (p = 0.038), whereas no significant differences in viral load were detected (Figures 1I–K). TE was 75%, with a median saliva viral load of 1.34 × 103 cDNA copies, which did not differ significantly from the monoinfected group (Figure 1L).In the DENV-2 + CHIKV simultaneous coinfection group (CD2), CHIKV IR reached 100% at 7 dpi, 80% at 14 dpi, and 100% at 21 dpi, with median viral loads of 7.61 × 103, 4.98 × 102, and 3.74 × 103 cDNA copies, respectively (Figures 1I–K). At 14 dpi, both CHIKV IR (p = 0.0098) and viral load (p = 0.0166) were significantly lower than those in the CHIKV monoinfected group (Figure 1J). TE was 70%, with a median saliva viral load of 7.77 × 102 cDNA copies, which did not differ significantly from the CHIKV monoinfected group (Figure 1L).3.2.DENV-1 and DENV-2 infection and transmission phenotypes following sequential exposure with CHIKVTo characterize DENV infection and transmission phenotypes following sequential arbovirus exposure, we measured DENV-1 and DENV-2 infection rates, viral loads, and transmission efficiency in mosquitoes exposed to each DENV serotype before or after CHIKV. These analyses allowed us to stratify DENV outcomes by serotype and order of virus acquisition.In the CD1 group, DENV-1 IR was 100% at both 7 and 14 dpci. In the CD2 group, DENV-2 IR was 93% at both time points. Median viral loads differed between the two groups at both time points (Figures 2A, B). At 7 dpci, viral loads were 7.54 × 102 cDNA copies in CD1 and 2.27 × 104 in CD2 (p < 0.0001). At 14 dpci, median viral loads were 4.16 × 103 versus 1.57 × 103 cDNA copies, respectively (p = 0.007) (Figures 2A, B). At 14 dpci, TE was 55% for DENV-1 and 65% for DENV-2, with viral loads of 1.40 × 102 and 2.28 × 102 cDNA copies, respectively (Figure 2C). Additionally, the ability of Ae. aegypti females to transmit the virus to vertebrate hosts by bite was assessed using BALB/c mice. In this assay, TE was 20% for DENV-1 and 10% for DENV-2 (Figure 2D).Figure 2DENV viral loads in mosquitoes sequentially coinfected with DENV-1 or DENV-2 and CHIKV. In the sequential coinfection experiments, DENV-2 exhibited lower replication levels than DENV-1 in both sequential infection scenarios, regardless of whether DENV was acquired before or after CHIKV. Likewise, DENV-2 showed lower transmission efficiency than DENV-1, and murine transmission assays confirmed reduced viral loads for DENV-2. Overall, our findings demonstrate that CHIKV–DENV coinfection in Ae. aegypti is associated with distinct infection and transmission outcomes depending on the DENV serotype and the infection scenario. In sequentially exposed mosquitoes, distinct phenotypes were observed according to the order of arbovirus acquisition. These results highlight the complexity of arboviral coinfections within this shared vector and emphasize the importance of considering different coinfection scenarios when evaluating vector competence and transmission risk in endemic settings.Keywords: Aedes aegypti, arbovirus coinfection, chikungunya virus, dengue virus serotypes, sequential infection, simultaneous infection, vector competence
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Materials and methods2.1. Ae. aegypti colony A well-established Brazilian colony of Ae. aegypti (strain BH), maintained at the Laboratory of Medical Entomology, Fiocruz-Minas, Brazil, was used in this study. Mosquito eggs were collected using ovitraps in the city of Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil, in 2019. Mosquitoes were reared and maintained under standard insectary conditions at 27 °C, with 80% relative humidity, and a (16-h light/8-h dark photoperiod).2.2.DENV-1, DENV-2 and CHIKVThe arboviruses CHIKV (GenBank: MH823668) (Vasconcellos et al., 2019), DENV-1, (GenBank: KP188540) and DENV-2 (GenBank: KP188569; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/KP188569) were maintained and propagated in C6/36 cells cultured in Leibovitz’s L-15 medium supplemented with 2% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS), 5 μg/mL amphotericin B, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (White, 1987). Virus titration was performed in Vero cells using a plaque assay (LaBarre and Lowy, 2001).2.3.Experimental infections in Ae. aegypti2.3.1.Monoinfection and simultaneous coinfectionThree- to five-day-old female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes were divided into five experimental groups (n = 200 per group) and infected by membrane feeding (Secundino et al., 2017). The infectious blood meal was prepared by mixing mouse blood and virus suspension at a 2:1 (v/v) ratio. The final blood meal contained 1 × 105 PFU/mL of virus. For the simultaneous coinfection groups, CHIKV and DENV were each present at the same final infectious titer (1 × 105 PFU/mL per virus).The following experimental groups of infected Ae. aegypti were established: (i) DENV-1 (D1); (ii) DENV-2 (D2); (iii) CHIKV (C); (iv) CHIKV+DENV-1 (CD1); and (v) CHIKV+DENV-2 (CD2). After feeding, engorged females were maintained on 10% glucose ad libitum for 21 days post-infection (dpi).2.3.2.Sequential coinfectionThree- to five-day-old female Ae. aegypti mosquitoes were divided into four experimental groups (n = 300 per group) and infected by membrane feeding as described above. The sequential coinfection assay was designed to simulate potential sequential arbovirus exposure scenarios in nature and characterize infection and transmission outcomes according to the order of virus acquisition. For the first infection, one group received DENV-1, another received DENV-2, and two groups received CHIKV. Seven days later, mosquitoes were exposed to a second blood meal containing the corresponding second virus as follows: (i) DENV-1 followed by CHIKV (D1C); (ii) DENV-2 followed by CHIKV (D2C); (iii) CHIKV followed by DENV-1 (CD1); and (iv) CHIKV followed by DENV-2 (CD2). After the second blood meal, engorged females were maintained on 10% glucose ad libitum for 14 days post-coinfection (dpci).2.3.3.Blood collection for mosquito infection assaysFor the mosquito infection assays described in this section, fresh blood was obtained from BALB/c mice by cardiac puncture. Animals were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of ketamine (200 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg). Blood was collected immediately after surgical anesthesia had been confirmed. Following blood collection, mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal administration of sodium thiopental (150 mg/kg), administered as an overdose (three times the anesthetic dose).2.4.RNA extraction and virus quantificationFor the monoinfection groups (DENV-1, DENV-2, and CHIKV) and the simultaneous coinfection groups (CD1 and CD2): 30 mosquitoes per group were randomly selected at 7, 14, and 21 dpi. For the sequential coinfection groups (CD1, CD2, D1C, and D2C), 30 mosquitoes were also randomly selected at 7 and 14 dpci. The selected mosquitoes were individually transferred into separate microtubes. Viral RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and stored at −70 °C. Viral RNA quantification was performed using quantitative RT-qPCR (7500 Fast Real-Time PCR, Applied Biosystems) using the TaqMan Fast Virus 1-Step kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Virus detection was based on specific TaqMan probes and primers, as previously described by Edwards et al. (2007) and Leparc-Goffart et al. (2009).2.5.Saliva collection and transmission efficiency (TE)TE was assessed at 14 dpi for all monoinfection and simultaneous coinfection groups and at 14 dpci for the sequential coinfection groups. At each time point, 10 mosquitoes from each experimental group were randomly selected for saliva collection. In one independent experiment, fewer than 10 mosquitoes were available for saliva analysis due to mortality following infection. Mosquitoes were cold anesthetized, and their legs and wings were removed. The proboscis of each mosquito was inserted into a filter tip containing 6 μL of a 1:1 mixture of sucrose solution and fetal bovine serum for 30 min. Saliva samples were collected into 1.5 mL tubes containing 100 μL of L-15 medium and stored at −70 °C until processing (do Nascimento et al., 2022). Saliva samples were analyzed using RT-qPCR to determine viral RNA loads. Viral load (VL), expressed as the number of viral RNA copies detected in each saliva sample, was used as a measure of infection intensity. Transmission efficiency (TE) was calculated as the proportion of mosquitoes with detectable viral RNA in their saliva relative to the total number of mosquitoes tested.2.6.Transmission by bite of coinfected Ae. aegyptiConcurrently with the forced salivation assay, a mosquito bite transmission assay was performed to confirm the presence of infectious virus in saliva and evaluate successful transmission to a vertebrate host during blood feeding. This assay was designed to assess virus transmission to the vertebrate host rather than infection status in individual mosquitoes. To increase the chances of successful blood feeding and virus transmission, ten female mosquitoes were used per mouse. Transmission by bite was evaluated at 14 dpci in the sequential coinfection groups (CD1, CD2, D1C, and D2C). For each experimental group, ten female Ae. aegypti mosquitoes were divided into two pools of five females. Each pool was transferred to a 3-dram plastic vial (4.8 cm in height × 1.8 cm in diameter) covered with 0.25-mm nylon mesh. One vial was placed against each ear of an anesthetized BALB/c mouse, and mosquitoes were allowed to feed for 1 h (Secundino et al., 2017).BALB/c mice were anesthetized with ketamine (200 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg). After adequate anesthesia was confirmed, animals were positioned in a custom restraint device with both ears exposed for mosquito feeding. At the end of the feeding period, mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal administration of sodium thiopental (150 mg/kg). Death was confirmed by the absence of respiratory movements and cardiac activity before tissue collection. A 4-mm punch biopsy was then collected from the mosquito-exposed area of each ear, and the right and left ear samples were transferred individually to microtubes for RNA extraction and RT-qPCR, as previously described.2.7.Statistical analysisThree independent biological experiments were performed under identical experimental conditions for both the monoinfection and the simultaneous and sequential coinfection assays. Inter-experiment variability was assessed using the Kruskal–Wallis test. As no significant differences were detected among the independent biological experiments (p > 0.05), data were pooled for the final statistical analyses. Data distribution normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Because viral load data did not follow a Gaussian distribution, comparisons between groups were performed using the Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test. Differences in infection rates (IR) and transmission efficiency (TE) were evaluated using the two-tailed χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test. full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Impact of simultaneous coinfection on the vector competence of Ae. aegypti for DENV and CHIKVTo assess the effects of simultaneous coinfection on vector competence, we compared monoinfected and simultaneously coinfected mosquitoes using infection rates (IR), viral loads in mosquito bodies at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, and transmission efficiency (TE) and saliva viral loads at 14 dpi. To further characterize the infection status of mosquitoes within the simultaneous coinfection groups, individual mosquitoes were classified according to the detection of DENV and CHIKV as positive for both viruses, positive only for DENV, positive only for CHIKV, or negative for both. Dual infection was the predominant outcome in both coinfection groups at most time points evaluated. At 21 dpi, dual positivity remained high in the DENV-1/CHIKV group (96.7%), whereas in the DENV-2/CHIKV group, 53.3% of mosquitoes were positive for both viruses and 46.7% were positive only for CHIKV. A small percentage of mosquitoes were positive for only one virus, whereas only one mosquito (from the DENV-2/CHIKV group at 14 dpi) was negative for both viruses (Supplementary Table 1).In the DENV-1 monoinfected group (D1), the IR was 100%, 97%, and 100% at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, whereas in the CHIKV+DENV-1 simultaneous coinfection group (CD1), IR was 87%, 90%, and 100% at the corresponding time points. At 7 dpi, the DENV-1 IR was significantly lower in the CD1 group than in the monoinfection group (p = 0.038), whereas no significant differences were observed at 14 or 21 dpi (Figures 1A–C). Median viral loads in the D1 group were 7.14 × 106, 1.25 × 107, and 3.75 × 107 viral cDNA copies at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, compared with 1.17 × 104, 2.58 × 104, and 6.75 × 103 copies in the CD1 group. A significantly lower viral load was observed in the CD1 group at 7 dpi (p = 0.0017), whereas no significant differences were detected at 14 or 21 dpi (Figures 1A–C). At 14 dpi, TE was 70% in the D1 group and 65% in the CD1 group, with median saliva viral loads of 3.29 × 102 and 7.44 × 103 copies, respectively. No significant difference in TE was observed between the two groups (Figure 1D).Figure 1Viral loads of Ae. aegypti-BH following monoinfection or simultaneous coinfection with DENV-1, DENV-2, and CHIKV at 7, 14, and 21 days post-infection (dpi). Each panel presents viral RNA copies for different groups and time points, with statistical significance indicated by asterisks. Pie charts below plots show infection or transmission efficiency percentages, with color coding to differentiate groups.In the DENV-2 monoinfection group (D2), IR was 93%, 87%, and 50% at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, whereas in the CHIKV+DENV-2 simultaneous coinfection group (CD2), IR was 80%, 90%, and 53% at the corresponding time points. No significant differences in IR were observed between the groups (Figures 1E–G). Median viral loads in the D2 group were 1.51 × 103, 4.69 × 102, and 1.08 × 101 cDNA copies at 7, 14, and 21 dpi, respectively, compared with 1.05 × 103, 1.16 × 103, and 1.21 × 102 cDNA copies in the CD2 group. No significant differences in viral loads were detected at any time point (Figures 1E–G). At 14 dpi, transmission efficiency (TE) was 35% (7/20 saliva-positive mosquitoes) in the D2 group and 55% in the CD2 group. Although TE did not differ significantly between groups, the median saliva viral load was significantly higher in the CD2 group (5.81 × 102 cDNA copies) than in the monoinfection group (p = 0.0390) (Figure 1H).In the CHIKV monoinfected group (C), IR was 100% at 7 and 14 dpi, and 93% at 21 dpi. Median viral loads were 1.93 × 104, 4.77 × 103, and 1.19 × 104 cDNA copies at the corresponding time points (Figures 1I–K). At 14 dpi, TE was 80%, with a median saliva viral load of 1.54 × 103 cDNA copies (Figure 1L).In the DENV-1 + CHIKV simultaneous coinfection group (CD1), CHIKV IR was 97% at 7 dpi, 87% at 14 dpi, and 97% at 21 dpi, with median viral loads of 2.90 × 103, 5.43 × 102, and 6.86 × 103 cDNA copies, respectively. Compared with the monoinfected group, CHIKV IR was significantly lower at 14 dpi (p = 0.038), whereas no significant differences in viral load were detected (Figures 1I–K). TE was 70%, with a median saliva viral load of 7.77 × 102 cDNA copies, which did not differ significantly from the CHIKV monoinfected group (Figure 1L).3.2.DENV-1 and DENV-2 infection and transmission phenotypes following sequential exposure with CHIKVTo characterize DENV infection and transmission phenotypes following sequential arbovirus exposure, we measured DENV-1 and DENV-2 infection rates, viral loads, and transmission efficiency in mosquitoes exposed to each DENV serotype before or after CHIKV. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study examines the transmission dynamics associated with two ecologically relevant coinfection scenarios, namely, simultaneous and sequential coinfection, using two epidemiologically significant arboviruses: dengue virus (DENV) and chikungunya virus (CHIKV). Under monoinfection conditions in vitro, DENV-2 has consistently demonstrated elevated viral replication levels relative to DENV-3 (Quintero-Gil et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2020) and DENV-1 (Quintero-Gil et al., 2018). Complementary in vivo studies employing Ae. aegypti and Aedes albopictus infected with the four DENV serotypes have similarly reported enhanced viral loads for DENV-1 and DENV-2 when compared with DENV-3 and DENV-4 (Ekwudu et al., 2020). These serotype-specific differences in viral replication kinetics may contribute to differences in vector competence, transmission efficiency, and overall epidemiological potential and should therefore be considered when interpreting coinfection experiments involving different DENV serotypes.These serotype-specific differences in viral replication kinetics may significantly modulate vector competence, transmission efficiency, and overall epidemiological potential, particularly in contexts of coinfection with CHIKV.Under coinfection conditions, the structural and functional distinctions between the genera Alphavirus and Orthoflavivirus may contribute to different outcomes in the infection and transmission processes of Ae. aegypti. Although both viruses share the same vector and are positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses, they differ in structural features, replication strategies, and interactions with the mosquito immune system. Alphaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm (Laurent et al., 2022; Girard et al., 2024), whereas orthoflaviviruses preferentially establish replication complexes associated with the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) (Welsch et al., 2009; Rückert and Ebel, 2018). These biological disparities may influence coinfection dynamics and could partially elucidate the antagonistic or synergistic interactions identified in our study.In simultaneous coinfection, CHIKV was associated with reductions in both the prevalence and viral load of DENV-1 at 7 dpi. These results suggest that CHIKV was associated with reduced DENV-1 replication when Ae. aegypti mosquitoes were co-infected with both viral species. However, this effect did not extend to viral loads in saliva or transmission efficiency, indicating that horizontal transmission to vertebrate hosts was not significantly affected. A potential area for further investigation is the impact of this interaction on vertical transmission of DENV-1, since reduced viral load and prevalence in the mosquito body may limit successful viral passage to progeny during the early post-infection period.This finding is consistent with studies that demonstrate a similar effect in interactions between CHIKV and ZIKV (Rückert et al., 2017) and between MAYV and ZIKV (Brustolin et al., 2023), in which ZIKV viral load was reduced. Differences in coinfection outcomes are also reflected in vitro. In C6/36 cells, when DENV-3 was introduced at a higher multiplicity of infection (MOI = 1.0) than CHIKV (MOI = 0.1), only DENV replication was detected, indicating inhibition of CHIKV replication (Potiwat et al., 2011). Conversely, in Vero and human liver cells, CHIKV replication increased while DENV replication decreased (Zaidi et al., 2018; Taraphdar et al., 2022). These findings emphasize that coinfection dynamics are context-dependent, with outcomes varying by host, cell type, and virus strain. Notably, in mosquitoes, CHIKV viral load also increased during simultaneous coinfection with orthoflaviviruses (Rodrigues et al., 2021).In contrast to DENV-1, simultaneous CHIKV coinfection did not increase whole-body DENV-2 viral loads but was associated with significantly higher viral loads in saliva. This finding suggests that CHIKV may facilitate DENV-2 dissemination to, or release from, the salivary glands without necessarily increasing systemic viral loads. However, this interpretation should be considered with caution because viral loads were quantified using whole mosquito homogenates rather than dissected salivary glands. Consequently, the present study cannot determine whether the increased salivary viral load resulted from enhanced dissemination to the salivary glands or from greater viral accumulation within this tissue. Nevertheless, elevated salivary viral loads remain epidemiologically relevant because a higher viral inoculum delivered during mosquito feeding is more likely to establish productive infections in vertebrate hosts by increasing the probability of overcoming early innate immune responses (Althouse et al., 2014; Le Coupanec et al., 2017).An additional observation was the marked reduction in DENV-2 detection at 21 dpi in both the monoinfection and simultaneous coinfection groups. Because independent groups of mosquitoes were analyzed at each sampling time point, this pattern should not be interpreted as evidence of viral clearance within individual mosquitoes. Rather, it indicates that a smaller proportion of mosquitoes had detectable DENV-2 infection at 21 dpi.At 14 dpi, DENV-1 coinfection was associated with reduced CHIKV prevalence, while DENV-2 coinfection was associated with reductions in both CHIKV prevalence and viral load. These results suggest that both dengue serotypes may negatively influence CHIKV replication and/or establishment during later infection stages. A decrease in prevalence may translate into reduced vertical transmission potential of CHIKV, given that fewer females remain infected and capable of transmitting virus to progeny. In the case of DENV-2, the reduction in CHIKV viral load further strengthens this hypothesis, as lower systemic loads may reduce the likelihood of viral dissemination to the ovaries and subsequent establishment of transovarial infection (Ciota and Kramer, 2010; Vazeille et al., 2010). However, transmission efficiency and CHIKV salivary load remained unaffected, suggesting that coinfection may not substantially alter horizontal transmission from mosquitoes to vertebrate hosts.An important consideration is that CHIKV transmission to vertebrate hosts may occur considerably earlier than 14 dpi. Previous studies have demonstrated the rapid progression of CHIKV through mosquito tissue barriers and its relatively short extrinsic incubation period, with infectious virus being detected in saliva during the first days after exposure. Moreover, arbovirus infection and transmission are dynamic processes, and salivary gland infection or viral release into saliva may vary substantially over time (Robison et al., 2020; Viginier et al., 2023; Sartsanga et al., 2025). Therefore, because transmission was assessed at a single, relatively late time point in the present study, transient differences in CHIKV transmission between monoinfected and coinfected mosquitoes may not have been detected. Our findings should thus be interpreted as showing no detectable effect on CHIKV transmission at 14 dpi, rather than demonstrating the absence of an effect throughout the extrinsic incubation period. Since both DENV-1 and DENV-2 were associated with reduced CHIKV infection outcomes, biological features shared across dengue serotypes, such as overlapping cell tropism or conserved patterns of immune stimulation, may represent potential explanations that warrant further investigation. Potential mechanisms underlying these viral interactions include: (i) competition for target cells in the midgut or secondary tissues; (ii) competition for cellular and metabolic resources, including the host translational machinery and energy pools; and (iii) modulation of mosquito immune responses, because arboviruses may differentially activate RNA interference pathways, Toll/IMD signaling, or other innate responses, thereby affecting the replication and dissemination of the secondary virus…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionOur findings demonstrate that simultaneous CHIKV and DENV coinfection and different orders of sequential arbovirus exposure are associated with distinct infection and transmission phenotypes in Ae. aegypti. These observations highlight the complexity of arbovirus coinfections within mosquito vectors and indicate that their outcomes may vary according to the DENV serotype and infection scenario.During simultaneous coinfection, DENV-1 showed greater reductions in systemic infection and viral replication than DENV-2, while the sequential exposure experiments revealed distinct infection and transmission phenotypes between groups involving DENV-1- and DENV-2 and across different orders of virus acquisition. Although differences in salivary viral loads were observed under specific conditions, transmission efficiency was evaluated only at a single, relatively late time point (14 dpi). Therefore, the present study cannot exclude the possibility that coinfection may affect earlier stages of viral dissemination to saliva or the duration of the extrinsic incubation period.The sequential infection experiments should, however, be interpreted within the limitations of the experimental design. Matched sequential controls in which mosquitoes received a non-infectious blood meal followed by DENV-1 or DENV-2 seven days later were not included. Consequently, the specific effect of prior CHIKV infection on each DENV serotype cannot be distinguished from other effects associated with sequential exposure. In addition, differences observed between DENV-1 and DENV-2 may reflect intrinsic differences in their vector competence and replication dynamics and should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of a differential CHIKV-mediated effect on the two serotypes.Additional limitations should also be considered. The use of a single Ae. aegypti population and one viral strain per arbovirus limits the generalizability of the findings, and the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the observed patterns were not directly investigated. Thus, it remains unclear to what extent intracellular competition, mosquito immune responses, tissue tropism, or other processes contribute to the observed coinfection phenotypes.Taken together, our findings characterize distinct infection and transmission phenotypes associated with simultaneous coinfection and different sequential arbovirus exposure scenarios under laboratory conditions. Future studies incorporating matched sequential controls, multiple mosquito populations and viral genotypes, additional transmission time points, and mechanistic approaches will be important to determine the specific contribution of virus–virus interactions to these phenotypes and establish whether the observed patterns extend to natural transmission settings where DENV and CHIKV cocirculate.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionVector-borne diseases (VBDs) are caused by parasites, viruses, and bacteria and are transmitted to humans and other vertebrates through the bite of infected blood-sucking arthropods, such as mosquitoes, ticks, and sandflies. Of the 1, 407 recognized species of human pathogens, 177 are classified as emerging or re-emerging, with approximately 73% of these being arboviruses transmitted by mosquitoes (Mbaoma et al., 2025). It is estimated that nearly 80% of the world’s population lives in areas at risk of exposure to at least one VBD, which collectively are responsible for more than 700, 000 deaths annually (Madewell, 2020; Manouana et al., 2024; World Health Organization, 2024a).Dengue virus (DENV) and Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) are primarily transmitted by mosquitoes of the genus Aedes, particularly Aedes aegypti the principal urban vector in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. However, Aedes albopictus has emerged as an important secondary vector, contributing to the maintenance and geographic expansion of both arboviruses, particularly in temperate regions and areas where Ae. aegypti is absent or less abundant (Bezerra et al., 2016; Resck et al., 2024). Among the 134 arboviruses known to cause disease in humans, DENV and CHIKV are among the most prevalent and clinically important (Gubler, 2001). DENV and CHIKV belong to the genera Orthoflavivirus (formerly Flavivirus) and Alphavirus, respectively (Postler et al., 2023).Historical accounts indicate that China first documented dengue as a disease as early as 265–420 CE. More reliable records of epidemics in North America, Asia, and Africa emerged between 1779 and 1780. The growth of international trade and transportation in the 19th century facilitated the global spread of dengue, particularly through port towns, and its incidence continued to increase during the 20th century. In contrast, chikungunya was first recognized during an outbreak in Tanzania in 1952, when CHIKV was subsequently isolated and identified. Today, both diseases are widespread worldwide (Lumsden, 1955; World Health Organization, 2024b).While outbreaks of diseases with clinical manifestations compatible with dengue have been reported for centuries, the first isolations of DENV-1 and DENV-2 serotypes occurred in 1943 in Japan and 1945 in Hawaii, respectively (Hotta, 1952)., DENV is currently classified into four serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4), which share approximately 65% ​​genomic sequence identity and are endemic in more than 100 countries (Messina et al., 2014; Sirisena et al., 2021). CHIKV was first isolated for the first time in 1952 in Tanzania, Africa, and has since spread worldwide (Lumsden, 1955; World Health Organization, 2024b). In Brazil, the circulation of DENV has been documented since the 1980s, with outbreaks recurring every two to five years (Brathwaite Dick et al., 2012; Salles et al., 2018). CHIKV was introduced into Brazil in 2014, resulting in regional outbreaks, particularly in the southeast of the country (Almeida et al., 2023).Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of DENV and CHIKV, is currently widespread throughout Brazil; a distribution driven by poor urban infrastructure, population growth, and socioeconomic inequality (Torres et al., 2024). Additionally, factors such as increased urban mobility, climate and environmental changes, and the lack of effective vector control policies have contributed to the expansion of this vector and, consequently, to the increasing incidence of arboviral diseases (Ministério da Saúde, 2025). According to official surveillance data from Brazil, there were approximately 6 million dengue cases in 2024, compared with approximately 1.5 million cases in 2025. Similarly, approximately 230, 000 chikungunya cases were reported in 2024, decreasing to approximately 100, 000 cases in 2025 (Ministério da Saúde, 2024, 2025).The coexistence of multiple arboviruses in endemic areas raises concerns about coinfections in both humans and vectors. Although CHIKV-affected areas often overlap with regions endemic for DENV (Mackenzie et al., 2001), the rarity of simultaneous outbreaks raises the question of whether such events are truly uncommon or simply underreported. Nevertheless, confirmed cases of DENV and CHIKV coinfection in humans have been reported in Brazil (Torres et al., 2024), Madagascar (Ratsitorahina et al., 2008), Gabon, Central Africa (Caron et al., 2012), the Caribbean (Omarjee et al., 2014) and the Colombia–Venezuela border region (Carrillo-Hernández et al., 2018).Coinfection can occur by two mechanisms: (i) simultaneous infection with multiple viruses through a single mosquito bite, or (ii) sequential infection, in which the host receives infective bites from mosquitoes infected with different arboviruses (Miralles et al., 2001; Chaves et al., 2018). Studies have reported that Ae. aegypti can simultaneously transmit Zika virus (ZIKV) and CHIKV through its saliva, with transmission rates as high as 12% for both viruses (Göertz et al., 2017). In Brazil, Ae. aegypti populations from Manaus are highly permissive to DENV/ZIKV coinfections and can transmit both pathogens during a single bite, with increased transmission efficiency observed for ZIKV to vertebrate hosts (Chaves et al., 2018). Furthermore, the dynamics of dual or triple coinfections can alter vector competence and the viral abundance of one or more viruses (Rodrigues et al., 2021). Evidence for the occurrence of coinfections in nature is provided by reports of vertical transmission from female mosquitoes to their offspring, resulting in larvae simultaneously infected with DENV and ZIKV (Teixeira et al., 2021).Sequential coinfections, in which a mosquito already infected with one arbovirus is later exposed to another, are considered more likely to occur than simultaneous coinfections. Importantly, the interactions between the vector and each virus under these conditions can differ substantially, sometimes leading to unexpected effects on vector competence (Peng et al., 2024). Primary arbovirus infections can modulate vector susceptibility to subsequent infections by influencing viral replication, dissemination, and transmission efficiency. Consequently, these interactions may alter viral abundance and vector competence, thereby influencing the circulation of co-circulating arboviruses and the dynamics of outbreaks in endemic regions (Rodrigues et al., 2021). In the case of DENV and ZIKV, an initial DENV infection has been shown to reduce ZIKV dissemination in C6/36 cells and in Ae. aegypti (Rückert et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2024). Conversely, synergistic interactions have also been reported. Ae. aegypti infected with CHIKV either before or after exposure to ZIKV exhibited increased ZIKV transmission at seven days after the second infection (Magalhaes et al., 2018). analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the effects of simultaneous coinfection with CHIKV and two DENV serotypes (DENV-1 and DENV-2) on the vector competence of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, addressing the knowledge gap regarding how co-infections might influence viral transmission dynamics in tropical regions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved experimental infections of three to five-day-old female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes divided into five groups (n = 200 per group) for simultaneous coinfection and four groups (n = 300 per group) for sequential coinfection. Mosquitoes were reared under standard insectary conditions and infected by membrane feeding.
analysis.methods: Mosquitoes were infected by membrane feeding using fresh blood from BALB/c mice. Viral RNA quantification was performed using RT-qPCR, and saliva samples were collected for transmission efficiency assessment. Statistical analyses included the Kruskal–Wallis test and Shapiro–Wilk test for normality.
analysis.main_results: At 7 dpi, DENV-1 infection rates and viral loads were significantly reduced in the CD1 group compared with monoinfections, while DENV-2 showed increased viral loads in saliva. No significant differences in viral loads were detected at any time point for sequential coinfections. CHIKV infection rates were significantly lower at 14 dpi in the monoinfected group compared to the DENV-1/CHIKV coinfection group.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that DENV-1 and DENV-2 exhibited different transmission dynamics when co-infected with CHIKV, with DENV-1 showing reduced infection rates and viral loads, and DENV-2 showing increased viral loads in saliva. This finding highlights the complex interactions between arboviruses in mosquitoes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform surveillance strategies and risk assessments for dengue and chikungunya co-infections, as they demonstrate how viral interactions may affect transmission efficiency and vector competence in Aedes aegypti.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study had three independent biological experiments, and inter-experiment variability was assessed, but no significant differences were detected, which may limit the confidence in the results. The evidence is moderate due to the controlled experimental setting and the use of statistical tests.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the effects of simultaneous and sequential coinfections of Aedes aegypti with DENV-1, DENV-2, and CHIKV on vector competence. The research aimed to understand how co-infections might influence viral transmission dynamics in tropical regions. Mosquitoes were infected by membrane feeding using fresh blood from BALB/c mice, and viral RNA was quantified using RT-qPCR. Results showed that DENV-1 infection rates and viral loads were significantly reduced in the CD1 group compared with monoinfections, while DENV-2 showed increased viral loads in saliva. No significant differences in viral loads were detected at any time point for sequential coinfections. CHIKV infection rates were significantly lower at 14 dpi in the monoinfected group compared to the DENV-1/CHIKV coinfection group. The findings suggest that DENV-1 and DENV-2 exhibit different transmission dynamics when co-infected with CHIKV, which could inform surveillance and risk assessment strategies for dengue and chikungunya co-infections. However, the study's evidence is moderate due to its controlled experimental setting and the lack of significant differences among independent experiments.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及 3 至 5 天大的雌性埃及伊蚊的实验感染,分为五组(每组 200 只)同时合并感染和四组(每组 300 只)顺序合并感染。蚊子在标准昆虫条件下饲养并通过膜饲感染。
elements_zh.methods: 使用 BALB/c 小鼠的新鲜血液通过膜饲法感染蚊子。使用 RT-qPCR 进行病毒 RNA 定量,并收集唾液样本用于 传播 效率评估。统计分析包括 Kruskal-Wallis 检验和 Shapiro-Wilk 正态性检验。
elements_zh.main_results: 7 dpi时,与单一感染相比,CD1组的DENV-1感染率和病毒载量显着降低,而DENV-2则显示唾液中的病毒载量增加。在连续共感染的任何时间点均未检测到病毒载量的显着差异。与 DENV-1/CHIKV 合并感染组相比,单一感染组在 14 dpi 时的 CHIKV 感染率显着降低。

papers.full_text: AbstractBackgroundDengue fever has become an epidemiological concern worldwide, with 531,617 cases reported in Argentina during the 2023–2024 season. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon has been linked to changes in dengue dynamics. This study assessed the relationships among ENSO, local climatic variables, and dengue outbreaks in Argentina from 2018 to 2024.MethodsA nationwide spatiotemporal analysis was conducted using dengue cases and monthly mean temperature, relative humidity, and rainfall. The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) was used as the ENSO indicator (El Niño phase ≤ −0.5, neutral phase = −0.5 to 0.5, and La Niña phase ≥ 0.5). We fitted Hierarchical Bayesian models with Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). A Negative Binomial distribution of dengue cases was used to account for overdispersion. Spatial dependence was modeled by using the Besag–York–Mollié 2 (BYM2) structure, adjusted for population.ResultsThe final model achieved a Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 of 0.537. Exposure-response curves of posterior probability and 95% credible intervals suggested that dengue risk increased when monthly mean temperatures were between 20° and 30° Celsius during the El Niño or neutral phase, with less consistent effects during the La Niña phase. Humidity >50% was associated with increased dengue risk during the La Niña phase, with less steep or absent associations during El Niño or neutral phases. Negative SOI scores were associated with an increased risk of dengue after controlling for the covariates.ConclusionDengue outbreaks in Argentina were independently associated with temperatures between 20 and 30 °C during the El Niño and neutral phases, humidity > 50% during the La Niña phase, and the El Niño phase of the ENSO. Incorporating ENSO indices into predictive models could enhance early warning systems and timely public health interventions in Argentina.Keywords: Aedes aegypti, Argentina, dengue fever, El Niño-Southern Oscillation, epidemic dynamics, SOI 2.Methods2.1.Data collectionWe conducted a nationwide analysis of dengue case distribution in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 at a monthly resolution. Argentina is in the southern part of South America, covers an area of 2,780,400 km2 of continental and insular territory, and has a population of just over 46 million inhabitants. Argentina stretches over 3,700 km from north to south, which explains why it spans a remarkable variety of climates, from subtropical in the north to subpolar in the far south (15). This great length also gives rise to diverse biomes, including rainforests, grasslands, deserts, and Patagonian tundra. The country is divided into 525 departments and an autonomous city, Buenos Aires (hereinafter referred to as departments). Data on dengue incidence were obtained from the National Ministry of Health Surveillance System 2.0, accessed through https://datos.salud.gob.ar/dataset/vigilancia-de-dengue-y-zika (Date of Accession: 2025-02-01). A dengue case was defined as any confirmed or probable dengue infection reported through the national health surveillance system. For each department, monthly dengue incidence was calculated as the number of cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Population and population density data for each department were sourced from the 2022 National Census conducted by the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INDEC, https://www.indec.gob.ar/, Date of Accession: 2025-02-01).Climatic data were obtained from NASA’s POWER Project (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources) (16). For each department and month, we used the monthly mean of daily values for temperature (measured in degrees Celsius, °C) and relative humidity (measured in %), both at 2 meters above ground, as well as the monthly accumulated rainfall (measured in millimeters, mm). The spatial resolution of the satellite data is 0.5° latitude × 0.625° longitude (approximately 50 km). Daily values were extracted for each centroid within each administrative department and subsequently averaged to obtain monthly means; for rainfall, daily values were summed to derive monthly totals.The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) was also considered as a measure of ENSO (17, 18). This index reflects differences in atmospheric pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia, and is used to characterize the El Niño and La Niña phases. SOI scores were used in the analyses as a measure of the magnitude and direction of ENSO variability, which facilitates the climatological interpretation of exposure–response relationships. SOI scores above 0.5 indicated the La Niña phase; scores below −0.5 indicated the El Niño phase, with values between −0.5 and 0.5 characterizing a neutral phase, following the threshold criteria used in previous ENSO dengue studies (14).2.2.Statistical analysisWe fitted hierarchical Bayesian models using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) framework in R 4.5 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria; R-INLA package).The response variable was the monthly number of dengue cases, and we assumed a Negative Binomial likelihood to account for overdispersion.The general model fitted was:Yit∼NegBin(μit,φ)log(μit)=log(Eit)+f1(Temperaturelag)+f2(Humiditylag)+f3(Rainfalllag)+f4(SOIlag)+fn(SOI−categorizedlag∗climate_variableslag)+β1log(pop.densityi)+ui+vi+γyear(t)+smonth(t)Where Yit denotes the number of dengue cases observed in department i during month t, assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution. The term log(Eit) denotes the logarithm of the population size and is used as an offset. Nonlinear effects of temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, and SOI, as well as their interactions, were modeled using second-order random walks (RW2), which impose smoothness by penalizing second differences between adjacent latent effects. The RW2 terms were fitted using the default INLA penalized complexity priors for the precision parameter. For the RW2 components, climate parameters and SOI were centered and transformed into ordered indices representing adjacent exposure levels. Temperature and relative humidity were rounded to the nearest integer and converted to sequential indices, rainfall was rounded to the nearest 5-mm interval and converted to sequential indices, and SOI anomalies were rounded to the nearest integer and indexed similarly. These indices were then used as the covariates in the RW2 smooth terms, allowing estimation of nonlinear exposure–response relationships across the observed range of values. Population density was log-transformed and standardized before being included as a linear fixed effect.Interactions between the ENSO phase and climatic variables were implemented using the replicate argument in INLA. Specifically, separate RW2 smooth functions were estimated for temperature and relative humidity within each SOI category (El Niño, Neutral, and La Niña), while sharing a common smoothing prior structure. The terms ui and vi represent the structured and unstructured spatial random effects, respectively, modeled using the Besag–York–Mollié 2 specification. Departmental neighborhood relationships were defined using a first-order contiguity adjacency matrix derived from the departmental polygon shapefile, in which two departments were considered neighbors if they shared a common boundary. This adjacency matrix was supplied to INLA through the BYM2 specification. The BYM2 spatial effect was fitted using the default penalized complexity (PC) priors implemented in R-INLA.Temporal dependence was modeled through a 12-month cyclic seasonal effect to account for recurrent intra-annual patterns, together with an independent random effect for year to capture interannual variability in dengue transmission.We explored the best-fitting lags for SOI and climate parameters by computing and comparing the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) and the Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) between the models. Candidate lags from 0 to 11 months were evaluated independently for each climatic variable and SOI. The lag yielding the lowest DIC and WAIC values was retained in the final model.The interactions between the SOI and the climatic variables at their best-fitting lags were explored by categorizing SOI values, as established in the literature into El Niño (<−0.5), Neutral (−0.5 to 0.5), and La Niña (>0.5) phases (14). Models were fitted, and DIC and WAIC were used to select the best model.The final model adequacy was assessed through posterior predictive checks, including the randomized Probability Integral Transform (PIT) histogram, Q–Q plots of the randomized PIT values, and simulation-based residual diagnostics using the DHARMa package. DHARMa diagnostics included quantile residual Q–Q plots and residual-versus-predicted value assessments to evaluate potential deviations from distributional assumptions, overdispersion, and residual structure. To assess model performance, we calculated a pseudo-R2 using Nagelkerke’s method, based on the deviance values from the fitted and null models. Final inferences are presented as posterior means and 95% credible intervals from the INLA posterior summaries. Exposure-response curves were then obtained. When interactions with SOI were present, exposure–response curves had three curves, one for each SOI category. 3.ResultsThe total number of dengue cases reported from 2018 to 2024 was 1,559, 2,754, 52,027, 3,852, 793, 139,525, and 492,287, respectively (Figure 1A). No major differences in mean temperature or relative humidity were observed between 2018 and 2024 (Figures 1B,C). In contrast, the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) exhibited marked temporal variability, with predominantly negative values between 2018 and 2020, followed by positive values from 2020 to 2023, and a decline thereafter.Figure 1Temporal patterns of dengue incidence and environmental variables in Argentina (2018–2024). Shaded areas represent the maximum and minimum values for climate parameters across the country.Five-panel time series graphic from 2018 to 2025: Panel A shows reported cases peaking twice in 2023 and 2024; Panel B depicts annual cyclical temperature fluctuations; Panel C represents steady relative humidity; Panel D presents variable rainfall with sporadic spikes; Panel E tracks fluctuating SOI anomalies.Table 1 shows the fit of models involving different lags for the climatic and SOI variables. The best-fitting lag for temperature and humidity was 2 months, for rainfall was 3 months, and for SOI, 5 months. The final model included the variables at the best-fitting lags. Table 2 compares the fit of the different models tested. The introduction of SOI-climate parameter interaction terms reduced DIC and WAIC values and increased Nagelkerke R2. When the SOI*temperature and SOI*humidity terms were considered together, the fitting measures improved. Conversely, when the SOI*precipitation term was added, WAIC increased considerably. Therefore, the model retained contained SOI*temperature and SOI*humidity interaction terms plus the main effect terms for all other variables.Table 1Identification of the best lags in climatic and SOI variables included in the model.Lag (months)TemperatureHumidityRainfallSOI056,566/56,73356,568/56,73456,568/56,73556,565/56,731156,321/56,50256,480/56,65356,562/56,73456,332/56,5092 56,138/56,332 56,265/56,483 56,368/56,55156,624/56,794356,427/56,63956,496/56,682 56,366/56,548 56,281/56,540456,326/56,54556,546/56,76356,425/56,61056,215/56,393556,369/56,54056,666/56,87356,540/56,705 55,929/56,182 656,279/56,45356,636/56,79856,520/56,70056,621/56,796756,349/56,53256,576/56,75456,431/56,61456,251/56,457856,263/56,50056,444/56,61256,455/56,63356,593/56,774956,197/56,42256,206/56,40656,493/56,66456,653/56,8181056,202/56,41256,278/56,59856,435/56,60356,766/56,9481156,208/56,42956,290/56,49456,388/56,56756,761/56,930DIC/WAIC values are shown for each variable at each lag. The minimum values, highlighting the best-fitting lags, are marked in bold.Table 2Exploration of models with principal effect terms and interactions.ModelDICWAICNagelkerke R2Base model: SOI + Temperature + Relative Humidity + Rainfall + Pop. Density55,87456,0730.512Base model + Temperature*SOI53,51453,6960.533Base model + Humidity*SOI53,67153,4640.533Base model + Rainfall*SOI53,73453,5680.532Base model + Temperature*SOI + Humidity*SOI53,22353,4630.537Base model + Temperature*SOI + Humidity*SOI + Rainfall*SOI53,22662,4550.537The final selected model was a Bayesian hierarchical negative binomial model in which temperature and relative humidity were modeled as nonlinear effects with a 2-month lag, rainfall as an effect with a 3-month lag, and SOI anomalies score as an effect with a 5-month lag, with interactions between SOI anomalies and both temperature and relative humidity. A complete summary of the final model specification is provided in Table 3. The final model equation is:u,,,log(μit)=log(Eit)+f1(Temperaturelag2)+f2(Humiditylag2)+f3(Rainfalllag3)+f4(SOIlag5)+f5(SOI−categorizedlag5∗Temperaturelag2)+f6(SOI−categorizedlag5∗Humiditylag2)+β1log(pop.densityi)+ui+vi+γyear(t)+smonth(t)Table 3Summary of the final Bayesian spatiotemporal model.Model componentSpecificationSignificanceLikelihoodNegative binomialCompensation for overdispersed countsResponseMonthly dengue countsStudy outcomeSpatial effectBYM2Spatial structured and unstructured heterogeneityTemporal effectSeasonal (month) + IID yearControls for seasonality and year-to-year variation.TemperatureRW2, lag 2Nonlinear main effectHumidityRW2, lag 2Nonlinear main effectRainfallRW2, lag 3Nonlinear main effectSOI scoreRW2, lag 5Nonlinear main effectTemperature × SOI-categoricalRW2 replicated by ENSO phaseNonlinear interaction termHumidity × SOI-categoricalRW2 replicated by ENSO phaseNonlinear interaction termPopulation densityLinear standardized effectLinear main effectOffsetlog(population)Incidence adjustmentBYM2, Besag–York–Mollié 2 structure; ENSO, El Niño–Southern Oscillation; SOI, Southern Oscillation Index; RW2, second-order random walk; AR1, first-order autoregressive process.Exposure-response curves for posterior estimates of dengue relative risk across the predictors, along with the corresponding 95% credible intervals, are shown in Figure 2. Temperature (Figure 2A) was a risk factor when the monthly means were between 20 and 30 °C for the El Niño and neutral phases. During the El Niño phase, a monthly mean temperature of 25 °C was associated with an estimated RR of 2.92 (95% CrI, 1.69–4.23). Above 30 °C, the estimated risk declined markedly. Credible intervals were wider for the La Niña phase, signaling less consistent effects. Humidity (Figure 2B) showed a strong relationship with dengue risk during the La Niña phase, with values exceeding 50% indicating a higher risk. At a monthly mean relative humidity of 70%, the estimated log RR was 2.31 (95% CrI, 1.78–2.92). This relationship was less steep or absent in the El Niño and neutral phases. Precipitation (Figure 2C) showed no clear association with dengue risk. The SOI score showed an inverse relationship with dengue risk after adjusting for the covariates (Figure 2D). (A–D) Show the nonlinear associations between dengue risk and (A) temperature (2-month lag), (B) humidity (2-month lag), (C) rainfall (3-month lag), and (D) SOI (5-month lag), modeled using second-order random walks (RW2). Panel C displays log relative risk versus relative humidity percentage, also stratified by SOI phase with colored lines and shaded confidence intervals. Panel D illustrates log relative risk versus SOI anomalies using a yellow line and grey confidence band. Panel E plots log relative risk against standardized log population density, shown as a black line with grey confidence shading. All panels use dashed horizontal lines for reference at zero log relative risk.Figure 3 shows the residual spatial variation captured by the BYM2 component after accounting for climatic, temporal, and demographic covariates.
