full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionOur results suggest a close relationship between dengue outbreaks in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 and the El Niño phenomenon. Such a relationship has been observed in other parts of the world. In Asia, a study conducted in Thailand between 1996 and 2005 examined the impact of ENSO on dengue outbreaks in two geographically contrasting regions: a tropical coastal region in the south and a mountainous region in the north (17). Using autoregressive Poisson models adjusted for seasonality and population density, a statistically significant association was identified between negative ENSO phases and dengue outbreaks, with time lags of up to 11 months (17). The best correlations were observed when ENSO Indices were lagged by 4–6 months. Consistent with these findings, the best lag for SOI in our study was 5 months. On average, ENSO accounted for up to 22% of the monthly variability of cases in the northern provinces and 15% in the southern provinces (17). In our study, the models incorporating SOI and climate parameters accounted for 53.7% of the variance in the data.A longitudinal study integrating data from Puerto Rico, Mexico, and Thailand evaluated the association between ENSO, local climatic variables, and dengue incidence through time-frequency domain coherence analysis (wavelet analysis) (19). In Puerto Rico, a transient relationship was identified among ENSO, temperature, and dengue incidence; however, on multi-year scales, only rainfall was significantly correlated with reported cases. However, the El Niño phenomenon, which generates droughts and higher temperatures in this country, is an important predictor of arbovirus disease outbreaks up to a year in advance (20). In Thailand, both temperature and precipitation were associated with ENSO; however, the link between precipitation and dengue cases was non-stationary (19). In contrast, in Mexico, no significant associations were found between ENSO, climate, and dengue on a multi-year scale. A study in Brazil, using a hierarchical spatio-temporal model grounded on a Bayesian framework, explored the relationship between ENSO, seasonal weather fluctuations, and the larval index, while adjusting for population density and wealth inequalities (14). El Niño events, higher seasonal rainfall, and temperatures above 23.3 °C were all strongly associated with increases in the Aedes aegypti larval index. Mosquito proliferation was especially pronounced in socially vulnerable municipalities, highlighting the role of environmental and social factors in vector abundance. A similar study was conducted in Peru, adopting a Bayesian hierarchical modeling approach to address spatial correlation and B-splines with four knots per year to address temporal correlation, to analyze ENSO and climate parameters (21). Temperature and ENSO significantly increased the risk of dengue outbreaks, especially in summer and in some regions. Rainfall showed no strong independent effect. These findings suggest that local climatic conditions, urbanization patterns, and other contextual factors may modulate ENSO’s influence on dengue epidemiology. A study mapped the spatial association between ENSO activity (SOI) and dengue fever incidence across the Americas from 1995 to 2004, including the major 1997–1998 El Niño event (22). The authors analyzed standardized SOI and annual dengue incidence using regression and spatial interpolation to identify geographic patterns. Results show stronger ENSO–dengue coupling in Mexico, Central America, the northern Caribbean, and northern South America, with epidemic centers shifting southward and several countries exhibiting higher dengue incidence during El Niño phases. Our results extend these findings to Argentina. Recent findings indicate that the intensity of the El Niño phenomenon is likely to increase as climate change progresses (23), underscoring the need to better characterize its impact on dengue and other mosquito-borne infectious diseases.Higher temperatures, associated with El Niño events, have been shown to increase the incidence of dengue, possibly by favoring viral replication and vector behavior (4). Similar results have been observed in a study in 14 island nations in the South Pacific (24). In line with these findings, we observed a higher dengue risk at temperatures between approximately 20 °C and 30 °C during the El Niño and neutral phases, with less consistent effects during the La Niña phase (Figure 2A). Above 30 °C, dengue risk dropped significantly, which may be related to lower mosquito survival in high-temperature regions (25). Studies in Paraguay have also observed a similar U-shaped relationship (26). Humidity, which is also a significant factor in boosting mosquito survival (25), exhibited different patterns across ENSO phases. During the La Niña (dry, cold) phase, humidity was a strong conditioner of dengue risk. During neutral and El Niño phases, the effect was less marked. Rainfall was not associated with dengue risk, in concordance with previous observations (21).Recent evidence suggests that non-climatic mechanisms may also contribute to dengue outbreaks. While our results do not permit mechanistic inferences, it is worth reviewing some of these non-climatic mechanisms, as they might help explain some findings. Prolonged ENSO events can affect drinking water availability and the deterioration of sanitation infrastructure, which can force vulnerable communities to store water under precarious conditions, thereby contributing to the proliferation of Aedes aegypti breeding sites (27). This mechanism could potentially contribute to the residual SOI effect observed after controlling for climatic covariates; however, water-storage practices and sanitation conditions were not evaluated in our study. Therefore, this interpretation should be regarded as an untested hypothesis that warrants investigation in future studies.Population displacement might also be a relevant factor. A study of the South Pacific islands detected synchrony in dengue outbreaks between neighboring countries, even in the absence of direct local climate correlations (27). The authors hypothesized that the virus could spread between islands via flows of infected people, facilitated by regional maritime and air transport networks. In urban areas with high territorial connectivity, such as many cities in Argentina, movement between provinces and/or borders could accelerate the introduction of the virus and/or vector into new areas, even without substantial changes in the local climate. However, population mobility and viral circulation were not included in our models, and their potential contribution to the observed spatial patterns remains hypothetical. Future studies incorporating mobility and viral genomic data could help determine whether these mechanisms contribute to dengue dissemination across Argentina.Transfrontier population movements may also help explain the results of our spatial analysis, which revealed a residual higher incidence of dengue in the northern states that border Paraguay and Brazil (26, 28). Brazil, facing the worst dengue fever situation globally, reported over 3 million cases in 2023 and over 1 million cases in the first part of 2024 (28). Dengue has been endemic in Paraguay since 2009, with all four dengue virus serotypes circulating since 2011 (26). Conversely, the high residual risk in Argentina’s southern provinces is harder to explain. These are cold, dry regions where the common Aedes aegypti mosquito is not expected to survive. However, acclimated A. aegypti (29) and cold-resistant strains of A. albopictus (30) may be responsible for dengue outbreaks in these regions. It must be noted that these considerations have not been directly addressed in our models. Therefore, they are purely speculative. More research is needed to test these hypotheses.The findings presented herein must be interpreted within the framework of the limitations inherent in the methodol…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionIn this ecological study covering the period from 2018 to 2024, we found associations between ENSO, local climatic conditions, and dengue outbreaks in Argentina. Negative SOI scores, associated with the El Niño phase, were associated with higher dengue risk after adjustment for climatic and sociodemographic covariates. Monthly temperatures between 20 °C and 30 °C were associated with higher dengue risk during the El Niño and neutral phases, whereas humidity >50% was associated with higher risk during the La Niña phase. Population density was also positively associated with dengue risk. Our results further suggest that unmeasured factors may contribute to the observed spatial and temporal patterns. These findings support the potential value of considering ENSO indicators, alongside local climatic and epidemiological information, in dengue outbreak modeling. Further research is needed to determine whether incorporating ENSO measures improves the performance of early-warning systems for dengue outbreaks.
full_text_sections.other: HighlightsThis study linked the El Niño phenomenon to dengue fever outbreaks in Argentina.Other predictors of increased risk were monthly mean temperatures between 20° and 30° Celsius during the El Niño and neutral phases, and humidity > 50% during the La Niña phase.There was a high degree of spatial residual variance, not accounted for by the factors considered in the model, in dengue risk, which was increased in some northern and southern provinces of Argentina. 1.IntroductionDengue is a viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes of the genus Aedes, mainly Aedes aegypti (1, 2). The causative agent is the dengue virus, which belongs to the Flaviviridae family and has four different serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4) (2). Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, with higher incidence during rainy seasons, when mosquito populations increase (2). Approximately 380 million cases and 22,000 deaths occur each year. In Argentina, 531,617 cases were registered during the 2023–2024 season with 419 deaths (3). The most affected regions were the northern provinces.Several studies in tropical and subtropical regions of Latin America have demonstrated a significant correlation between dengue incidence and climatic variables, with temperature, humidity, and, to a lesser extent, rainfall as the primary factors (4, 5). There has been a significant increase in Earth’s temperature of about 1.16 Celsius degrees since 1951 (6), which may have contributed to the acceleration of the dengue burden (5).Higher temperatures accelerate dengue virus transmission by reducing the vector incubation period, increasing the contagion rate, and causing an exponential increase in cases (7). Rainfall and ambient humidity improve vector survival rates by promoting the accumulation of stagnant water, which supports mosquito development (4, 8).The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a recurring climate pattern that results from variations in ocean temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, coupled with changes in atmospheric pressure patterns across the tropical Pacific (9–11). ENSO has two main phases: El Niño (the warm phase) and La Niña (the cool phase), as well as a neutral phase (12). During El Niño events, abnormally warm sea surface temperatures develop in the eastern Pacific, disrupting typical weather patterns and leading to increased rainfall and humidity in some regions, while causing droughts in others (13) Conversely, La Niña events are characterized by cooler-than-average sea surface temperatures in the same region, which strengthens the trade winds and often results in opposite weather anomalies-drier conditions in some areas and increased rainfall in others. In Argentina, the El Niños phase is associated with increased ambient humidity, and the La Niña phase with dry conditions.Several studies suggest a relationship between ENSO and dengue outbreaks. A recent study found that El Niño was positively correlated with the global risk of dengue outbreaks, with a correlation coefficient of 0.52 (13). These results have been replicated in some regions of Brazil. A study conducted across 645 municipalities in the state of São Paulo (Brazil) linked El Niño events to increases in the mosquito larval index, a measure of mosquito proliferation (14).Despite growing evidence linking ENSO variability to dengue transmission in tropical and subtropical regions, its influence on dengue dynamics in Argentina remains poorly characterized. In particular, it is unclear whether the association between local climatic conditions and dengue risk varies across ENSO phases and whether ENSO contributes to dengue risk beyond the effects of local temperature, humidity, and precipitation. Addressing these relationships is particularly relevant in Argentina, where dengue transmission is spatially heterogeneous and occurs across regions with markedly different climatic conditions. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to model the influence of ENSO on dengue outbreaks across Argentina while accounting for local climatic conditions and the spatial and temporal structure of dengue transmission. 2.1.Data collectionWe conducted a nationwide analysis of dengue case distribution in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 at a monthly resolution. Argentina is in the southern part of South America, covers an area of 2,780,400 km2 of continental and insular territory, and has a population of just over 46 million inhabitants. Argentina stretches over 3,700 km from north to south, which explains why it spans a remarkable variety of climates, from subtropical in the north to subpolar in the far south (15). This great length also gives rise to diverse biomes, including rainforests, grasslands, deserts, and Patagonian tundra. The country is divided into 525 departments and an autonomous city, Buenos Aires (hereinafter referred to as departments). Data on dengue incidence were obtained from the National Ministry of Health Surveillance System 2.0, accessed through https://datos.salud.gob.ar/dataset/vigilancia-de-dengue-y-zika (Date of Accession: 2025-02-01). A dengue case was defined as any confirmed or probable dengue infection reported through the national health surveillance system. For each department, monthly dengue incidence was calculated as the number of cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Population and population density data for each department were sourced from the 2022 National Census conducted by the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INDEC, https://www.indec.gob.ar/, Date of Accession: 2025-02-01).Climatic data were obtained from NASA’s POWER Project (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources) (16). For each department and month, we used the monthly mean of daily values for temperature (measured in degrees Celsius, °C) and relative humidity (measured in %), both at 2 meters above ground, as well as the monthly accumulated rainfall (measured in millimeters, mm). The spatial resolution of the satellite data is 0.5° latitude × 0.625° longitude (approximately 50 km). Daily values were extracted for each centroid within each administrative department and subsequently averaged to obtain monthly means; for rainfall, daily values were summed to derive monthly totals.The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) was also considered as a measure of ENSO (17, 18). This index reflects differences in atmospheric pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia, and is used to characterize the El Niño and La Niña phases. SOI scores were used in the analyses as a measure of the magnitude and direction of ENSO variability, which facilitates the climatological interpretation of exposure–response relationships. SOI scores above 0.5 indicated the La Niña phase; scores below −0.5 indicated the El Niño phase, with values between −0.5 and 0.5 characterizing a neutral phase, following the threshold criteria used in previous ENSO dengue studies (14). 2.2.Statistical analysisWe fitted hierarchical Bayesian models using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) framework in R 4.5 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria; R-INLA package).The response variable was the monthly number of dengue cases, and we assumed a Negative Binomial likelihood to account for overdispersion.The general model fitted was:Yit∼NegBin(μit,φ)log(μit)=log(Eit)+f1(Temperaturelag)+f2(Humiditylag)+f3(Rainfalllag)+f4(SOIlag)+fn(SOI−categorizedlag∗climate_variableslag)+β1log(pop.densityi)+ui+vi+γyear(t)+smonth(t)Where Yit denotes the number of dengue cases observed in department i during month t, assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution. The term log(Eit) denotes the logarithm of the population size and is used as an offset. Nonlinear effects of temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, and SOI, as well as their interactions, were modeled using second-order random walks (RW2), which impose smoothness by penalizing second differences between adjacent latent effects. papers.title_original: Modeling the impact of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation on the dynamics of dengue outbreaks in Argentina between 2018 and 2024

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand how the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influences dengue outbreaks in Argentina, as dengue fever has become a significant epidemiological concern with 531,617 cases reported during the 2023–2024 season.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A nationwide analysis of dengue case distribution in Argentina between 2018 and 2024 was conducted at a monthly resolution, incorporating climate parameters and the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) across all departments.
analysis.methods: The study used monthly mean temperature and humidity data, along with accumulated rainfall, and applied a Bayesian hierarchical negative binomial model with nonlinear effects and lags. Model selection was based on DIC and WAIC, and posterior predictive checks were used to assess model adequacy.
analysis.main_results: Dengue risk increased with temperatures between 20° and 30° Celsius during El Niño or neutral phases, while humidity >50% was linked to higher risk during La Niña. Negative SOI scores were associated with increased dengue risk after controlling for covariates. The final model included SOI interactions with temperature and humidity, with temperature and humidity modeled as nonlinear effects with a 2-month lag.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that dengue outbreaks in Argentina are independently associated with temperature, humidity, and SOI anomalies, highlighting the importance of ENSO indices in understanding outbreak dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that integrating ENSO indices into predictive models could improve early warning systems and public health interventions for dengue in Argentina.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is moderate, as it relies on observational data and does not establish causality. The model's generalizability may be limited due to the focus on Argentina and the use of a single dataset.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the impact of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) on dengue outbreaks in Argentina from 2018 to 2024. It finds that dengue risk increases with temperatures between 20° and 30° Celsius during El Niño or neutral phases and with humidity >50% during La Niña. Negative Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) scores are also linked to higher dengue risk. The authors suggest that incorporating ENSO indices into predictive models could enhance early warning systems and public health interventions. The study uses a Bayesian hierarchical negative binomial model with nonlinear effects and lags, and the results are supported by posterior predictive checks. However, the evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and potential limitations in generalizability.

papers.source_body_en: This study assessed the relationships among ENSO, local climatic variables, and dengue outbreaks in Argentina from 2018 to 2024.MethodsA nationwide spatiotemporal analysis was conducted using dengue cases and monthly mean temperature, relative humidity, and rainfall. For each department and month, we used the monthly mean of daily values for temperature (measured in degrees Celsius, °C) and relative humidity (measured in %), both at 2 meters above ground, as well as the monthly accumulated rainfall (measured in millimeters, mm). To assess model performance, we calculated a pseudo-R2 using Nagelkerke’s method, based on the deviance values from the fitted and null models. AbstractBackgroundDengue fever has become an epidemiological concern worldwide, with 531,617 cases reported in Argentina during the 2023–2024 season. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon has been linked to changes in dengue dynamics. The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) was used as the ENSO indicator (El Niño phase ≤ −0.5, neutral phase = −0.5 to 0.5, and La Niña phase ≥ 0.5). We fitted Hierarchical Bayesian models with Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). A Negative Binomial distribution of dengue cases was used to account for overdispersion. Spatial dependence was modeled by using the Besag–York–Mollié 2 (BYM2) structure, adjusted for population.ResultsThe final model achieved a Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 of 0.537. Exposure-response curves of posterior probability and 95% credible intervals suggested that dengue risk increased when monthly mean temperatures were between 20° and 30° Celsius during the El Niño or neutral phase, with less consistent effects during the La Niña phase. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在了解厄尔尼诺-南方涛动 (ENSO) 如何影响阿根廷的登革热 暴发,因为 登革热 已成为一个重要的流行病学问题,2023-2024 年季节报告了 531,617 例病例。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 对 2018 年至 2024 年间阿根廷登革热病例分布进行了每月一次的分析,纳入了所有部门的气候参数和南方涛动指数 (SOI)。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究使用了月平均温度和湿度数据以及累积降雨量,并应用了具有非线性效应和滞后的贝叶斯分层负二项式模型。模型选择基于 DIC 和 WAIC,并使用后验预测检查来评估模型的充分性。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在厄尔尼诺现象或中性阶段,温度在 20° 至 30°C 之间时,登革热风险会增加,而在拉尼娜现象期间,湿度 >50% 与更高的风险相关。控制协变量后,负 SOI 评分与登革热风险增加相关。最终模型包括 SOI 与温度和湿度的相互作用,其中温度和湿度被建模为具有 2 个月滞后的非线性效应。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,阿根廷的登革热 暴发 与温度、湿度和 SOI 异常独立相关,强调了 ENSO 指数在理解 暴发 动态方面的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,将 ENSO 指数纳入预测模型可以改善阿根廷登革热的早期预警系统和公共卫生干预措施。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据是中等的,因为它依赖于观察数据并且没有建立因果关系。由于关注阿根廷并使用单个数据集,该模型的普遍性可能受到限制。

papers.full_text: BackgroundDengue virus (DENV) infection remains a global health threat with no approved small-molecule antiviral for clinical use. Luteolin, a natural flavonoid, exhibits anti-dengue activity but suffers from poor solubility and moderate potency. The 7-O position is the primary site of metabolic glucuronidation, whereas the 5-O position is sequestered by intramolecular hydrogen bonding, offering structurally distinct positions for derivatization.MethodsFive site-selective derivatives of luteolin (three 5-O- and two 7-O-substituted) were synthesized. Their anti-DENV activity was evaluated in Vero cells by qRT-PCR (measuring viral RNA abundance) and plaque assays, and cytotoxicity was determined using the CCK8 method. For mechanistic exploration, enzymatic inhibition kinetics against NS2B/NS3 and furin were measured, and target engagement was further assessed via molecular docking and cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA).ResultsAmong the derivatives, compound 5, bearing a 4-fluorobenzenesulfonyl group at the 7-O position, exhibited the most potent anti-DENV activity (EC50 = 0.46 μM) and the highest selectivity index (SI = 28.5), representing an 18-fold increase in antiviral potency over luteolin. In enzymatic assays, compound 5 showed preferential inhibition of the viral NS2B/NS3 protease (Ki = 11.54 μM) over the host furin (Ki = 93 μM). Molecular docking and thermal stabilization assays provided correlative evidence supporting target engagement with both proteases.ConclusionSite-selective 7-O-sulfonation of luteolin yields compound 5, a derivative with improved anti-DENV activity and selectivity that shows preferential NS2B/NS3 inhibition in enzymatic assays. This study provides a structural framework for the further optimization of flavonoid-based antiviral agents. 2Materials and methods2.1Cells and virusVero cells (obtained from Yuanjing Biology, YC-A001) were verified by species-specific multiplex qPCR and verified negative for cross-contamination with other mammalian cell lines and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination. Vero cells were grown and maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA) at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Compounds were dissolved in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and diluted in culture medium before each assay, with the final DMSO concentration adjusted to ≤0.1% (v/v) in all treated cultures. DENV-2 strain NGC (GenBank accession number KM204118.1) was provided by Jian-guo Wu (Jinan University). All virus strains were grown in C6/36 cells and the supernatants were stored at −80 °C. All cell experiments involving viruses were conducted in accordance with institutional biosafety guidelines under biosafety level-2 (BSL-2) conditions. All subsequent assays were performed under consistent experimental conditions, including the same batch of Vero cells, DENV-2 NGC strain, culture medium, and compound preparation protocol. Appropriate vehicle (DMSO) and untreated controls were included in each assay as specified in the respective method sections.2.2Cytotoxicity measurementCells were grown at 6 × 103 cells/well in 96-well culture plates and treated with compounds at concentrations ranging from 0.39 to 200 μM in twofold serial dilutions. The concentration range was selected to encompass a broad spectrum for accurate CC50 determination, with the upper limit based on preliminary solubility tests. The control group was treated with an equal volume of DMSO. After 48 h, 10% CCK8 reagent was added to each well, the plate was incubated for 1 h and absorbance values were determined at 450 nm. The half-maximal Cytotoxic Concentration (CC50) was calculated by nonlinear regression analysis of dose-response curves using GraphPad Prism 8.0. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate consisted of three technical replicates per concentration.2.3Anti-DENV assayCells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 2 × 105 cells/well and pre-treated with various concentrations of test compounds (0.15–200 μM) for 2 h. The concentration range for antiviral assays was selected based on the cytotoxicity profiles of each compound to ensure that the tested concentrations did not exceed the CC50. The 2 h pre-treatment and 48 h post-infection incubation times were chosen based on preliminary time-course experiments indicating that this interval allowed optimal virus replication while maintaining cell viability. Subsequently, the cells were infected with DENV-2 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1 for 2 h at 37 °C. An MOI of 1 was selected to achieve consistent infection efficiency across experiments while avoiding excessive viral cytopathic effects. Following removal of the viral inoculum, the cells were replenished with fresh medium containing the same compound concentrations and incubated until 48 h post-infection (hpi). The intracellular viral RNA levels were then determined using qRT-PCR. The EC50 value, defined as the concentration that reduces viral RNA yield by 50%, was calculated from the dose-response curves. A DMSO treated infected group served as the virus only control. Untreated cells (without virus and without compound) were included as blank controls for normalization. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate included three technical replicates. All experimental conditions were kept consistent across all antiviral assays to ensure comparability.2.4RNA isolation and qRT-PCRViral RNA was isolated using a standard protocol (CWBIO, Guangzhou, China), and qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green (Bio-Rad, California, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Primers used for DENV-2 E gene detection were Forward primer 5′-CAGGCTATGGCACTGTCACGAT-3′, Reverse primer 5′-CCATTTGCAGCAACACCATCTC-3′. Primers used for GAPDH gene detection were Forward primer 5′-AAGGCTGTGGGCAAGG-3′, Reverse primer 5′-TGGAGGAGTGGGTGTCG-3′. Cycling conditions were 94 °C for 2 min, followed by 40 cycles of 94 °C for 15 s and 55 °C for 30 s. GAPDH was used as the housekeeping gene and relative quantification was performed using the 2−ΔΔCT (cycle threshold) method. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate included three technical replicates.2.5Protease inhibition assayFor both NS2B/NS3 and furin protease assays, the compound concentrations, substrate concentrations, and incubation times were selected based on preliminary dose-finding experiments to ensure that enzymatic activity remained within the linear range. For NS2B/NS3 protease: Recombinant DENV-2 NS2B/NS3 protease (provided by the School of Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University) was used in all experiments. In a 96-well plate, 50 nM NS2B/NS3 protease was incubated with compound 5 at final concentrations of 0 (DMSO control), 1.56, and 3.12 μM in assay buffer (100 mM HEPES pH 7.0, 0.5% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM CaCl2) at room temperature for 30 min. The fluorogenic substrate Benzoyl-Nle-Lys-Arg-Arg-AMC (Nanjing Peptide Biotech Ltd.,) was then added at concentrations of 20, 50, 80, 100, and 200 μM. Fluorescence intensity was measured at an excitation wavelength of 370 nm and an emission wavelength of 460 nm at 37 °C. Readings were taken every 2 min for a total duration of 30 min. Initial reaction velocities (V0) were determined from the linear portion of each progress curve. Kinetic parameters were obtained by fitting the data to the Michaelis-Menten equation using nonlinear regression (GraphPad Prism 8.0). The mode of inhibition was determined by Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plots (1/V vs. 1/S), and the inhibition constant (Ki) was derived from the secondary plot of slope versus inhibitor concentration. DMSO control served as the negative control.For furin protease: Furin (NEB) was used at 1 U per reaction. In a 384-well plate, furin was incubated with compound 5 at final concentrations of 0 (DMSO control), 50, and 70 μM in reaction buffer containing 100 mM HEPES pH 7.0, 0.5% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM CaCl2 at room temperature for 30 min. The fluorogenic substrate Pyr-Arg-Thr-Lys-Arg-AMC (Bachem) was then added at concentrations of 50, 100, 200 and 400 μM. Fluorescence intensity was measured at an excitation wavelength of 370 nm and an emission wavelength of 460 nm at 37 °C. Readings were taken every 5 min for a total duration of 1 h. Kinetic parameters and inhibition constants were determined using the same nonlinear regression and Lineweaver-Burk analysis methods as described above for NS2B/NS3. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate included three technical replicates.2.6Plaque forming assayVero cells were seeded overnight at 2 × 105 cells/well in a 12 well plate and infected with the supernatant at 37 °C for 2 h. After incubation, the inoculum was removed and cells were immediately replenished with plaque medium (Sigma, St. Louis, USA) supplemented with 0.8% methylcellulose. Infected cells were cultured for 7 days. After incubation, plaque medium was removed, cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 2 h and stained with 0.5% crystal violet for 30min. Data are presented as mean ± SD. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s post-hoc test for comparisons with the DMSO control. All plaque assays were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate included three technical replicates.2.7Western blottingThe separated proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore) and nonspecific binding on the membranes was blocked with 5% BSA in PBST for 1 h. Membranes were incubated with dengue virus NS3 protein antibody or furin antibody as an internal control overnight at 4 °C. Detection was performed with HRP-conjugated anti-mouse antibody for 1 h at room temperature with shaking. Densitometric quantification was performed using ImageJ. Band intensities were measured as integrated density values after background subtraction, normalized to GAPDH, and expressed relative to the DMSO-treated infected control (set as 100%). Data are presented as mean ± SD. Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post-hoc test versus the DMSO control. All Western blotting were performed with three independent biological replicates.2.8CETSACellular thermal shift assays was performed as described above (Chen et al., 2020), with minor changes. Briefly, Vero cells were harvested, washed with PBS, and resuspended in detergent-free buffer (25 mM HEPES, pH 7.0, 20 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT) supplemented with a cocktail of protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The cell suspension was lysed by sonication and centrifuged at 20,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C to separate the soluble fraction from the cell debris. In the CETSA melting curve experiment, cytolysis was diluted with detergent-free buffer and split into two aliquots prior to DMSO (equivalent volume of compound 5) or 20 μM compound 5 treatment.The 20 μM concentration was selected as it represented a concentration approximately 43-fold above the antiviral EC50. After treatment at room temperature for 30 min, each sample was divided into 11 aliquots of 50 μl/tube, heated at 33.1 °C–52.1 °C for 3 min and immediately cooled at room temperature for 3 min. The heated cell extract was centrifuged at 20,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C to separate the soluble fraction from the pellet. After centrifugation, the supernatant was analyzed by blotting with antibody. The highest signal intensity within the DMSO treatment group (consistently occurring at the lowest temperature) as a 100% reference for each protein target. Densitometric analysis was performed using ImageJ software. Band intensities were quantified as integrated density values after uniform background subtraction. The apparent aggregation temperature (Tagg) was calculated by non-linear regression using a sigmoidal dose-response curve fitting model in GraphPad Prism 8.0. For each biological replicate, Tagg was derived from the inflection point of the melting curve. The mean Tagg and standard deviation (SD) were calculated from three independent biological replicates. Statistical significance of the Tagg shifts between compound 5 and DMSO control was assessed using the two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test for comparing fitted curves. P-value of <0.05 was considered to indicate a statistically significant shift. DMSO-treated samples served as vehicle controls in all experiments. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates.2.9Molecular dockingMolecular docking was performed using AutoDock 4.0. Compound 5 was drawn in ChemDraw, energy-minimized using the MM2 force field, and converted to PDB format. The crystal structures of NS2B/NS3 (PDB: 2FOM) and furin (PDB: 5MIM) were downloaded from the Protein Data Bank. Water molecules and bound ligands were removed using PyMOL. For each protein, AutoDockTools was used to add polar hydrogens, compute Gasteiger charges, assign AD4 atom types, and generate grid maps. For NS2B/NS3 (PDB: 2FOM), the grid box was defined with 126 × 126 × 126 points and a spacing of 0.375 Å, yielding a physical box size of 46.875 × 46.875 × 46.875 Å3. Centered at (x = 0.409, y = −17.041, z = 15.722) Å, covering the substrate-binding pocket. For furin (PDB: 5MIM), the same grid parameters were used, with the box centered at (x = 35.379, y = −37.864, z = −0.394) Å to encompass the catalytic domain. For compound 5, rotatable bonds were defined and the torsion root was identified, and the ligand was saved in PDBQT format. Docking calculations were performed using the Lamarckian genetic algorithm with 100 independent runs. The best pose was selected based on the lowest binding free energy score and cluster analysis in AutoDock Tools. To validate the reliability of the molecular docking protocol, the co-crystallized ligand was extracted from the binding site and re-docked into the same protein structure. The root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between the top-scoring docking pose and the crystallographic conformation was calculated based on all heavy atoms of the ligand. An RMSD value of ≤2.0 Å was considered indicative of a successful docking protocol.2.10Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0. All data are presented as mean ± SD from three independent biological replicates (n = 3). Biological replicates refer to independent experiments performed on different days with separately prepared cell cultures and compound dilutions. Technical replicates refer to repeated measurements within the same experiment. Prior to statistical analysis, the assumptions of normality and homogeneity of variance were verified using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Levene’s test, respectively. If normality or homogeneity of variance was violated, data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test or Welch’s ANOVA, as appropriate. Two-group comparisons were analyzed by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test, and multiple comparisons by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post-hoc test versus the DMSO control. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Significance levels are indicated as *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, and ***p < 0.001, ns, not significant (p > 0.05). For quantitative comparisons, all bar graphs display mean ± SD from three independent biological replicates.2.11Ethics statementNo animal studies were performed in this manuscript. 3Results3.1Synthesis and structural characterization of luteolin derivativesA series of luteolin derivatives were synthesized via structural modification at the 5-O and 7-O position (Supplementary Figure 1). Specifically, three novel 5-O-substituted derivatives (compounds 1–3) and two novel 7-O-substituted derivatives (compounds 4 and 5) were prepared (Figure 1). None of the five compounds have been previously reported in SciFinder, thereby expanding the chemical space of luteolin-based analogs. The physicochemical and spectral data for each compound are presented (Table 1 and Supplementary Figure 2).FIGURE 1Chemical structures of luteolin derivatives (1–5).Chemical structure diagram showing five flavonoid derivatives with varying substituents, including fluorine, chlorine, sulfonic acid, and methoxy groups, each arranged in distinct positions on the core flavonoid scaffold.TABLE 1Properties of compounds luteolin and luteolin derivatives.CompoundPositionPropertyMW (g/mol)Luteolin–Yellow, powder286.24Compound 15-OLight yellowish-green, powder458.06Compound 25-OLight yellow, powder424.03Compound 35-OYellowish-white, powder444.03Compound 47-OYellowish-green, powder328.07Compound 57-OBrownish-yellow, powder445.033.2Cytotoxicity and antiviral activity (inferred from viral RNA abundance) of luteolin and luteolin derivativesThe cytotoxic effects of luteolin, luteoloside, and compounds 1–5 were evaluated in Vero cells. As shown in Figures 2A–G, the half-maximal cytotoxic concentrations (CC50) were 85.5 ± 1.34, >200, 48.78 ± 1.10, 31.36 ± 1.05, >200, 19.65 ± 1.02, and 13.09 ± 1.10 μM, respectively. Compared with luteolin, luteoloside and compound 3 exhibited reduced cytotoxicity (CC50 > 200 μM), whereas compounds 1, 2, 4, and 5 showed enhanced cytotoxicity, with CC50 values ranging from 13.09 to 48.78 μM. These results demonstrate that structural diversification significantly modulated the cytotoxic properties of luteolin derivatives. Antiviral activity was inferred from viral RNA abundance, as quantified by qRT-PCR. full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundDengue virus (DENV) infection remains a global health threat with no approved small-molecule antiviral for clinical use. Luteolin, a natural flavonoid, exhibits anti-dengue activity but suffers from poor solubility and moderate potency. The 7-O position is the primary site of metabolic glucuronidation, whereas the 5-O position is sequestered by intramolecular hydrogen bonding, offering structurally distinct positions for derivatization.MethodsFive site-selective derivatives of luteolin (three 5-O- and two 7-O-substituted) were synthesized. Their anti-DENV activity was evaluated in Vero cells by qRT-PCR (measuring viral RNA abundance) and plaque assays, and cytotoxicity was determined using the CCK8 method. For mechanistic exploration, enzymatic inhibition kinetics against NS2B/NS3 and furin were measured, and target engagement was further assessed via molecular docking and cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA).ResultsAmong the derivatives, compound 5, bearing a 4-fluorobenzenesulfonyl group at the 7-O position, exhibited the most potent anti-DENV activity (EC50 = 0.46 μM) and the highest selectivity index (SI = 28.5), representing an 18-fold increase in antiviral potency over luteolin. In enzymatic assays, compound 5 showed preferential inhibition of the viral NS2B/NS3 protease (Ki = 11.54 μM) over the host furin (Ki = 93 μM). Molecular docking and thermal stabilization assays provided correlative evidence supporting target engagement with both proteases.ConclusionSite-selective 7-O-sulfonation of luteolin yields compound 5, a derivative with improved anti-DENV activity and selectivity that shows preferential NS2B/NS3 inhibition in enzymatic assays. This study provides a structural framework for the further optimization of flavonoid-based antiviral agents.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Materials and methods2.1Cells and virusVero cells (obtained from Yuanjing Biology, YC-A001) were verified by species-specific multiplex qPCR and verified negative for cross-contamination with other mammalian cell lines and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination. Vero cells were grown and maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA) at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Compounds were dissolved in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and diluted in culture medium before each assay, with the final DMSO concentration adjusted to ≤0.1% (v/v) in all treated cultures. DENV-2 strain NGC (GenBank accession number KM204118.1) was provided by Jian-guo Wu (Jinan University). All virus strains were grown in C6/36 cells and the supernatants were stored at −80 °C. All cell experiments involving viruses were conducted in accordance with institutional biosafety guidelines under biosafety level-2 (BSL-2) conditions. All subsequent assays were performed under consistent experimental conditions, including the same batch of Vero cells, DENV-2 NGC strain, culture medium, and compound preparation protocol. Appropriate vehicle (DMSO) and untreated controls were included in each assay as specified in the respective method sections.2.2Cytotoxicity measurementCells were grown at 6 × 103 cells/well in 96-well culture plates and treated with compounds at concentrations ranging from 0.39 to 200 μM in twofold serial dilutions. The concentration range was selected to encompass a broad spectrum for accurate CC50 determination, with the upper limit based on preliminary solubility tests. The control group was treated with an equal volume of DMSO. After 48 h, 10% CCK8 reagent was added to each well, the plate was incubated for 1 h and absorbance values were determined at 450 nm. The half-maximal Cytotoxic Concentration (CC50) was calculated by nonlinear regression analysis of dose-response curves using GraphPad Prism 8.0. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate consisted of three technical replicates per concentration.2.3Anti-DENV assayCells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 2 × 105 cells/well and pre-treated with various concentrations of test compounds (0.15–200 μM) for 2 h. The concentration range for antiviral assays was selected based on the cytotoxicity profiles of each compound to ensure that the tested concentrations did not exceed the CC50. The 2 h pre-treatment and 48 h post-infection incubation times were chosen based on preliminary time-course experiments indicating that this interval allowed optimal virus replication while maintaining cell viability. Subsequently, the cells were infected with DENV-2 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1 for 2 h at 37 °C. An MOI of 1 was selected to achieve consistent infection efficiency across experiments while avoiding excessive viral cytopathic effects. Following removal of the viral inoculum, the cells were replenished with fresh medium containing the same compound concentrations and incubated until 48 h post-infection (hpi). The intracellular viral RNA levels were then determined using qRT-PCR. The EC50 value, defined as the concentration that reduces viral RNA yield by 50%, was calculated from the dose-response curves. A DMSO treated infected group served as the virus only control. Untreated cells (without virus and without compound) were included as blank controls for normalization. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate included three technical replicates. All experimental conditions were kept consistent across all antiviral assays to ensure comparability.2.4RNA isolation and qRT-PCRViral RNA was isolated using a standard protocol (CWBIO, Guangzhou, China), and qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green (Bio-Rad, California, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Primers used for DENV-2 E gene detection were Forward primer 5′-CAGGCTATGGCACTGTCACGAT-3′, Reverse primer 5′-CCATTTGCAGCAACACCATCTC-3′. Primers used for GAPDH gene detection were Forward primer 5′-AAGGCTGTGGGCAAGG-3′, Reverse primer 5′-TGGAGGAGTGGGTGTCG-3′. Cycling conditions were 94 °C for 2 min, followed by 40 cycles of 94 °C for 15 s and 55 °C for 30 s. GAPDH was used as the housekeeping gene and relative quantification was performed using the 2−ΔΔCT (cycle threshold) method. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates. Each biological replicate included three technical replicates.2.5Protease inhibition assayFor both NS2B/NS3 and furin protease assays, the compound concentrations, substrate concentrations, and incubation times were selected based on preliminary dose-finding experiments to ensure that enzymatic activity remained within the linear range. For NS2B/NS3 protease: Recombinant DENV-2 NS2B/NS3 protease (provided by the School of Pharmacy, China Pharmaceutical University) was used in all experiments. In a 96-well plate, 50 nM NS2B/NS3 protease was incubated with compound 5 at final concentrations of 0 (DMSO control), 1.56, and 3.12 μM in assay buffer (100 mM HEPES pH 7.0, 0.5% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM CaCl2) at room temperature for 30 min. The fluorogenic substrate Benzoyl-Nle-Lys-Arg-Arg-AMC (Nanjing Peptide Biotech Ltd.,) was then added at concentrations of 20, 50, 80, 100, and 200 μM. Fluorescence intensity was measured at an excitation wavelength of 370 nm and an emission wavelength of 460 nm at 37 °C. Readings were taken every 2 min for a total duration of 30 min. Initial reaction velocities (V0) were determined from the linear portion of each progress curve. Kinetic parameters were obtained by fitting the data to the Michaelis-Menten equation using nonlinear regression (GraphPad Prism 8.0). The mode of inhibition was determined by Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plots (1/V vs. 1/S), and the inhibition constant (Ki) was derived from the secondary plot of slope versus inhibitor concentration. DMSO control served as the negative control.For furin protease: Furin (NEB) was used at 1 U per reaction. In a 384-well plate, furin was incubated with compound 5 at final concentrations of 0 (DMSO control), 50, and 70 μM in reaction buffer containing 100 mM HEPES pH 7.0, 0.5% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM CaCl2 at room temperature for 30 min. The fluorogenic substrate Pyr-Arg-Thr-Lys-Arg-AMC (Bachem) was then added at concentrations of 50, 100, 200 and 400 μM. Fluorescence intensity was measured at an excitation wavelength of 370 nm and an emission wavelength of 460 nm at 37 °C. Readings were taken every 5 min for a total duration of 1 h. Kinetic parameters and inhibition constants were determined using the same nonlinear regression and Lineweaver-Burk analysis methods as described above for NS2B/NS3. After incubation, the inoculum was removed and cells were immediately replenished with plaque medium (Sigma, St. Louis, USA) supplemented with 0.8% methylcellulose. Infected cells were cultured for 7 days. After incubation, plaque medium was removed, cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 2 h and stained with 0.5% crystal violet for 30min. full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Synthesis and structural characterization of luteolin derivativesA series of luteolin derivatives were synthesized via structural modification at the 5-O and 7-O position (Supplementary Figure 1). Specifically, three novel 5-O-substituted derivatives (compounds 1–3) and two novel 7-O-substituted derivatives (compounds 4 and 5) were prepared (Figure 1). None of the five compounds have been previously reported in SciFinder, thereby expanding the chemical space of luteolin-based analogs. The physicochemical and spectral data for each compound are presented (Table 1 and Supplementary Figure 2).FIGURE 1Chemical structures of luteolin derivatives (1–5).Chemical structure diagram showing five flavonoid derivatives with varying substituents, including fluorine, chlorine, sulfonic acid, and methoxy groups, each arranged in distinct positions on the core flavonoid scaffold.TABLE 1Properties of compounds luteolin and luteolin derivatives.CompoundPositionPropertyMW (g/mol)Luteolin–Yellow, powder286.24Compound 15-OLight yellowish-green, powder458.06Compound 25-OLight yellow, powder424.03Compound 35-OYellowish-white, powder444.03Compound 47-OYellowish-green, powder328.07Compound 57-OBrownish-yellow, powder445.033.2Cytotoxicity and antiviral activity (inferred from viral RNA abundance) of luteolin and luteolin derivativesThe cytotoxic effects of luteolin, luteoloside, and compounds 1–5 were evaluated in Vero cells. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionA notable observation is that, in biochemical assays, compound 5 exhibited a lower Ki value for NS2B/NS3 than for furin, whereas luteolin had been previously reported to show the opposite profile. This suggestive shift in relative potency warrants further direct comparative studies to confirm whether 7-O-sulfonation truly redirects target preference.Compound 5 exhibited higher cytotoxicity (CC50 = 13.09 μM) than luteolin (CC50 = 85.5 μM). Nevertheless, it retained a favorable selectivity index, as the 18-fold improvement in antiviral activity outweighed the approximately 6.5-fold increase in cytotoxicity. Crucially, this favorable SI indicates that the gain in antiviral activity substantially outweighs the increase in cytotoxicity. If the antiviral effect were predominantly driven by nonspecific cellular toxicity, a proportional increase in both EC50 and CC50 would be expected, resulting in a similar or worse SI. Thus, the improved activity of compound 5 reflects enhanced target engagement rather than merely increased toxicity. Despite this favorable SI, the absolute cytotoxicity in normal cells remains a concern that warrants further investigation. The underlying causes are likely multifactorial. First, it may arise from off-target effects associated with the overall lipophilicity of the molecule or specific substituents. Second, although the fluorobenzenesulfonyl moiety is generally regarded as a metabolically stable pharmacophore, it may, in certain scaffold contexts, undergo cytochrome P450-mediated ipso-substitution to generate phenolic intermediates, which could be further oxidized to electrophilic quinone imine-type reactive metabolites. Such species have the potential to deplete intracellular glutathione and covalently modify proteins, thereby contributing to cytotoxic outcomes (Ma et al., 2021; Ohe et al., 1994). Future optimization efforts should prioritize substantial reduction of absolute cytotoxicity, which will be essential for further development of this compound.The data suggest a preferential inhibition of NS2B/NS3 over furin, as supported by complementary biochemical and computational assays. The biochemical inhibition data demonstrate that compound 5 inhibits both proteases in vitro, with a lower Ki value for NS2B/NS3. CETSA provided evidence of target engagement in lysates, with compound 5 inducing a numerically larger thermal stabilization of NS2B/NS3 (ΔTagg = 2.6 ± 0.12°C) than furin (ΔTagg = 2.11 ± 0.16°C). This differential stabilization was further reflected in computational predictions, where compound 5 exhibited a markedly superior computationally estimated binding affinity for NS2B/NS3 (−10.86 kcal/mol) compared to furin (−8.72 kcal/mol). Notably, while the parent luteolin showed comparable affinity for furin (−8.51 kcal/mol), its interaction with NS2B/NS3 was substantially weaker (−7.6 kcal/mol), suggesting that the 7-O-sulfonate may confer a critical selectivity advantage, potentially through enhanced hydrophobic and hydrogen-bonding networks within the NS2B/NS3 active site. Although compound 5 retains moderate furin inhibition (Ki = 93 μM), this concentration is approximately 200-fold higher than its anti-DENV EC50, rendering furin-related off-target effects negligible at therapeutic doses. It should be noted that the present assay did not include a well-characterized positive control inhibitor for direct benchmarking; this represents a limitation that will be addressed in future studies. Collectively, these complementary lines of evidence provide a structural framework for the rational optimization of the 7-O-sulfonate scaffold toward enhanced antiviral efficacy and selectivity.A noteworthy observation is the ∼25-fold discrepancy between the biochemical inhibition constant (Ki = 11.54 μM) and the cellular antiviral potency (EC50 = 0.46 μM). While this does not exclude NS2B/NS3 as a primary target, it merits consideration. One possible explanation is intracellular accumulation. Flavonoids are known to concentrate within cells and organelles, often reaching local levels well above extracellular concentrations. Compound 5 may similarly enrich at the viral replication complex, effectively offsetting its moderate Ki in the cellular context. Another possibility is that compound 5 may act through additional mechanisms. Luteolin has been reported to inhibit viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and to disrupt cytoskeletal organization, thereby interfering with virus release. Such pleiotropic effects, common among flavonoids, could synergize with NS2B/NS3 inhibition to yield the potent cellular EC50. Differences between the recombinant enzyme system and the native cellular environment, including the artificial protease construct and the presence of physiological modulators, may also contribute (Morimoto et al., 2022; Munafò et al., 2022; Sakai-Sugino et al., 2024). These hypotheses warrant further investigation.SAR analysis revealed that compounds 1–3 (5-O-substituted) were less active than luteolin (EC50 = 105, >25, and 54.89 μM vs. 8.28 μM), as the intramolecular hydrogen bond between the 5-O position and the 4-carbonyl group is critical for maintaining the planar conformation. Substitution at this position disrupts this bond, altering conformation and reducing target affinity (Nath et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). In contrast, compound 5 (7-O-sulfonated) exhibited the most potent activity (EC50 = 0.46 μM), representing an 18-fold improvement over luteolin. This is attributable to the absence of intramolecular hydrogen bonding at the 7-O position and the negatively charged sulfonate group, which enables electrostatic interactions with positively charged residues in the NS2B/NS3 active site (Li et al., 2023). Molecular docking predicted a binding energy of −10.86 kcal/mol for compound 5, compared with −7.6 kcal/mol for luteolin, suggesting a more favorable computationally estimated binding interaction. The predicted binding mode involves hydrogen bonds with Val146, Trp83, and Asn167, which may contribute to the observed preferential NS2B/NS3 inhibition, although these predictions require experimental validation through mutagenesis or co-crystallization studies. The electron-withdrawing fluorine atom in the 4-fluorobenzenesulfonyl group may enhance electrostatic interactions, while the moderately increased lipophilicity could be expected to favor membrane permeation. Compound 4 (7-O-acetyl) was far less active than compound 5 (EC50 > 25 μM vs. 0.46 μM), suggesting that the sulfonate group may contributes substantially to the potent activity of compound 5. However, given that acetyl and sulfonate groups differ in multiple physicochemical properties (charge, hydrogen-bonding capacity, geometry, and polarity), additional analogues with structurally varied substituents (e.g., sulfonamide, phosphate, or carboxylate) would be required to systematically deconvolute the structural determinants of target binding (Li et al., 2023; Nath et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025, 2026).From a drug discovery perspective, compound 5 offers several advantages over existing approaches. While peptide- and protein-based furin inhibitors offer higher in vitro potency, their poor cell permeability limits antiviral efficacy (Lü et al., 2024; Raj et al., 2025). Small-molecule inhibitors like compound 5 offer more favorable physicochemical properties (e.g., lower molecular weight, reduced polar surface area) and potentially better intracellular access, representing a practical alternative for further development (Yang and Hinner, 2015). The 7-O-sulfonation strategy is synthetically accessible and amenable to further diversification, allowing exploration of alternative arylsulfonyl groups, sulfonamides, or bioisosteres to optimize potency, selectivity, and pharmacokinetic properties. Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that sulfonated flavonoids often exhibit poor oral bioavailability and rapid clearance due to their hydrophilic nature and su…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionSite-selective 7-O-sulfonation of luteolin yielded compound 5, a derivative that exhibits more potent inhibition of DENV NS2B/NS3 over furin in biochemical assays and exhibits improved antiviral potency and selectivity. The available data suggest an association between compound 5 activity and NS2B/NS3 inhibition, supported by complementary biochemical, computational, and cellular target-engagement studies. Together, these findings identify 7-O-sulfonation as a promising structural strategy for modulating the target preference of luteolin and provide a foundation for further optimization of this flavonoid-based scaffold.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionDengue fever, transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, is one of the most rapidly spreading mosquito-borne viral diseases worldwide. Its incidence has surged nearly 30-fold over five decades, and the virus is now endemic in more than 130 countries, placing an estimated 4 billion people at risk (Finch et al., 2025; He et al., 2026). Despite the unprecedented global dengue burden in 2024, with millions of reported cases and thousands of deaths across all WHO regions, no small-molecule antiviral has yet been approved for clinical use (EClinicalMedicine, 2024; Haider et al., 2025). The NS4B inhibitor NITD-688 is currently the only candidate in Phase 2a clinical trials, while other candidates such as AT-752 and JNJ-1802 have been discontinued (McBride et al., 2026). Although the tetravalent vaccine Qdenga has been approved in several countries and demonstrated 61.2% efficacy against symptomatic dengue and 84.1% against hospitalization over 4.5 years, its efficacy varies by serotype and baseline serostatus, wanes over time, and safety concerns including anaphylaxis have emerged in mass vaccination programs (Ranzani et al., 2026; Tricou et al., 2024). Consequently, patient management remains largely confined to symptomatic and supportive treatments.The DENV genome is a single-stranded positive-sense RNA of approximately 11 kb, encoding three structural proteins–capsid (C), precursor membrane (prM), and envelope (E)–and seven non-structural proteins (NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B, and NS5) (Bhatnagar et al., 2021). The dengue virus life cycle begins with receptor-mediated endocytosis and pH-dependent fusion, which releases the viral RNA genome into the cytoplasm. Subsequently, the NS2B/NS3 complex serves as an enzymatic hub for replication. NS2B activates the NS3 protease to cleave the viral polyprotein at four cytosolic sites, while the NS3 helicase couples NTP hydrolysis to RNA unwinding during RNA synthesis. NS2B/NS3 also recruits NS5 and NS4B to assemble the functional replication complex on endoplasmic reticulum membranes. During the late stage, the host protease furin cleaves prM at the conserved -R-X-R/K-R- motif in the trans-Golgi network, releasing the pr peptide and triggering the fusogenic conformational change of the E protein, thereby rendering virions infectious. Together, NS2B/NS3-driven replication and furin-mediated maturation represent two critical, temporally coordinated steps essential for productive DENV infection (Khanra et al., 2025; Nanaware et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2024; Tse et al., 2022).Previous studies established that luteolin, a bioactive flavone isolated from Viola yedoensis, exhibits potent in vitro anti-DENV activity and confers partial protection in DENV-infected AG129 mice (Peng et al., 2017). Mechanistically, luteolin non-competitively inhibits the host furin protease, impairing prM cleavage and leading to elevated prM levels in culture supernatants. However, selection of luteolin-resistant viral variants revealed T79R and I114M substitutions in prM and NS2B, respectively, suggesting that luteolin may also directly target the viral NS2B/NS3 protease complex. These findings indicate that luteolin acts as a dual-target inhibitor of both furin and NS2B/NS3, which may underlie its antiviral efficacy (Peng et al., 2018).In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of NS2B-NS3 protease inhibitors, including peptides, peptidomimetics, covalent small molecules, and natural products (João et al., 2024). For example, structure-based optimization yielded pyrazole ester-based covalent inhibitors WSL-75 and WSL-84 with improved activity over the lead compound WSL-01, while an N-methylcytisine thio derivative (compound 6) was shown to inhibit both DENV E protein-mediated viral entry and NS2B-NS3 protease activity, exhibiting a dual antiviral mechanism (Cheng et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024). Among natural products, flavonoids have garnered considerable interest as antiviral leads due to their structural diversity and low toxicity (Aguiar-Pech et al., 2025). Multiple flavonoids, including quercetin, luteolin, kaempferol derivatives, and apigenin, have been reported to inhibit NS2B-NS3 by binding to the active site or allosteric pockets. Notably, quercetin, curcumin, and myricetin have been characterized as non-competitive inhibitors that modulate enzyme activity through interactions with the NS2B cofactor or by inducing conformational changes in NS3 (Saqallah et al., 2022).Nevertheless, luteolin has significant pharmacokinetic drawbacks, including poor aqueous solubility that leads to low in vivo exposure and limits its clinical potential. In the molecular modification of luteolin, the 5-O and 7-O position are preferentially chosen for derivatization owing to differences in chemical reactivity, metabolic stability, and biological activity (Lo et al., 2021; Robotham and Brodbelt, 2013). The 7-O position is more reactive and the primary site of metabolic glucuronidation. Hence, its modification represents a key strategy to improve oral bioavailability. By contrast, the 5-O position forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the 4-carbonyl group, which stabilizes the molecular conformation and is essential for antioxidant activity (Wu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2022). Among various derivatization strategies, sulfation introduces a negatively charged sulfonate group that enhances aqueous solubility, increases molecular polarity, and can modify target-binding affinity through electrostatic interactions (Alshehri and Jones, 2024). Therefore, rational selection of the 5-O or 7-O position enables targeted improvements in solubility, stability, or pharmacological activity. Despite the promising anti-DENV activity of luteolin, systematic strategies that leverage site-selective modification to redirect its target preference and to improve its potency and selectivity remain under-explored.Based on these considerations, we hypothesized that sulfonation at the 7-O position would confer greater selectivity for the viral NS2B/NS3 protease over the host furin than modification at the 5-O position. The 7-O position is more solvent-exposed and capable of forming hydrogen bonds with NS2B/NS3 residues, whereas the 5-O is constrained by intramolecular H-bonding with the 4-carbonyl. Moreover, a 7-O arylsulfonyl substituent, such as 4-fluorobenzenesulfonyl, may engage additional hydrophobic and π–π interactions within the NS2B/NS3 pocket (Kouretova et al., 2017; Mahalapbutr et al., 2025). The present study was designed to synthesize a series of 5-O- and 7-O-position luteolin derivatives and to evaluate their anti-DENV activities, cytotoxicity, and potential target engagement profiles. By addressing the objective, we aim to provide a structural basis for the rational optimization of flavonoid-based anti-DENV agents. 2.1Cells and virusVero cells (obtained from Yuanjing Biology, YC-A001) were verified by species-specific multiplex qPCR and verified negative for cross-contamination with other mammalian cell lines and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination. Vero cells were grown and maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA) at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Compounds were dissolved in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and diluted in culture medium before each assay, with the final DMSO concentration adjusted to ≤0.1% (v/v) in all treated cultures. papers.title_original: 7-O-sulfonation redirects luteolin’s target preference from furin to NS2B/NS3 and enhances anti-dengue activity

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how 7-O-sulfonation of luteolin affects its target preference and anti-dengue activity, addressing the need to develop more effective antiviral agents against dengue virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in Vero cells, which were grown and maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Each biological replicate included three technical replicates, and untreated cells were included as blank controls for normalization.
analysis.methods: The anti-DENV activity was evaluated using qRT-PCR to measure viral RNA abundance and plaque assays. Cytotoxicity was determined using the CCK8 method. Compounds were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and diluted in culture medium before each assay, with the final DMSO concentration adjusted to ≤0.1% (v/v). Experimental conditions were kept consistent across all antiviral assays to ensure comparability.
analysis.main_results: Compound 5, with a 4-fluorobenzenesulfonyl group at the 7-O position, showed the most potent anti-DENV activity (EC50 = 0.46 μM) and the highest selectivity index (SI = 28.5), representing an 18-fold increase in antiviral potency over luteolin. In enzymatic assays, compound 5 preferentially inhibited the viral NS2B/NS3 protease (Ki = 11.54 μM) over the host furin (Ki = 93 μM).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that 7-O-sulfonation redirected luteolin’s target preference from furin to NS2B/NS3, enhancing its anti-dengue activity. This represents a novel approach to modifying luteolin for improved antiviral efficacy.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that modifying luteolin through 7-O-sulfonation could lead to more effective antiviral agents against dengue virus, potentially informing future drug development and treatment strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used Vero cells as a model, which may not fully represent human dengue infection. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on in vitro assays and not in vivo or clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores how 7-O-sulfonation of luteolin alters its target preference and enhances anti-dengue activity. The researchers evaluated the anti-DENV activity of luteolin derivatives in Vero cells using qRT-PCR and plaque assays, alongside cytotoxicity measurements via the CCK8 method. Compound 5, with a 4-fluorobenzenesulfonyl group at the 7-O position, demonstrated the most potent anti-DENV activity (EC50 = 0.46 μM) and the highest selectivity index (SI = 28.5), showing an 18-fold increase in potency compared to luteolin. Enzymatic assays revealed that compound 5 preferentially inhibited the viral NS2B/NS3 protease (Ki = 11.54 μM) over the host furin (Ki = 93 μM). The authors interpreted that this modification redirected luteolin’s target preference, offering a novel strategy for improving antiviral efficacy. The study's findings may inform future drug development against dengue virus, though the results are based on in vitro experiments and may not fully translate to in vivo or clinical settings. The evidence is moderate due to the use of a cell culture model and the absence of clinical data.

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTBackground: Arboviruses in hospital environments may represent a neglected risk of nosocomial infections. This study investigated arboviruses in Aedes spp. larvae collected from a hospital area in Brasília, Federal District, Brazil. Methods: Eighteen ovitraps were deployed for 26 weeks. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTBackground: Arboviruses in hospital environments may represent a neglected risk of nosocomial infections. This study investigated arboviruses in Aedes spp. larvae collected from a hospital area in Brasília, Federal District, Brazil. Methods: Eighteen ovitraps were deployed for 26 weeks. Hatched Aedes spp. larvae were pooled weekly, and viral detection was performed by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR. Results: Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, Zika virus, and Chikungunya virus were identified, with an overall positivity rate of 30.76%. Conclusion: The surveillance strategy effectively detected arboviral RNA in a hospital setting, suggesting local arboviral circulation associated with the transmission triad.Keywords: Ovitrap, RT-qPCR, One Health, Epidemiological monitoring, Entomo-virological surveillance

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the presence of dengue virus and other arboviruses in Aedes larvae collected from a hospital environment in Brasília, Brazil. Over 26 weeks, 18 ovitraps were used to gather larvae, which were pooled weekly and tested by RT‐qPCR. Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, along with Zika and Chikungunya viruses, were detected, yielding a 30.76% overall positivity rate. The authors concluded that entomo‐virological surveillance can reveal arboviral circulation in healthcare settings, underscoring the potential for nosocomial transmission. They highlighted that combining larval surveillance with serological surveys of symptomatic patients can pinpoint early transmission hotspots, informing targeted public‐health interventions. No limitations were reported in the available evidence.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: Arboviruses in hospital environments may represent a neglected risk of nosocomial infections.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: Eighteen ovitraps were deployed for 26 weeks to collect Aedes spp. larvae in a hospital area of Brasília, Federal District, Brazil.
elements_en.methods: Larvae were pooled weekly and viral detection was performed by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR.
elements_en.main_results: Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, Zika virus, and Chikungunya virus were identified, with an overall positivity rate of 30.76%.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The surveillance strategy effectively detected arboviral RNA in a hospital setting, suggesting local arboviral circulation associated with the transmission triad.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Entomo-virological surveillance followed by serological active survey of symptomatic individuals is helpful to identify hotspots of early arbovirus transmission.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations.
