news.content: Featured Columns Shorts Podcasts Sterile Processing Burnout and Cognitive Overload: How Interruptions, IFUs, and Human Factors Affect Patient Safety Sterile processing professionals face constant interruptions, cognitive overload, increasingly complex devices, and hundreds of IFUs. Randalyn Harreld, CRCST, FHSPA, explains why health care organizations must address the human factors behind SPD performance rather than expecting frontline professionals to simply absorb ever-increasing complexity. From “Gotcha” to Coaching: Using RTLS to Improve Hand Hygiene In this podcast with ICT, Danielle Updegraff, MBA, BSN, RN, discusses real-time location systems, which can give infection prevention teams greater visibility into hand hygiene, workflow, and infectious disease exposures, but sustainable improvement still depends on staff engagement, leadership, education, and culture. AIDS 2026: Malawi Program Achieves 10-fold Reduction in HIV Positivity Among Exposed Infants In this complete interview, ICT speaks with Endale Tilahun, MD, MPH, about a Malawi community program that reduced missed HIV testing and achieved 0.2% positivity among exposed infants through household follow-up, individualized case management, and coordinated health and social support. Experts Call for Standardized Cleaning of Reusable Lead Aprons Environmental testing found bacterial contamination on many lead garments and described what lead garment cleaning technicians routinely encounter during servicing. McKnight, MHA, BSN, CRCST, CER, examines how infection prevention and sterile processing can identify process drift, assess disruptions, and strengthen shared oversight of medical device reprocessing. Artist and designer Matthew Caliman shares how personal loss inspired the Cleanup Crew, a handwashing education project using cartoon faucets, songs, and games to help families revisit an essential health message. Through a personal reflection on gaming, AI, and biological research, an infection preventionist explores why faster answers make human judgment, peer consultation, and accountability increasingly important. A study of 193,260 individuals found overlapping tick-borne antibody levels more frequently among those with Lyme antibodies, highlighting diagnostic challenges when active coinfections are not confirmed. A shifting mask or fogged eyewear can interrupt focus when precision matters most. Dana Weaver Storm, MHA, BSN, RN, examines the challenges of prolonged surgical mask use and how perioperative leaders can support comfort, visibility, and consistent adherence. What happens when one disinfectant cannot satisfy every IFU? At AHE in New Orleans, Diane Cullen discusses weighted risk assessment, documenting difficult decisions, and why infection prevention and EVS need to work together. Turnover pressure can leave critical OR cleaning steps unfinished. Karen deKay, MSN, RN, EBP-C, CNOR, CIC, FAPIC, examines common gaps in environmental hygiene and how shared responsibilities, attention to disinfectant contact time, and ongoing education can help teams strengthen practices between cases. A patient with fever and no recent travel could still have dengue. Florida’s local transmission highlights why clinicians and infection preventionists should look beyond travel history and recognize warning signs. High contact follow-up rates suggest progress, but who is being missed? Sterile processing professionals face constant interruptions, cognitive overload, increasingly complex devices, and hundreds of IFUs. Randalyn Harreld, CRCST, FHSPA, explains why health care organizations must address the human factors behind SPD performance rather than expecting frontline professionals to simply absorb ever-increasing complexity. Long-acting HIV therapies promise greater convenience, but fewer doses alone may not solve adherence or access challenges. Lloyd Bibby and Pooja Goyal, MS(Pharm), discuss patient choice, weekly oral and injectable therapies, health system capacity, equitable access, and the real-world measures that will define success. This week on Infection Control Today, the stories ranged from emerging drug-resistant pathogens circling the globe to a landmark decade of surface science—all against a backdrop of ongoing outbreaks and a hard look at what the profession owes its own workforce

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 16, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dengue-Carrying Mosquitoes Signal High Yellow Fever Risk in Northern Ghana Outbreak Zone by October 16, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Dengue-Carrying Mosquitoes Signal High Yellow Fever Risk in Northern Ghana Outbreak Zone Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram An extensive entomological investigation into the 2021 yellow fever outbreak in Ghana’s Savannah Region has revealed a landscape primed for arbovirus transmission, even though the mosquitoes collected during the response tested negative for the virus itself. The study, published in PLOS Global Public Health by a team of Ghanaian researchers led by Joseph Harold Nyarko Osei of the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, documents dense populations of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, an overwhelming dominance of the sylvatic subspecies Aedes aegypti formosus, and container-breeding conditions that placed the affected communities squarely above World Health Organization outbreak thresholds. The findings carry significant implications for how West African nations monitor and contain a virus that continues to erupt unpredictably across the continent. The outbreak that prompted the investigation was severe by any measure. Health authorities recorded 202 suspected cases, of which 70 were laboratory confirmed, with 35 deaths attributed to the disease. The case fatality rate among suspected cases stood at 17 percent, but among confirmed cases it reached a startling 50 percent, meaning that half of the people whose infections were confirmed by testing did not survive. Such mortality is consistent with the clinical course of yellow fever, a viral hemorrhagic disease that progresses from an initial febrile phase, in many severe cases, to a toxic phase marked by jaundice, organ failure, internal bleeding, and shock. The Savannah Region, one of Ghana’s newest administrative areas carved from the former Northern Region in 2019, had not previously been regarded as a yellow fever hotspot, and the sudden eruption of cases demanded an urgent, multidisciplinary response. A team assembled specifically for its expertise in yellow fever outbreak response was tasked with assessing the extent of vector activity and identifying practical measures to contain or control the rapid spread of the virus. The entomological component of that response formed the backbone of the published study. In arbovirus epidemiology, entomological investigations serve a dual purpose: they quantify the density and distribution of competent vectors, which determines the force of transmission, and they attempt to isolate virus from field-caught mosquitoes, which provides direct evidence of ongoing transmission. The team employed a combination of larval surveys and adult mosquito collections designed to capture the full picture of vector abundance across the affected communities. The larval survey was exhaustive. Investigators examined 12,264 potential breeding containers in and around houses, a scale of surveillance that speaks to the density of water-holding receptacles in the surveyed settlements. From these containers, they recovered 3,885 larvae and 1,186 pupae distributed across 173 positive containers, yielding a container positivity rate of 1.26 percent. Of the 1,001 houses surveyed, 130 harbored larvae or pupae, a house positivity rate of 12.99 percent. These raw counts were converted into the classical World Health Organization larval indices: the House Index, the Container Index, the Breteau Index, and the Pupal Demographic Index. Collectively, these metrics assess the risk of arbovirus transmission, with established thresholds separating low-risk from high-risk conditions. The indices recorded in the Savannah Region exceeded the levels generally regarded as indicative of epidemic risk, meaning that the density of Aedes breeding was sufficient to sustain and amplify viral transmission had competent, infected mosquitoes been present in sufficient numbers. Morphological identification of the immature stages followed standard taxonomic criteria. The larvae were recognized by their short and stout siphons, the breathing tubes characteristic of Aedes species, which distinguish them from the longer, more slender siphons of Culex larvae. Pupae were identified by the short but distinctly serrated spicules along the paddle fringe and by the branched, fanlike seta 9-VIII bearing six to seven branches, anatomical characters that allow entomologists to separate Aedes pupae from those of other medically important culicines. Such morphological work remains the practical foundation of outbreak entomology in resource-limited settings, where molecular identification of every specimen is rarely feasible and where rapid, accurate triage of mosquitoes determines how sampling proceeds. The composition of the breeding containers offered a revealing portrait of peridomestic risk. Plastic containers accounted for the largest share, 6,529 receptacles or 46.95 percent of those examined, followed by metallic containers at 6,024, or 43.32 percent. Clay jars contributed 753 receptacles, or 5.42 percent, while discarded tires made up 565, or 4.06 percent, and open wells the remaining 34, or 0.24 percent. This distribution reflects the water storage practices common in rural northern Ghana, where households store water in a variety of containers that, if left uncovered or allowed to collect rainwater, become ideal developmental sites for Aedes aegypti. Plastic and metallic containers dominate the profile, underscoring how modern materials have multiplied breeding opportunities in communities where water supply is intermittent and storage is essential. Discarded tires, long recognized as among the most productive Aedes habitats worldwide, added another layer of risk. Adult mosquito collections added a crucial dimension to the assessment. The team deployed BG-Sentinel traps, a design that uses visual cues and chemical attractants to lure host-seeking Aedes, and supplemented these with oral aspirators, hand-held suction devices that collect mosquitoes resting on walls and other surfaces, and Prokopack aspirators, motorized backpack units that allow rapid collection from elevated indoor and outdoor resting sites. A total of 1,571 adult mosquitoes were identified in the collections. The species composition was striking: 35 were Aedes aegypti aegypti, the domesticated subspecies that prefers to feed on humans and breeds in human-made containers, while 619 were Aedes aegypti formosus, the wild, sylvatic form that typically feeds on non-human hosts in forest cycles. The remaining 917 specimens were Culex species, vectors of filariasis and West Nile virus but not primary yellow fever vectors. Outdoor collections overwhelmingly outnumbered indoor ones, accounting for 86.4 percent of the adult catch against 13.6 percent indoors. The dominance of Aedes aegypti formosus is arguably the study’s most significant entomological finding. The formosus subspecies is the ancestral, feral form of the yellow fever vector, adapted to breeding in tree holes and feeding on primates and other wild animals in the sylvatic cycle, the forest transmission loop in which the yellow fever virus circulates between monkeys and canopy-dwelling mosquitoes. Yet formosus populations in West Africa are known to occupy a transitional ecological role: they colonize peridomestic containers, feed opportunistically on humans when wild hosts are scarce or when humans encroach on forest edges, and can therefore act as bridge vectors, carrying virus from sylvatic reservoirs into human populations. The authors suggest that this subspecies may have been the driver of the outbreak and of yellow fever transmission in the Savannah Region, a hypothesis consistent with the pattern seen in several recent African epidemics where spillover from sylvatic cycles into unvaccinated rural communities ignited explosive human-to-mosquito-to-human amplification. Despite the abundance of vectors, the virological screening came back empty. All mosquitoes collected during the investigation were tested by real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction for four arboviruses: yellow fever, dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. The assay’s detection limit of fewer than 10 RNA copies per reaction meant that even very low-level infections would likely have been detected. No arbovirus was found in any specimen. This negative result does not contradict the outbreak; rather, it reflects the practical realities of arbovirus field investigation. Adult mosquito collections typically take place after the peak of transmission, once control measures, case isolation, and insecticide spraying have reduced both vector density and infection prevalence. Infection rates in wild mosquito populations during endemic transmission are often on the order of one infected individual per thousand or fewer, so capturing an infected mosquito requires collecting very large numbers of adults, something a short outbreak-response survey can rarely achieve. The absence of virus in the sampled mosquitoes therefore reinforces, rather than undermines, the study’s central conclusion drawn from the vector indices: that conditions in the region posed a high risk of arbovirus transmission. The wider context sharpens the public health urgency of these findings. Yellow fever, dengue, Zika, and chikungunya are among the most consequential emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases on the planet, and by recent estimates half the world’s population lives at risk of infection by the viruses that mosquitoes of the Aedes complex transmit. Recent African epidemics have confirmed 19,569 cases with 820 deaths, a toll that underscores both the persistence of sylvatic yellow fever reservoirs and the vulnerability of communities with incomplete vaccination coverage. The Savannah Region outbreak, with its 50 percent case fatality rate among confirmed cases, fits a familiar pattern: a rural population with low immunity, abundant vectors, and proximity to sylvatic transmission cycles. The study’s authors argue that the entomological evidence, dominated by Aedes aegypti formosus breeding above epidemic thresholds, poses a continuing public health threat that demands robust Aedes mosquito surveillance systems and sustained vector control strategies, including source reduction of plastic and metallic water-storage containers, larviciding of productive habitats, and vaccination campaigns to close the immunity gap. Without such measures, the region remains primed for the next spillover. The team deployed BG-Sentinel traps, a design that uses visual cues and chemical attractants to lure host-seeking Aedes, and supplemented these with oral aspirators, hand-held suction devices that collect mosquitoes resting on walls and other surfaces, and Prokopack aspirators, motorized backpack units that allow rapid collection from elevated indoor and outdoor resting sites. A total of 1,571 adult mosquitoes were identified in the collections. The species composition was striking: 35 were Aedes aegypti aegypti, the domesticated subspecies that prefers to feed on humans and breeds in human-made containers, while 619 were Aedes aegypti formosus, the wild, sylvatic form that typically feeds on non-human hosts in forest cycles. The remaining 917 specimens were Culex species, vectors of filariasis and West Nile virus but not primary yellow fever vectors. Outdoor collections overwhelmingly outnumbered indoor ones, accounting for 86.4 percent of the adult catch against 13.6 percent indoors. The dominance of Aedes aegypti formosus is arguably the study’s most significant entomological finding. The formosus subspecies is the ancestral, feral form of the yellow fever vector, adapted to breeding in tree holes and feeding on primates and other wild animals in the sylvatic cycle, the forest transmission loop in which the yellow fever virus circulates between monkeys and canopy-dwelling mosquitoes. Yet formosus populations in West Africa are known to occupy a transitional ecological role: they colonize peridomestic containers, feed opportunistically on humans when wild hosts are scarce or when humans encroach on forest edges, and can therefore act as bridge vectors, carrying virus from sylvatic reservoirs into human populations. The authors suggest that this subspecies may have been the driver of the outbreak and of yellow fever transmission in the Savannah Region, a hypothesis consistent with the pattern seen in several recent African epidemics where spillover from sylvatic cycles into unvaccinated rural communities ignited explosive human-to-mosquito-to-human amplification. Despite the abundance of vectors, the virological screening came back empty. All mosquitoes collected during the investigation were tested by real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction for four arboviruses: yellow fever, dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. The assay’s detection limit of fewer than 10 RNA copies per reaction meant that even very low-level infections would likely have been detected. No arbovirus was found in any specimen. This negative result does not contradict the outbreak; rather, it reflects the practical realities of arbovirus field investigation. Adult mosquito collections typically take place after the peak of transmission, once control measures, case isolation, and insecticide spraying have reduced both vector density and infection prevalence. Infection rates in wild mosquito populations during endemic transmission are often on the order of one infected individual per thousand or fewer, so capturing an infected mosquito requires collecting very large numbers of adults, something a short outbreak-response survey can rarely achieve. The absence of virus in the sampled mosquitoes therefore reinforces, rather than undermines, the study’s central conclusion drawn from the vector indices: that conditions in the region posed a high risk of arbovirus transmission. The wider context sharpens the public health urgency of these findings. Yellow fever, dengue, Zika, and chikungunya are among the most consequential emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases on the planet, and by recent estimates half the world’s population lives at risk of infection by the viruses that mosquitoes of the Aedes complex transmit. Recent African epidemics have confirmed 19,569 cases with 820 deaths, a toll that underscores both the persistence of sylvatic yellow fever reservoirs and the vulnerability of communities with incomplete vaccination coverage. The Savannah Region outbreak, with its 50 percent case fatality rate among confirmed cases, fits a familiar pattern: a rural population with low immunity, abundant vectors, and proximity to sylvatic transmission cycles. The study’s authors argue that the entomological evidence, dominated by Aedes aegypti formosus breeding above epidemic thresholds, poses a continuing public health threat that demands robust Aedes mosquito surveillance systems and sustained vector control strategies, including source reduction of plastic and metallic water-storage containers, larviciding of productive habitats, and vaccination campaigns to close the immunity gap. Without such measures, the region remains primed for the next spillover. analysis.time: The study was conducted in response to the 2021 yellow fever outbreak in the Savannah Region of Ghana, with the publication date being October 16, 2026. The investigation was carried out in 2021, and the findings were published in 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred in the Savannah Region of Ghana, a newly formed administrative area since 2019. The affected communities included households and settlements where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes were prevalent, particularly Aedes aegypti formosus, which is associated with sylvatic cycles.
analysis.event: An extensive entomological investigation was conducted to assess the risk of arbovirus transmission, including yellow fever, in the Savannah Region of Ghana. The study found that the mosquito populations were above WHO outbreak thresholds, indicating a high potential for viral spread, though the mosquitoes tested negative for yellow fever virus.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Health authorities recorded 202 suspected cases, with 70 laboratory-confirmed cases and 35 deaths. The case fatality rate was 17% among suspected cases and 50% among confirmed cases. The study identified 12,264 breeding containers, with 1.26% being positive for Aedes larvae and pupae, and 12.99% of houses harboring these mosquitoes.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The investigation was part of a multidisciplinary response to the outbreak. The study documented the entomological findings and their implications for monitoring and containing the virus. However, the mosquitoes tested negative for yellow fever virus, and the study focused on the risk factors rather than confirming active transmission.

analysis.brief_en: In October 2026, an entomological investigation into the 2021 yellow fever outbreak in Ghana’s Savannah Region revealed high mosquito breeding activity, though the mosquitoes tested negative for the yellow fever virus. The study, led by Joseph Harold Nyarko Osei of the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, found that 12,264 potential breeding containers were examined, with 1.26% being positive for Aedes larvae and pupae. Of the 1,001 houses surveyed, 12.99% harbored these mosquitoes, indicating a significant risk for arbovirus transmission. Health authorities reported 202 suspected cases, 70 confirmed, and 35 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 50% among confirmed cases. The outbreak prompted an urgent, multidisciplinary response, including the use of BG-Sentinel traps, oral aspirators, and Prokopack aspirators to collect adult mosquitoes. The findings highlight the role of Aedes aegypti formosus in the sylvatic cycle and the risk posed by modern water storage practices in rural areas. The study underscores the need for improved surveillance and containment strategies in regions with limited vaccination coverage.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 16, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dengue Deaths Hide in Unconfirmed Cases, 13-Year Philippine Surveillance Study Reveals by October 16, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Dengue Deaths Hide in Unconfirmed Cases, 13-Year Philippine Surveillance Study Reveals Check Symptoms Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A sweeping 13-year analysis of dengue surveillance data from Davao City, Philippines, has revealed a striking paradox at the heart of routine disease monitoring: while laboratory-confirmed dengue cases rose significantly over time, the vast majority of recorded dengue deaths occurred among patients who were never laboratory-confirmed at all. The study, published in Frontiers in Tropical Diseases, examined 81,075 dengue notifications reported through the Philippine Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (PIDSR) system between January 2012 and December 2024, and found that the three surveillance case classifications—suspected, probable, and confirmed—each told a distinctly different story about the epidemic unfolding in this major southern Philippine city. Dengue remains one of the most formidable public health challenges in tropical and subtropical regions. The mosquito-borne viral disease ranges in clinical presentation from a self-limiting febrile illness to severe disease marked by plasma leakage, hemorrhage, organ dysfunction, and death. In 2024 alone, more than 13 million dengue cases and over 8,700 dengue-related deaths were reported globally. The Philippines ranks among the most affected countries in Southeast Asia, where cyclical outbreaks continue to strain healthcare and public health systems. Yet interpreting long-term dengue trends has always been complicated by changes in case definitions, reporting practices, and the availability of laboratory confirmation—factors that can reshape the apparent epidemiological landscape without any true change in transmission. The research team, led by Alfredo A. Hinay Jr. of the University of the Immaculate Conception in Davao, conducted a retrospective observational study using the official citywide surveillance database coordinated by the City Epidemiology and Surveillance Unit. In the Philippine system, dengue is a nationally notifiable disease, and healthcare providers must report cases meeting national surveillance definitions. The three-tier classification system distinguishes suspected cases—previously healthy individuals with acute febrile illness of two to seven days duration and clinical signs consistent with dengue—from probable cases, which additionally show a positive dengue IgM antibody test, and confirmed cases, which require positive results from viral culture isolation, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or dengue NS1 antigen testing. Each tier represents a different level of diagnostic certainty, and each captured a different slice of the epidemic. Donate to Research Discover more Check Symptoms Find Grief Support deaths Deaths death Of the 81,075 notifications analyzed after data cleaning, 59,021 were classified as suspected cases, 20,559 as probable cases, and only 1,495 as confirmed cases. Suspected cases therefore dominated the surveillance record throughout the entire 13-year period, accounting for nearly three-quarters of all notifications. Demographically, the burden fell hardest on children: individuals younger than 15 years represented 59.4 percent of suspected cases, 61.4 percent of probable cases, and 62.7 percent of confirmed cases. Males comprised a slightly higher proportion of notifications than females across all classifications, ranging from 51.2 to 52.2 percent. Hospital admission was reported in more than 90 percent of notifications across every classification, indicating that patients classified at all levels of diagnostic certainty received comparable clinical attention within the healthcare system. Buy First Aid Kits The temporal analysis, performed using the Mann–Kendall trend test—a non-parametric method for detecting monotonic trends in time-series data that does not require assumptions of normality—produced the study’s most consequential finding. Confirmed dengue incidence increased significantly over the study period (p = 0.003), while probable dengue incidence remained stable with no significant trend (p = 0.855), and suspected dengue incidence showed a decreasing, though not statistically significant, tendency (p = 0.059). In other words, the same city, the same virus, and the same surveillance system produced three divergent trend lines depending solely on how cases were classified. Had the analysis been restricted to laboratory-confirmed cases alone, observers would have concluded that dengue was steadily worsening; had it relied on suspected cases, the conclusion might have been one of gradual improvement. Discover more Buy First Aid Kits Read Security News Protect Privacy The increasing trend in confirmed dengue incidence proved remarkably consistent across every stratum examined. All three congressional districts of Davao City showed significant upward trends—Congressional District I (p = 0.005), Congressional District II (p = 0.016), and Congressional District III (p = 0.002)—and the increase was significant among both children under 15 (p = 0.005) and adults aged 15 or older (p = 0.014), as well as among both females (p = 0.005) and males (p = 0.003). This uniformity suggests that the rise in confirmed cases was not confined to particular neighborhoods or demographic groups but reflected a broad, citywide phenomenon. The authors attribute such increases in other dengue-endemic settings to a combination of changing transmission dynamics, expanded availability of diagnostic testing, improvements in laboratory capacity, and enhanced surveillance practices. Notably, the Department of Health only formally recognized positive NS1 antigen test results as a criterion for laboratory-confirmed dengue in 2024, so its influence on the long-term trend is likely limited, though it may have shaped the distribution of classifications in the final year. Check Symptoms The COVID-19 pandemic casts a long shadow over any interpretation of these trends. Consistent with reports from other dengue-endemic countries, dengue notifications in Davao City declined during the pandemic, likely reflecting movement restrictions, school closures, altered healthcare-seeking behavior, and disruptions to routine surveillance and healthcare services. The subsequent increase following the relaxation of public health measures may represent a post-pandemic rebound driven by resumed population mobility, renewed opportunities for virus transmission, and improved case detection. However, the authors emphasize that the increasing trend in laboratory-confirmed dengue remained evident beyond the immediate post-pandemic period, suggesting the pattern cannot be explained solely by pandemic effects. Perhaps the most sobering finding concerns mortality. Dengue mortality incidence showed no significant temporal trends in any classification—suspected (p = 0.089), probable (p = 0.242), or confirmed (p = 0.282)—yet the distribution of deaths across classifications was deeply asymmetric. Probable cases exhibited the highest cumulative case fatality rate at 0.85 percent (rising to 0.89 percent among admitted patients), followed by confirmed cases at 0.67 percent, and suspected cases at just 0.26 percent. Because suspected and probable cases vastly outnumbered confirmed ones, they accounted for the overwhelming majority of deaths recorded among reported dengue notifications. Among non-admitted patients, case fatality rates were low across all classifications, and no deaths were recorded among non-admitted confirmed notifications. The pattern suggests that diagnostic certainty and clinical severity do not necessarily align: patients may die of clinically compatible dengue without ever receiving the laboratory test that would place them in the confirmed category. The authors caution that routine passive surveillance systems carry inherent biases, including underreporting, delayed reporting, and misclassification. Patients with more severe presentations may have been more likely to undergo confirmatory testing and thus be classified as probable or confirmed, while those with milder illness or limited access to laboratory services may have remained classified as suspected. The study also could not clinically validate deaths recorded within the surveillance system, evaluate alternative diagnoses, or determine the extent to which individual deaths were directly attributable to dengue infection. Without an external reference standard, surveillance performance measures such as sensitivity and positive predictive value could not be assessed. These limitations temper but do not erase the central conclusion. For low- and middle-income countries, where dengue surveillance systems frequently operate under constraints related to diagnostic availability and laboratory capacity, the implications are substantial. Analyses restricted exclusively to confirmed cases may underestimate severe outcomes recorded within routine surveillance systems, since probable and suspected cases accounted for most deaths despite stable incidence trends over time. The authors argue that surveillance classifications beyond laboratory-confirmed dengue continue to provide meaningful epidemiological information about disease burden and severe outcomes in resource-constrained settings. As dengue continues its global expansion driven by urbanization, population growth, climate variability, and expanding mosquito habitats, the Davao City experience offers a cautionary lesson: the picture of an epidemic depends profoundly on where in the diagnostic pipeline one chooses to look, and public health decisions built on a single classification may miss the deaths that matter most. analysis.time: The study analyzed dengue surveillance data from January 2012 to December 2024, with the publication date being October 16, 2026. The temporal analysis revealed trends in confirmed dengue incidence over the study period, with significant increases observed in 2024.
analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on Davao City, Philippines, examining 81,075 dengue notifications. The population affected included individuals of all ages, with children under 15 representing the largest proportion of suspected, probable, and confirmed cases.
analysis.event: A 13-year surveillance study in Davao City, Philippines, revealed that while laboratory-confirmed dengue cases increased, the majority of dengue deaths occurred among unconfirmed cases. The study highlighted the impact of case classification on interpreting dengue trends and mortality.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In 2024, over 13 million dengue cases and more than 8,700 dengue-related deaths were reported globally. In Davao City, suspected cases dominated the surveillance record, accounting for nearly 75% of all notifications. The cumulative case fatality rate was highest for probable cases (0.85%) and confirmed cases (0.67%), with suspected cases having the lowest (0.26%).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted using the official citywide surveillance database and the PIDSR system. The authors emphasized that the increasing trend in laboratory-confirmed dengue incidence remained evident beyond the pandemic period, suggesting the pattern is not solely due to pandemic effects. The study's findings are based on retrospective observational data.

analysis.brief_en: A 13-year surveillance study in Davao City, Philippines, revealed a striking paradox in dengue monitoring: while laboratory-confirmed cases increased, the majority of dengue deaths occurred among unconfirmed cases. The study, published in Frontiers in Tropical Diseases, analyzed 81,075 dengue notifications from 2012 to 2024, finding that suspected cases dominated the records, accounting for nearly 75% of all notifications. The three-tier classification system—suspected, probable, and confirmed—produced divergent trends, with confirmed cases showing a significant upward trend (p = 0.003) and suspected cases showing a slight decline. Mortality rates were highest among probable cases (0.85%) and confirmed cases (0.67%), with suspected cases having the lowest (0.26%). The authors attribute the rise in confirmed cases to improved diagnostic testing, expanded laboratory capacity, and enhanced surveillance practices. The study also noted that the decline in dengue notifications during the COVID-19 pandemic was likely due to movement restrictions and altered healthcare-seeking behavior, but the increase in confirmed cases persisted beyond the pandemic, indicating broader trends in dengue transmission and detection.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, October 20, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology IgM antibodies curb Zika and dengue enhancement in laboratory studies by October 20, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 IgM antibodies curb Zika and dengue enhancement in laboratory studies Study Biology Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A recombinant IgM monoclonal antibody reduced antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of Zika virus infection across a panel of IgG antibodies in laboratory assays, including at concentrations below those required for viral neutralization. A second pentameric IgM antibody produced a similar, though less uniform, effect against Zika virus and all four dengue virus serotypes. The findings indicate that reducing IgG-driven enhancement may be a function of IgM antibodies that is partly distinct from neutralization, but the experiments did not test protection in animals or people. ADE occurs when antibodies increase rather than reduce viral infection by promoting uptake of virus particles into Fc-gamma receptor-bearing cells. The phenomenon is well documented in dengue and has been implicated in severe disease during secondary infections. It has also been observed in laboratory studies of Zika virus, whose E-glycoprotein antibodies can enhance infection of monocytes, macrophages and other cells. The clinical importance of enhancement during Zika infection remains uncertain, although evidence from pregnant non-human primates, mice and ex vivo human placentas has led researchers to consider whether it could contribute to placental infection and vertical transmission. Study Biology For the current study, investigators used DH1017.IgM, a native pentameric IgM antibody isolated 71 days after symptom onset from a pregnant woman who had Zika infection and subsequently delivered a healthy baby. The antibody recognizes a discontinuous quaternary epitope on the Zika virus envelope E-protein dimer, spanning domain II and the interface between domains I and II. Its potent neutralization depends on its multimeric structure. Researchers proposed two possible binding arrangements: an umbrella-like configuration in which the pentamer contacts several E dimers on one virion, and a planar configuration in which it cross-links multiple virions. Earlier work estimated that only three such IgM molecules could bind simultaneously to one virion in the umbrella-like arrangement, leaving part of the recognized epitope space available to other antibodies. Study Biology Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Compare Lab Gear Bioengineering careers guide The researchers first examined whether IgG monoclonal antibodies and DH1017.IgM would compete for binding to intact Zika virus particles. A panel of 14 characterized IgG antibodies targeted several regions of the envelope protein, including domain I, domain II, domain III, the fusion loop, the domain I/III linker and the E-dimer epitope 1. Two antibodies were excluded from reciprocal competition assays because they could not compete with their own labeled versions. The competition was incomplete in both directions. Some IgG antibodies displaced DH1017.IgM, while DH1017.IgM efficiently outcompeted several others, but even at saturating concentrations it generally did not eliminate IgG binding. Six of the 12 antibodies tested reduced DH1017.IgM binding by more than 75%, whereas only three blocked more than 75% of IgG binding with DH1017.IgM. This partial overlap is consistent with the large footprint of multivalent IgM and suggests that it can alter how many IgG molecules bind a virion without occupying every potentially accessible epitope. Study Biology These binding effects did not come at the expense of neutralization. When DH1017.IgM was combined with neutralizing or non-neutralizing Zika IgG antibodies in assays using GFP-expressing Zika reporter virus particles, its expected neutralizing activity remained intact. Combinations of DH1017.IgM with neutralizing IgG antibodies also tracked the increasing neutralization produced by the IgG alone. A control IgM antibody that did not recognize Zika did not alter the IgG neutralization profiles. The results therefore indicate that the cross-competition between IgM and IgG did not produce an obvious detrimental effect on either antibody class’s capacity to reduce viral infectivity. Discover more Earth’s Earth Science The more pronounced effect appeared in assays of ADE, in which antibodies were tested with Fc-gamma receptor-expressing K562 cells. At a fixed concentration corresponding to its reporter-virus neutralization midpoint, DH1017.IgM lowered peak IgG-mediated enhancement by an average of 2.7-fold, with reductions ranging from 1.8- to 3.8-fold. It did not simply shift the concentration at which peak enhancement occurred. Reversing the assay design and holding each IgG antibody at its peak enhancement concentration showed that DH1017.IgM reduced enhancement in a dose-dependent manner. Concentrations of 100 nanograms per milliliter or lower completely abrogated enhancement across the tested antibodies, regardless of which envelope epitope they recognized. The concentration required to reduce enhancement by 50% had a mean of 2.1 nanograms per milliliter and ranged from 0.4 to 9.1 nanograms per milliliter. Comparisons with neutralization potency showed that the enhancement-reducing action was not simply a consequence of virus neutralization. For most antibodies tested, DH1017.IgM reduced enhancement at sub-neutralizing concentrations, defined in the study by a ratio of the 50% enhancement-reduction concentration to the 50% reporter-virus neutralization concentration of no more than 0.75. Ratios ranged from 0.18 for the E-dimer epitope 1 antibodies C8 and C10 to 0.68 for the domain II antibody MZ20. The fusion-loop antibody 2A10G6 narrowly missed the threshold at 0.78 and showed substantial variation between replicates. A second recombinant IgM, C8.IgM, also reduced IgG-driven Zika enhancement in a dose-dependent fashion and did so at sub-neutralizing concentrations for six of 11 tested antibodies. Its profile differed from that of DH1017.IgM, showing that the effect depends on the particular IgM–IgG pairing rather than being a uniform property of all IgM antibodies. Study Biology Discover more Bioengineering News Subscription Bioengineering Career Guide Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Because C8 also recognizes dengue virus, the investigators extended its testing to dengue reporter virus particles representing serotypes 1 through 4. C8.IgM reduced enhancement mediated by six tested IgG antibodies for every dengue serotype, although the potency varied with both the IgG antibody and the serotype. It reduced enhancement at sub-neutralizing concentrations in 16 of 24 antibody–serotype combinations. This pattern was consistent for three antibodies—MZ20, C10 and the IgG version of C8—across all four serotypes. The antibody was generally less effective against IgG antibodies targeting the fusion loop. For example, the enhancement-reduction to neutralization ratio for 4G2 ranged from 1.2 for dengue 1 to 5.11 for dengue 2, indicating that concentrations sufficient to neutralize the virus were required to substantially reduce enhancement in those combinations. DH1017.IgM was also tested against unfractionated sera from a controlled human Zika infection study. Participants received either the SJRP/2016-184 or Nicaragua/2016 Zika strain, with nine and 10 infected participants respectively, while seven additional individuals received placebo. At 90 days after infection, sera from all 19 infected participants produced measurable enhancement of a heterologous Zika strain in vitro, whereas placebo sera did not. Adding DH1017.IgM reduced serum-mediated enhancement in a dose-dependent manner. The mean concentration required for 50% reduction was 6.2 nanograms per milliliter for the SJRP cohort and 6.0 nanograms per milliliter for the Nicaragua cohort, with no statistically significant difference between groups. DH1017.IgM reduced enhancement at sub-neutralizing concentrations in 16 of 19 sera, or 84.2% of the tested samples. The authors interpret the findings as evidence that IgM antibodies can mitigate IgG-mediated ADE through mechanisms that are probably multifactorial. Altered antibody-binding stoichiometry may contribute, but the strongest reductions also occurred with IgG antibodies whose epitopes were not efficiently displaced by DH1017.IgM, implying that additional mechanisms remain to be defined. The results support further investigation of multivalent IgM biologics for Zika and dengue, including possible effects on placental infection and vertical transmission. They do not establish clinical benefit. All experiments were conducted in vitro or ex vivo, without animal or human efficacy testing, and the activity of DH1017.IgM will be difficult to separate from its exceptionally potent neutralization in vivo. The work therefore identifies a measurable antibody function and a basis for further study, rather than demonstrating that an IgM treatment can prevent severe dengue, Zika disease or fetal harm. analysis.time: The study was conducted and reported by October 20, 2026, with the publication date being October 20, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study involved laboratory assays using Zika virus and dengue virus serotypes, with participants infected with either the SJRP/2016-184 or Nicaragua/2016 Zika strain, and seven individuals receiving placebo.
analysis.event: A recombinant IgM monoclonal antibody, DH1017.IgM, was isolated from a pregnant woman who had Zika infection and was found to reduce antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of Zika virus infection in laboratory assays, including at concentrations below those required for viral neutralization. The study also tested a second IgM antibody, C8.IgM, against dengue virus serotypes.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study showed that DH1017.IgM reduced ADE by an average of 2.7-fold, with reductions ranging from 1.8- to 3.8-fold. It also demonstrated that the effect depends on the specific IgM–IgG pairing rather than being a uniform property of all IgM antibodies. The clinical importance of enhancement during Zika infection remains uncertain.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The findings are based on laboratory assays and do not demonstrate that an IgM treatment can prevent severe dengue, Zika disease, or fetal harm.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on October 20, 2026, by Bioengineer.org reports that a recombinant IgM monoclonal antibody, DH1017.IgM, isolated from a pregnant woman with Zika infection, reduced antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of Zika virus in laboratory assays. The antibody was tested against a panel of IgG antibodies and showed a significant reduction in ADE, with an average of 2.7-fold decrease. The study also examined a second IgM antibody, C8.IgM, which demonstrated similar effects against dengue virus serotypes. However, the research did not assess protection in animals or humans, and the clinical significance of these findings remains unclear. The results suggest that IgM antibodies may have a distinct role in reducing ADE, independent of neutralization, but further studies are needed to confirm their efficacy in real-world scenarios. The study involved participants infected with either the SJRP/2016-184 or Nicaragua/2016 Zika strain, with seven individuals receiving placebo. The findings highlight a potential therapeutic avenue for managing ADE in flaviviruses but do not provide evidence for preventing severe dengue or Zika disease.
analysis.summary_en: A study published on October 20, 2026, by Bioengineer.org reports that a recombinant IgM monoclonal antibody, DH1017.IgM, isolated from a pregnant woman with Zika infection, reduced antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of Zika virus in laboratory assays. The antibody was tested against a panel of IgG antibodies and showed a significant reduction in ADE, with an average of 2.7-fold decrease. The study also examined a second IgM antibody, C8.IgM, which demonstrated similar effects against dengue virus serotypes. However, the research did not assess protection in animals or humans, and the clinical significance of these findings remains unclear. The results suggest that IgM antibodies may have a distinct role in reducing ADE, independent of neutralization, but further studies are needed to confirm their efficacy in real-world scenarios. The study involved participants infected with either the SJRP/2016-184 or Nicaragua/2016 Zika strain, with seven individuals receiving placebo. The findings highlight a potential therapeutic avenue for managing ADE in flaviviruses but do not provide evidence for preventing severe dengue or Zika disease.

analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The findings are based on laboratory assays and do not demonstrate that an IgM treatment can prevent severe dengue, Zika disease, or fetal harm.

news.title_zh: IgM抗体抑制寨卡病毒和登革热增强作用——Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A study published on October 20, 2026, by Bioengineer.org reports that a recombinant IgM monoclonal antibody, DH1017.IgM, isolated from a pregnant woman with Zika infection, reduced antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of Zika virus in laboratory assays. The antibody was tested against a panel of IgG antibodies and showed a significant reduction in ADE, with an average of 2.7-fold decrease. The study also examined a second IgM antibody, C8.IgM, which demonstrated similar effects against dengue virus serotypes. However, the research did not assess protection in animals or humans, and the clinical significance of these findings remains unclear. The results suggest that IgM antibodies may have a distinct role in reducing ADE, independent of neutralization, but further studies are needed to confirm their efficacy in real-world scenarios. The study involved participants infected with either the SJRP/2016-184 or Nicaragua/2016 Zika strain, with seven individuals receiving placebo. The findings highlight a potential therapeutic avenue for managing ADE in flaviviruses but do not provide evidence for preventing severe dengue or Zika disease.
news.content_zh: 一项于2026年10月20日由Bioengineer.org发表的研究报告称,一种从寨卡病毒感染孕妇体内分离出的重组IgM单克隆抗体DH1017.IgM,在实验室检测中减少了寨卡病毒的抗体依赖性增强(ADE)作用。该抗体在与一系列IgG抗体的对比测试中显示出显著的ADE减少效果,平均减少了2.7倍。研究还测试了第二种IgM抗体C8.IgM,其对登革病毒型病毒也表现出类似效果。然而,该研究并未评估其在动物或人体中的保护作用,这些发现的临床意义尚不明确。研究结果表明,IgM抗体可能在减少ADE方面具有独特作用,且不依赖于中和作用,但需要进一步研究以确认其在实际场景中的有效性。该研究涉及感染了SJRP/2016-184或尼加拉瓜/2016型寨卡病毒的参与者,其中七人接受了安慰剂。这些发现指出了针对黄病毒属病毒ADE管理的潜在治疗途径,但并未提供预防重症登革热或寨卡病的证据。

supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Destination Đà Nẵng Da Nang proactively prevents dengue fever starting from residential areas. DANANG - The increasing number of dengue cases in localities, along with the pressure on hospital treatment, indicates that dengue fever is becoming more complex as Da Nang enters the rainy season. To prevent widespread transmission, relevant forces are proactively monitoring the area and coordinating with local health facilities to strengthen disease prevention efforts. Báo Đà Nẵng•21/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Cam Le Ward Health Station organizes mosquito spraying at the dengue fever outbreak site. Photo: Huu Trung Stay close to the local area and control risks. Upon receiving information about dengue fever cases in the area, Neighborhood Group 8 (Cam Le Ward) coordinated with functional forces to assess the situation, guide patients to medical facilities, and organize environmental sanitation and mosquito control spraying in the affected area. Ms. Vo Thi Len, Deputy Head of Neighborhood Group 8, shared that receiving information early from residents helps the local authorities coordinate with medical forces to promptly handle the risk of spread. Besides monitoring the disease situation, the neighborhood committee regularly encourages households to check water containers, remove items that collect water, and actively participate in environmental sanitation campaigns to eliminate mosquito larvae and pupae. [ VIDEO ] - Community officials share information about residents' awareness of dengue fever prevention: In September 2026, Cam Le ward recorded 71 cases of dengue fever and 7 small outbreaks. The ward's health station intensified surveillance in high-risk areas and coordinated with neighborhood groups to implement comprehensive disease prevention and control measures. Ms. Nguyen Thi Tuyet, the officer in charge of disease prevention and control at the Cam Le Ward Health Station, said that information on cases is continuously updated through the Ministry of Health 's infectious disease surveillance system and feedback from residential groups. Upon detecting a case, health authorities coordinate with local governments to inform the public about the situation, guide people on disease prevention, and handle the outbreak according to regulations. Health station staff in Cam Le ward, along with local residents, inspect and remove mosquito breeding grounds. Photo: TRAM ANH You may also like The campaign to eliminate mosquito larvae is also integrated into the "Green, Clean, and Beautiful Sunday" program. Along with encouraging residents to collect waste and remove mosquito breeding grounds, the local authorities are intensifying propaganda through the electronic information portal, the Cam Le News fanpage, and community meetings. As a result, environmental sanitation is maintained regularly, instead of being only dealt with passively when cases of disease appear. Community-based monitoring helps the health sector proactively grasp the situation, identify high-risk areas, and implement timely response measures. However, for effective disease prevention, environmental sanitation and the elimination of mosquito larvae and pupae need to be maintained regularly, not just when cases have already occurred in the area. Coordinate disease prevention efforts at the grassroots level. In fact, hospitals have also recorded an increase in the number of children with dengue fever. Dr. Nguyen Hai Thinh, Head of the Tropical Medicine Department ( Da Nang Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital), said that the number of children with dengue fever in the department has increased by about 30-50% compared to the previous month, with an average of 5-10 cases admitted each day. Among the pediatric patients being treated at the hospital, there was a 9-year-old child from Hoi An Tay ward who was admitted with blood concentration, thrombocytopenia, and blood pressure disorders, requiring intensive treatment. Doctors note that dengue fever can become complicated even after the patient's fever subsides. Therefore, people need to monitor their health, seek timely medical attention if they suspect they have the disease, and follow the instructions of healthcare professionals. Many dengue fever cases have become severe and require treatment at Da Nang Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital. Photo: TRAM ANH Da Nang is entering the rainy season, creating favorable conditions for disease-carrying mosquitoes to breed and multiply. The health sector predicts that the number of cases may continue to rise if disease prevention and control measures are not consistently maintained. According to the Da Nang City Center for Disease Control, in the first nine months of 2026, the city recorded 4,251 cases of dengue fever and 283 outbreaks, representing increases of 2.4 times and 3.9 times respectively compared to the same period in 2025. Test results showed that 39 out of 56 samples tested positive for Dengue virus type 2 (DENV-2), accounting for nearly 70% of the samples tested. This is one of the virus types that can cause severe illness and requires attention in surveillance and treatment. In response to this situation, the Da Nang City Center for Disease Control focused on advising on solutions for monitoring, detecting, and handling outbreaks early; coordinating with the health sector to improve the quality of examination and treatment, ensuring timely referrals; and strengthening communication to help people recognize disease symptoms and proactively prevent infection. In this context, community-based monitoring is particularly important. Information from neighborhood committees, feedback from residents, and infectious disease surveillance data help health authorities understand the situation, identify risk areas, and implement appropriate response measures. You may also like Mr. Nguyen Dai Vinh, Director of the Da Nang City Center for Disease Control, emphasized that although a dengue fever vaccine is now available, controlling the mosquitoes that transmit the disease remains the core measure. People need to cover water containers tightly, check flower vases and bottles, remove items that collect water, and proactively take measures to prevent mosquito bites. In areas where outbreaks occur, specialized forces will deploy efforts to eliminate mosquito larvae and pupae, combined with spraying chemicals to kill mosquitoes when necessary. According to Mr. Vinh, dengue prevention cannot wait until someone is infected to take action. Regularly cleaning the environment and eliminating mosquito breeding grounds is the most practical measure to limit the risk of disease spread in the community. (WINK) — Dengue fever cases are rising in Florida, with a new hotspot emerging in Pinellas County. The Florida Department of Health reports a total of 368 cases of locally-acquired dengue this year across seven counties as of Thursday. The majority are in Hillsborough County, but the latest data shows Pinellas County is becoming a new area of concern. "We're still seeing an increase in those numbers, especially in the Hillsborough and now actually the Pinellas area," said Jenifer McBride, communication director for Lee County Mosquito Control District. Mosquito experts say they haven't seen localized cases like this since the 1930s. Right now, there are no locally-acquired dengue fever cases reported in any Southwest Florida counties. The mosquito-borne virus can cause aches, nausea and rashes, though it is rarely deadly. McBride explained how the disease spreads from one area to another. "This mosquito... it only travels from backyard to backyard. It doesn't go very far," McBride said. "What we're seeing now is that as humans move, they're moving it around counties." For months, Lee County Mosquito Control has been helping fight the outbreak with education and larvacide sprays across county lines. McBride emphasized that the actual number of cases is likely much higher than reported. "368 may not seem like a lot of people, but the reality is, this virus only 80% of people are actually symptomatic," McBride said. "So, for us, we know that number is actually much higher." Preston Gosa, a Lee County neighbor and mobile mechanic, has lived in Florida for decades and served 40 years in the army. He said he's familiar with mosquito-borne diseases from his time in service. "Been 40 years in the army. I've been to every mosquito-infested place with malaria, and the disease you're talking about is getting bad," Gosa said. As a mobile mechanic, Gosa sees common breeding grounds for mosquitos at people's homes. He pointed out items that collect standing water as major contributors to mosquito populations. "I've been around a lot of people's houses because I go to their house to work on vehicles. I've seen a lot of old tires laying around, anything buckets, any containers that are left outside, and you see the water stagnant," Gosa said. "It's a breeding field for it." Mosquito experts say dumping standing water is key to stopping the spread. McBride offered simple advice for residents to help control mosquito populations. "What I suggest is once a week, just take a walk around your backyard," McBride said. "We're going to get this under control. We just need everybody's help," McBride said. supplementary_news.content: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Ten News Network About Us Ten News Network Journey Ten News Network Family Advertise with us Contact Us Careers More Publisher - Ten News Network Home National Business Tech Education Entertainment Lifestyle Features Ten News Hindi Delhi Noida Greater Noida Yamuna Expressway Area More Posts Categories Tags Home Health Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa reports 100 dengue cases in 24 hours Health Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa reports 100 dengue cases in 24 hours On Oct 21, 2026 Share Islamabad, Oct 20 (IANS) Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province has reported around 100 new dengue cases in the past 24 hours, the highest number reported in a single day in 2026, local media reported on Tuesday. The total number of dengue cases in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2026 rose to 4,091 after 99 new cases were reported, according to a report by the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response System (IDSRS), leading Pakistani daily Dawn reported. According to the report by IDSRS, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has 144 dengue cases while 3,946 people have recovered from the disease. October has proved challenging for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as the province has been reporting a rise in dengue cases, especially in Kohat, which is in the grip of a dengue outbreak. Kohat has reported 80 cases since October 1, followed by Bannu with 24 and Peshawar with 18. The health department has been taking measures to control and prevent the spread of dengue in Kohat, where a sharp increase in cases has placed pressure on hospitals. Meanwhile, Pakistan’s Islamabad has reported 42 dengue cases since January, with authorities making efforts to prevent the spread of the disease by identifying hotspots and high-risk areas. As many as 32 cases were reported in rural areas, while 10 were reported in urban areas of Islamabad from January 1 to October 16, according to the data. Anti-dengue teams carried out 382,452 surveillance and control activities in Islamabad in October, Dawn reported. According to officials, the teams identified and eliminated 7,669 sites with mosquito larvae during the operations conducted in October. The teams visited 10,084 places, while indoor vector-surveillance teams carried out inspections at 72,305 houses to identify possible breeding sites as part of the hotspot surveillance campaign, as per the report. Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV), which is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Prevention and control of dengue rely on vector control, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO) statement. There is no specific treatment for dengue/severe dengue, and early detection and access to proper medical care greatly lower fatality rates of severe dengue. –IANS akl/as Share FacebookTwitterGoogle+ReddItWhatsAppPinterest Email TenNews Team 121449 posts 0 comments Prev Post Flights remain disrupted as airlines face risk due to Middle East conflict Next Post Qualcomm to begin global job cuts from November amid push for stronger performance culture Comments are closed. (James Gathany/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention via AP, File) By Michael Cuglietta | mcuglietta@orlandosentinel.com | Orlando Sentinel PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026 at 1:57 PM EDT | UPDATED: October 21, 2026 at 3:11 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... A person in Seminole County is the latest in Central Florida to have contracted dengue fever, according to health officials who are urging Central Florida residents to take precautions against mosquito-borne illnesses. The Florida Department of Health in Seminole County issued the advisory Wednesday. It comes following five cases of dengue fever reported in Orange County since the beginning of September. Orange announced on Tuesday that it resumed aerial spraying to reduce mosquito populations in an effort to contain the spread of the virus. The Department of Health and Seminole County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance, prevention and control efforts, according to their advisory. Dengue fever, found in tropical and subtropical climates, including southern parts of the United States, is transmitted to humans through mosquito bites. Each year about 400 million people worldwide contract dengue, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For decades, most continental U.S. infections had been found among people who caught the virus while traveling internationally. But experts say the Aedes aegypti mosquito has been expanding its geographic reach because of climate change. Dengue is not fatal. Symptoms, which usually occur within two weeks of being bitten, include aches and pains, nausea, vomiting and rashes, according to the CDC. Florida is suffering a statewide outbreak of the disease, with the Tampa Bay area alone seeing 351 confirmed cases this year, according to the state, mostly in Hillsborough County. Overall, it’s the most cases in a calendar year for any state since at least the 1940s. Residents are advised to avoid being bitten by using insect repellent when going outdoors and removing standing water from their properties, since that is where mosquitoes breed. Orange on Tuesday conducted aerial spraying over Apopka and Pine Hills, two areas where dengue cases were reported. The county will conduct another round of spraying over the same areas at 7pm on Saturday. The spraying is expected to reduce the targeted mosquito population by 99%, officials said. Residents are also being asked to report any dead birds they find to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s site, as they can be an indicator of mosquito-borne illnesses. The Associated Press contributed to this report. supplementary_news.content: EPAPER LIVE TV DAWNNEWS URDU Images Herald Aurora CityFM89 Advertise Events Supplements Careers Obituaries Dawn E-Paper | October 22, 2026 Home Latest US-Iran War Pakistan Opinion Business Images Prism World Sport Breathe Magazines Tech Videos Popular Archive Flood Donations Home Latest US-Iran War Pakistan Opinion Business Images Prism World Sport Breathe Magazines Tech Videos Popular Archive Flood Donations Search Search Subscribe to notifications Get the latest news and updates from Dawn Not Now Allow Notifications KP records 100 dengue cases in 24 hours Ashfaq Yusufzai Published October 20, 2026 Updated 2 days ago Email Story Your Name * Recipient Email * Send Email Cancel 0 This file photo shows a dengue mosquito. — AFP/File comments Join our Whatsapp Channel PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Monday recorded around 100 new dengue cases in the last 24 hours, the highest daily tally this year, as the province continues to pass through the high-risk month of October. Recently, one person, a resident of Tank, died of the mosquito-borne disease in the Dera Ismail Khan district. According to a report by the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response System (IDSRS), the provincial tally of dengue this year reached 4,091 after 99 new cases were reported. Kohat is leading with 2,567 cases, followed by Peshawar with 566, Bannu 192, Khyber 120, Haripur 112, Charsadda 75, Abbottabad 71, Nowshera 51, Karak 43, Mansehra 38, Dera Ismail Khan 35, Swabi 28 and Mohmand 14. Other districts recorded single-digit cases. Health dept says measures being taken for dengue control, prevention October has proved challenging, especially in Kohat, which is in the grip of a dengue outbreak. The district has recorded 80 cases since October 1, followed by Bannu with 24 and Peshawar with 18. The report said the health department was carrying out measures to control and prevent dengue in Kohat where a sharp rise in cases had put pressure on hospitals. It said currently, the province had 144 dengue cases, while 3,946 patients had recovered from the disease. Experts said the situation remained better than last year when dengue affected more than 6,000 people, including over 1,000 in Charsadda, following an outbreak in a few union councils. They said this year, Kohat had emerged as a new hotspot, with the reasons for the high number of cases already identified by the health department. The experts, however, said the coming weeks remained crucial as conditions favourable for mosquito breeding could lead to further infections. They added that the government prepared a dengue prevention plan every year and that the 2026 action plan had been issued on time, allowing field activities to begin early in the year. The experts, however, said the recent rise in cases in some districts was largely attributable to a lack of coordination among government departments, which needed to work together at the district, tehsil and union council levels to devise micro-plans for containing the disease. They said testing patients, confirming diagnoses and treating dengue cases were the health department’s responsibilities, while measures such as insecticidal spraying, eliminating stagnant water and ensuring an uninterrupted electricity supply fell within the remit of other government departments. The experts said a few weeks ago, the health department asked the district administrations in Kohat, Mansehra and Haripur to level the ground and fill ditches where rainwater accumulated, creating mosquito breeding sites. They said mosquitoes were the carriers and transmitters of the dengue virus. The experts said the health department had been implementing the dengue action plan since 2017, updating it every year with changes to the previous version. The experts said coordination among government departments and public awareness campaigns remained its main pillars, meant to reduce the incidence of dengue and ultimately eliminate the recurring public health threat in the province. They said around a decade ago, dengue struck Peshawar severely, killing dozens of people and infecting more than 50,000 others.
