supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, October 20, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology IgM antibodies curb Zika and dengue enhancement in laboratory studies by October 20, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 IgM antibodies curb Zika and dengue enhancement in laboratory studies Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A recombinant IgM monoclonal antibody reduced antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of Zika virus infection across a panel of IgG antibodies in laboratory assays, including at concentrations below those required for viral neutralization. A second pentameric IgM antibody produced a similar, though less uniform, effect against Zika virus and all four dengue virus serotypes. The findings indicate that reducing IgG-driven enhancement may be a function of IgM antibodies that is partly distinct from neutralization, but the experiments did not test protection in animals or people. ADE occurs when antibodies increase rather than reduce viral infection by promoting uptake of virus particles into Fc-gamma receptor-bearing cells. The phenomenon is well documented in dengue and has been implicated in severe disease during secondary infections. It has also been observed in laboratory studies of Zika virus, whose E-glycoprotein antibodies can enhance infection of monocytes, macrophages and other cells. The clinical importance of enhancement during Zika infection remains uncertain, although evidence from pregnant non-human primates, mice and ex vivo human placentas has led researchers to consider whether it could contribute to placental infection and vertical transmission. For the current study, investigators used DH1017.IgM, a native pentameric IgM antibody isolated 71 days after symptom onset from a pregnant woman who had Zika infection and subsequently delivered a healthy baby. The antibody recognizes a discontinuous quaternary epitope on the Zika virus envelope E-protein dimer, spanning domain II and the interface between domains I and II. Its potent neutralization depends on its multimeric structure. Researchers proposed two possible binding arrangements: an umbrella-like configuration in which the pentamer contacts several E dimers on one virion, and a planar configuration in which it cross-links multiple virions. Earlier work estimated that only three such IgM molecules could bind simultaneously to one virion in the umbrella-like arrangement, leaving part of the recognized epitope space available to other antibodies. The researchers first examined whether IgG monoclonal antibodies and DH1017.IgM would compete for binding to intact Zika virus particles. A panel of 14 characterized IgG antibodies targeted several regions of the envelope protein, including domain I, domain II, domain III, the fusion loop, the domain I/III linker and the E-dimer epitope 1. Two antibodies were excluded from reciprocal competition assays because they could not compete with their own labeled versions. The competition was incomplete in both directions. Some IgG antibodies displaced DH1017.IgM, while DH1017.IgM efficiently outcompeted several others, but even at saturating concentrations it generally did not eliminate IgG binding. Six of the 12 antibodies tested reduced DH1017.IgM binding by more than 75%, whereas only three blocked more than 75% of IgG binding with DH1017.IgM. This partial overlap is consistent with the large footprint of multivalent IgM and suggests that it can alter how many IgG molecules bind a virion without occupying every potentially accessible epitope. These binding effects did not come at the expense of neutralization. When DH1017.IgM was combined with neutralizing or non-neutralizing Zika IgG antibodies in assays using GFP-expressing Zika reporter virus particles, its expected neutralizing activity remained intact. Combinations of DH1017.IgM with neutralizing IgG antibodies also tracked the increasing neutralization produced by the IgG alone. A control IgM antibody that did not recognize Zika did not alter the IgG neutralization profiles. The results therefore indicate that the cross-competition between IgM and IgG did not produce an obvious detrimental effect on either antibody class’s capacity to reduce viral infectivity. The more pronounced effect appeared in assays of ADE, in which antibodies were tested with Fc-gamma receptor-expressing K562 cells. At a fixed concentration corresponding to its reporter-virus neutralization midpoint, DH1017.IgM lowered peak IgG-mediated enhancement by an average of 2.7-fold, with reductions ranging from 1.8- to 3.8-fold. It did not simply shift the concentration at which peak enhancement occurred. Reversing the assay design and holding each IgG antibody at its peak enhancement concentration showed that DH1017.IgM reduced enhancement in a dose-dependent manner. Concentrations of 100 nanograms per milliliter or lower completely abrogated enhancement across the tested antibodies, regardless of which envelope epitope they recognized. The concentration required to reduce enhancement by 50% had a mean of 2.1 nanograms per milliliter and ranged from 0.4 to 9.1 nanograms per milliliter. Comparisons with neutralization potency showed that the enhancement-reducing action was not simply a consequence of virus neutralization. For most antibodies tested, DH1017.IgM reduced enhancement at sub-neutralizing concentrations, defined in the study by a ratio of the 50% enhancement-reduction concentration to the 50% reporter-virus neutralization concentration of no more than 0.75. Ratios ranged from 0.18 for the E-dimer epitope 1 antibodies C8 and C10 to 0.68 for the domain II antibody MZ20. The fusion-loop antibody 2A10G6 narrowly missed the threshold at 0.78 and showed substantial variation between replicates. A second recombinant IgM, C8.IgM, also reduced IgG-driven Zika enhancement in a dose-dependent fashion and did so at sub-neutralizing concentrations for six of 11 tested antibodies. Its profile differed from that of DH1017.IgM, showing that the effect depends on the particular IgM–IgG pairing rather than being a uniform property of all IgM antibodies. Because C8 also recognizes dengue virus, the investigators extended its testing to dengue reporter virus particles representing serotypes 1 through 4. C8.IgM reduced enhancement mediated by six tested IgG antibodies for every dengue serotype, although the potency varied with both the IgG antibody and the serotype. It reduced enhancement at sub-neutralizing concentrations in 16 of 24 antibody–serotype combinations. This pattern was consistent for three antibodies—MZ20, C10 and the IgG version of C8—across all four serotypes. The antibody was generally less effective against IgG antibodies targeting the fusion loop. For example, the enhancement-reduction to neutralization ratio for 4G2 ranged from 1.2 for dengue 1 to 5.11 for dengue 2, indicating that concentrations sufficient to neutralize the virus were required to substantially reduce enhancement in those combinations. DH1017.IgM was also tested against unfractionated sera from a controlled human Zika infection study. Participants received either the SJRP/2016-184 or Nicaragua/2016 Zika strain, with nine and 10 infected participants respectively, while seven additional individuals received placebo. At 90 days after infection, sera from all 19 infected participants produced measurable enhancement of a heterologous Zika strain in vitro, whereas placebo sera did not. Adding DH1017.IgM reduced serum-mediated enhancement in a dose-dependent manner. The mean concentration required for 50% reduction was 6.2 nanograms per milliliter for the SJRP cohort and 6.0 nanograms per milliliter for the Nicaragua cohort, with no statistically significant difference between groups. DH1017.IgM reduced enhancement at sub-neutralizing concentrations in 16 of 19 sera, or 84.2% of the tested samples. The authors interpret the findings as evidence that IgM antibodies can mitigate IgG-mediated ADE through mechanisms that are probably multifactorial. Altered antibody-binding stoichiometry may contribute, but the strongest reductions also occurred with IgG antibodies whose epitopes were not efficiently displaced by DH1017.IgM, implying that additional mechanisms remain to be defined. The results support further investigation of multivalent IgM biologics for Zika and dengue, including possible effects on placental infection and vertical transmission. They do not establish clinical benefit. All experiments were conducted in vitro or ex vivo, without animal or human efficacy testing, and the activity of DH1017.IgM will be difficult to separate from its exceptionally potent neutralization in vivo. The work therefore identifies a measurable antibody function and a basis for further study, rather than demonstrating that an IgM treatment can prevent severe dengue, Zika disease or fetal harm. supplementary_news.content: News Space Sports Restaurants Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCAL Dengue fever returns to Brevard Jim Waymer Florida Today Oct. 16, 2026, 3:43 p.m. ET A locally-acquired case of dengue fever has been confirmed in Brevard County, Florida. Health officials are increasing surveillance, prevention efforts, and targeted mosquito treatments. Residents are advised to take precautions to avoid mosquito bites, especially at dawn and dusk. Dengue fever is back in Brevard. The Florida Department of Health in Brevard County announced Friday, Oct. 16, a confirmed human case of locally-acquired dengue. "DOH-Brevard andBrevard County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts byenhanced monitoring for mosquitoes and diseases as well as targeted mosquito treatment and overnight spraying to reduce the risk of disease transmission," state health officials said in a release. What is dengue? Dengue (break-bone fever) is a viral infection that spreads from mosquitoes to people. It is more common in tropical and subtropical climates, according to the World Health Organization. About one in four people infected with dengue get sick, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Dengue can present "as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash. Usually, there are no respiratory symptoms." Symptoms appear within 15 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. State health offficials continue to conduct statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses, including West Nile virus infections, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria, chikungunya, and dengue. Residents of Florida are encouraged to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s site. Florida health officials warned early last month about risks to Brevard County residents from rabies and the West Nile virus. Several sentinel chickens within the county have recently tested positive for West Nile virus, triggering a health advisory. Health officials urge the public to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes by taking basic precautions, such as avoiding being outdoors at dawn and dusk, using mosquito repellants and/or wearing long-sleaves and pants to cover the skin. Brevard County led the state in locally transmitted dengue fever cases in 2025 and remains under a health alert for mosquito-borne diseases. At least 35 of the state's 62 dengue cases caught in Florida in 2025 were in Brevard, which also had two travel-related dengue cases. The locally caught cases have puzzled experts who are trying to figure out why a disease typically found in the tropics is spreading for the fist time in and from Brevard. This year, there have been some 300 cases of dengue in Hillsborough County. Brevard also still under rabies alert On Sept. 3, state health officials issued a 60-day rabies alert in Brevard in response to a confirmed case of the viral infection in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. supplementary_news.content: News Space Sports Restaurants Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Florida dengue cases up to 368. Counties under alerts, advisories Sarah Perkel Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 16, 2026, 9:58 a.m. ET More than 360 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report. The report for the period from Oct. 4 through Oct. 10 says that "368 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from eight counties" in 2026. More than 360 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report. The report for the period from Oct. 4 through Oct. 10 says that "368 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from eight counties" in 2026. From Oct. 4 through Oct. 10 alone, 72 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. Hillsborough County, home of Tampa, saw 310 of the 252 reported dengue cases this year. Miami-Dade County saw nine cases, Orange County saw five, Palm Beach County saw one, Pasco County saw four, Pinellas County saw 37, Polk County saw one and Broward County saw one. Dengue is also known as dengue fever or breakbone fever, the latter due to the pain it can cause. It can present as "a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain," along with fever and "sometimes" a rash, according to the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade County. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not contagious, and is transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts As of Oct. 10, Bay, Brevard, Broward, Holmes, Leon, Manatee, Martin, Palm Beach, Polk and Walton counties are under mosquito-borne illness advisories. Alachua, Duval, Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Pasco and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts. Dengue still surging in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 10, there have been 368 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported from eight counties, which is up from 296 reported Oct. 3. There have also been seven positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 368 cases 310 in Hillsborough County 37 in Pinellas County 9 in Miami-Dade County 5 in Orange County 4 in Pasco County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: 7 cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County How to best prevent mosquito-borne illnesses In June, Miami-Dade County encouraged residents to "take proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water." That's the best protection against "container-breeding mosquitoes," said a press release by the county, which are the "likeliest species to transmit the viruses that cause dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever," illnesses that are among those most commonly transmitted by mosquitoes. Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. "As little as one teaspoon or bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to breed and multiply," according to a flyer provided by the FDOH. As for individual protection, mosquito repellent can help prevent bites while outdoors, especially between "dusk and dawn," when mosquitoes are most active. The county also suggests: Covering entrances to one's home, including windows and doors, with mesh screens. Wearing clothes with long sleeves and pant legs to "maximize skin protection." Regularly cleaning rain gutters to avoid water pooling within them. Filling up indentations in one's lawn, air conditioner drain areas and tree holes. Regularly replacing water in outdoor pet dishes and birdbaths. Requesting a mosquito inspection via the county’s online portal. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Drone-integrated biosensor detects dengue antigen in five seconds by October 21, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Drone-integrated biosensor detects dengue antigen in five seconds Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A lightweight drone fitted with a gold-nanoparticle biosensor detected dengue virus antigen in human serum with a reported limit of detection of 0.91 micrograms per milliliter and a visible test-line signal within five seconds. The prototype combines a lateral-flow assay, a compact unmanned aerial vehicle, image analysis based on YOLOv5 and a QR-code-linked reporting system. Researchers characterized the sensor in laboratory tests and limited field conditions, rather than demonstrating autonomous surveillance during a dengue outbreak. In the assay, dengue antigen separated a DNA aptamer from its gold-nanoparticle conjugate, allowing the released nanoparticles to bind immobilized lysozyme and produce a red band visible to the naked eye. The study was designed as a proof-of-concept for decentralized dengue screening. Its central idea is to carry a small diagnostic strip to a location that can be reached by drone, perform the test near the collection point and transmit the result through a digital workflow. The platform used a DJI Mini 3 Pro weighing less than 249 grams, with dimensions of 251 by 362 by 70 millimetres, an intelligent-flight battery capacity of 2,453 milliampere-hours and a stated top speed of 16 metres per second in S mode under sea-level, no-wind conditions. The lateral-flow strip was attached to the drone with a double-sided adhesive and enclosed in translucent Plexiglas to protect it during flight. A QR code placed on the aircraft opened a reporting webpage through which a user could transmit results to laboratory personnel. At the biochemical core of the system is a 34-base DNA aptamer designed to recognize polyvalent dengue antigen. Researchers synthesized gold nanoparticles by reducing chloroauric acid with trisodium citrate, then mixed 24 microlitres of aptamer with 500 microlitres of the nanoparticle suspension at a pH of 9.2 to 9.6. After incubation, bovine serum albumin was added as a blocking agent, and the conjugate was washed, resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline and stored at 4 degrees Celsius. Zeta-potential analysis gave the unmodified particles a mean surface charge of minus 37.56 millivolts, consistent with strong electrostatic repulsion and colloidal stability. Dynamic light scattering measured an average hydrodynamic diameter of 11.59 nanometres, while transmission electron microscopy gave a particle diameter of 12.43 plus or minus 0.20 nanometres. The particles were well dispersed and spherical. Discover more Bioengineering careers guide Bioengineering News Subscription Bioengineering Career Guide Learn Engineering Track Biotech Aptamer attachment altered the nanoparticles in ways that were consistent with successful functionalization. Their surface-plasmon-resonance band shifted from 521 to 526 nanometres after conjugation, accompanied by a decrease in absorbance, indicating a change in the local environment around the gold surface. Dynamic light scattering also recorded an increase in hydrodynamic diameter to 17.11 nanometres, which the authors attributed to the aptamer coating rather than aggregation. The investigators characterized the interaction between the aptamer and dengue antigen through molecular docking and an electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Docking produced a score of minus 326.89, which the authors interpreted as strong predicted binding affinity, although a ligand root-mean-square deviation of 66.33 angstroms indicated considerable conformational flexibility or imperfect structural alignment after docking. In the mobility assay, the conjugate shifted relative to the free aptamer, as did the aptamer–antigen complex, supporting the formation of the intended molecular complexes. The lateral-flow sensor used a sample pad, conjugate pad, nitrocellulose membrane and absorbent pad mounted in a plastic cassette. A 70-microlitre sample was applied to the pad and moved by capillary action. When dengue antigen was present, it bound the aptamer and promoted release of the gold nanoparticles from the complex. The free nanoparticles then reached a test line containing immobilized lysozyme and formed a visible red signal. In the absence of dengue antigen, the gold–aptamer complex remained associated and did not produce the test-line band. During a separate verification using 80-microlitre samples, dengue antigen and phosphate-buffered saline controls were run at room temperature for 30 seconds. Of three tested stages—free nanoparticles, gold–aptamer conjugate and gold–aptamer–dengue antigen complex—only the complete three-component stage generated a signal. Scanning electron microscopy showed the porous and fibrous structures of the strip components and the deposition of biomaterial on the test line. Discover more Tour Colleges Earth’s Earth The researchers optimized the pH and aptamer loading before evaluating analytical performance. The gold nanoparticles performed well at pH 7, while increasing the amount of aptamer initially strengthened the test-line signal before reaching a plateau or modest decline at higher loadings. The investigators attributed that downturn to steric hindrance or excessive surface capping, which could impede the release of nanoparticles required by the competitive assay format. Strips were then tested across dengue-antigen concentrations from 1 to 100 micrograms per milliliter. Test-band intensity rose with concentration, and ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy was used to examine the associated changes in nanoparticle dispersion. Densitometric analysis with ImageJ produced a calibration coefficient of determination of 0.994 within the working range, allowing the authors to describe the assay as suitable for semiquantitative antigen measurement. Each concentration was tested in seven replicates for the intensity analysis. The reported limit of detection was calculated as three times the standard deviation of the response divided by the slope of the calibration curve, using seven observations. It was 0.91 micrograms per milliliter, and the study’s highlights state that a visible result could be obtained within five seconds. Recovery tests produced values of 92.79% and 105.96%, with relative standard deviations of 1.61% and 2.33%. Student’s t-values of 0.850 and 0.442 were below the critical value of 2.447 for six degrees of freedom at a two-tailed 0.05 significance level. In separate repeatability measurements, the reported intra-day mean was 112.41% plus or minus 1.18%, with an RSD of 1.05%, while the inter-day mean was 113.32% plus or minus 1.45%, with an RSD of 1.28%. These are analytical assay results rather than measurements of accuracy against a broad clinical population. Selectivity experiments tested chikungunya virus and hepatitis C virus at 1 microgram per milliliter, the lowest dengue-antigen concentration used in the reported comparison. Neither produced a test-line signal, supporting specificity for the intended target under the conditions tested. The researchers also evaluated three independently collected human-serum samples, each tested in triplicate, and observed dengue signals in spiked serum. A commercial gold-standard lateral-flow kit was used for comparison, although the supplied article does not provide a detailed clinical agreement table. The human-serum work was approved by the Jamia Hamdard Institutional Ethics Committee, and participants provided written informed consent. The study nevertheless involved a small set of specimens, so the serum results support feasibility rather than establishing performance across diverse patients or a validated clinical diagnosis. Automated image analysis was added to reduce dependence on subjective visual interpretation. The YOLOv5 small model was used first to locate the predefined result window, not to diagnose patients. On a 47-image working set, the region-of-interest localization achieved a mean average precision at an intersection-over-union threshold of 0.5 of about 0.995 and a value across thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 of about 0.945. A separate linear support-vector-machine classifier assessed positive or negative strips. Its 25-image test set contained 18 positive and seven negative images, producing six true negatives, one false positive, no false negatives and 18 true positives. Reported accuracy was 96.00%, sensitivity 100.00%, specificity 85.71%, precision 94.74% and F1 score 97.30%, with a reported ROC-AUC and average precision of 1.000. The authors cautioned that the reconstructed image dataset was small and that historical independence of the training and test sets could not be guaranteed, making these results preliminary model-development performance rather than independent clinical validation. The reporting layer, called the Delhi Against Dengue platform, links a QR code to a mobile webpage showing the result, a unique barcode for an electronic prescription and summary counts of positive and negative reports. It also presents dengue information and graphs of reported trends from 2020 to 2024. This digital element is designed to support communication with clinicians and laboratory authorities, but the platform’s surveillance value was not established through a prospective outbreak trial. The authors identify several constraints to operational use: drone flight endurance of roughly 20 to 30 minutes, payload limits, adverse-weather sensitivity, communication range and bandwidth, crash risk, and aviation, privacy and security requirements in populated or sensitive areas. Large multicenter clinical studies, environmental robustness tests, field trials, regulatory clearance and optimized hardware would be needed before deployment. The demonstrated result is therefore a technically characterized drone-integrated diagnostic prototype, while autonomous outbreak surveillance, real-time epidemiological mapping and large-scale remote deployment remain future objectives. Subject of Research: Proof-of-concept drone-integrated lateral-flow biosensor for dengue antigen detection Article Title: Intelligent drone-based biosensor for the detection of dengue virus antigen towards smart unmanned aerial-vehicle platform-based virus diagnosis Article References: Hasan, M. R., Khan, S., Naithani, D., Sharma, P., Mehta, Y., Ansari, S., kumar, S., Naikoo, U. M., Baliyan, A., Abbas, M., Parayangat, M., Kalathil, S., & Narang, J. (2026). Intelligent drone-based biosensor for the detection of dengue virus antigen towards smart unmanned aerial-vehicle platform-based virus diagnosis. Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology, 14, Article 1907197. https://doi.org/10.3389/fbioe.2026.1907197 Image Credits: AI Generated DOI: 10.3389/fbioe.2026.1907197 Keywords: dengue virus, biosensor, lateral-flow assay, gold nanoparticles, DNA aptamer, unmanned aerial vehicle, YOLOv5, point-of-need testing, digital reporting, Intelligent, drone-based, detection News Source: Kristina Jarvis. The demonstrated result is therefore a technically characterized drone-integrated diagnostic prototype, while autonomous outbreak surveillance, real-time epidemiological mapping and large-scale remote deployment remain future objectives. supplementary_news.content: KU Leuven Home News On Campus Research News Policy News Public Debate Media Resources Staff Resources More EN Nederlands English Home Content 2026 Promising antiviral drug candidate against dengue gets new opportunity for further development Promising antiviral drug candidate against dengue gets new opportunity for further development Mosnodenvir, a promising Phase 2a-tested oral antiviral against dengue with demonstrated antiviral activity in humans, is ready to move into a new phase of development. All rights to mosnodenvir have been transferred back to KU Leuven. As a next step, KU Leuven and the Centre for Drug Design and Discovery (CD3) aim to identify partners to build on more than a decade of research and extensive preclinical and clinical studies with mosnodenvir. https://nieuws.kuleuven.be/en/content/2026/promising-antiviral-drug-candidate-against-dengue-gets-new-opportunity-for-further-development-1 https://nieuws.kuleuven.be/en/content/2026/promising-antiviral-drug-candidate-against-dengue-gets-new-opportunity-for-further-development-1/@@images/image-1200-9bd22d2dba9e467f6fcf4deaa7a507d1.jpeg Promising antiviral drug candidate against dengue gets new opportunity for further development 20 Oct 2026 Mosnodenvir, a promising Phase 2a-tested oral antiviral against dengue with demonstrated antiviral activity in humans, is ready to move into a new phase of development. All rights to mosnodenvir have been transferred back to KU Leuven. As a next step, KU Leuven and the Centre for Drug Design and Discovery (CD3) aim to identify partners to build on more than a decade of research and extensive preclinical and clinical studies with mosnodenvir. In a new study published this week in The New England Journal of Medicine, professor Anna Durbin (Johns Hopkins University) and colleagues report findings that further demonstrate the efficacy for mosnodenvir against dengue infections, including its potential for once-weekly dosing. Since there are no antiviral drugs against dengue, mosnodenvir may address a major unmet global health need. Dengue is a major and growing global health threat, with an estimated 400 million infections and 100 million people developing dengue disease each year. Close to 4 billion people in over 129 countries are at risk. There is no antiviral drug to prevent or treat dengue, leaving a major unmet global health need. Mosnodenvir is an orally available small-molecule antiviral with equipotent activity against all four dengue virus serotypes. Mosnodenvir is the first antiviral drug candidate with proven activity against dengue in humans; as demonstrated in a Phase 2a human challenge study published in 2025 in The New England Journal of Medicine. New clinical findings, also published in The New England Journal of Medicine, further strengthen the evidence for mosnodenvir, including its potential for once-weekly dosing. Mosnodenvir has been dosed to about 900 people, it is safe and well tolerated. The rights to this advanced drug candidate are returned to KU Leuven allowing mosnodenvir its further development. A promising drug for a growing global health challenge Dengue is one of the world's fastest-growing infectious disease threats with approximately 400 million infections each year. While the greatest burden remains in tropical and subtropical regions, locally acquired dengue cases have also increased in Europe in recent years, particularly in southern Europe. Climate change creates increasingly favourable conditions for the mosquitoes that transmit the virus. Yet there is still no specific antiviral treatment or prophylactic drug available for dengue. Mosnodenvir may help fill that gap. The oral small-molecule antiviral originated from joint research efforts from the Laboratory of Virology and Antiviral Research at the Rega Institute and drug discovery experts at the Centre for Drug Design and Discovery (CD3) of KU Leuven with financial support from Wellcome. The programme was subsequently advanced by a global pharmaceutical company and underwent extensive preclinical and clinical development. In a Phase 2a controlled human infection study [Durbin et al., The New England Journal of Medicine (2025)] treatment with mosnodenvir significantly reduced the number of infected individuals and lowered dengue virus levels in those who were infected, compared with placebo-treated participants. New clinical findings reported by Prof. Anna Durbin (Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health) and colleagues confirm the dose-dependent antiviral activity of daily mosnodenvir and extend these findings to once-weekly dosing [Van Wesenbeeck et al., The New England Journal of Medicine (2026)]. More than 900 people received mosnodenvir in studies to date, with no safety concerns identified. When we started this research more than 10 years ago, there was no guarantee we would ever get this far. Seeing a molecule that originated in our laboratory demonstrate antiviral activity in people, even following once weekly dosing, is exactly why we keep searching for new ways to tackle infectious diseases. Prof. Johan Neyts of the KU Leuven Rega Institute An opportunity to take an advanced programme forward The rights to the programme have recently reverted to KU Leuven, creating a new opportunity to take this advanced drug candidate forward. Together with Wellcome, we are now seeking a partner with the expertise and capacity to continue the development of mosnodenvir. This is a rare opportunity to build on a decade of drug discovery and development rather than to start from scratch. Mosnodenvir has already demonstrated antiviral activity in humans. We now need the right partner to build on that evidence and take the programme through the next stages towards patients. Dr. Patrick Chaltin, Managing Director of CD3 CD3, KU Leuven and Wellcome remain strongly committed to move the development of mosnodenvir forward and are looking for the right partner to do so. Mosnodenvir has the potential to make a real difference to people living with the constant threat of dengue. An effective antiviral could add a much-needed tool in the fight against dengue. We now have an opportunity to bring one closer to the people who need it. Dr. Sally Nicholas, Head of Vector Control and Therapeutics at Wellcome More information: Daily Mosnodenvir as Dengue Prophylaxis in a Controlled Human Infection Model – NEJM, 2025 Once-Weekly Mosnodenvir as Dengue Prophylaxis in a Human Infection Model – NEJM, 2026 Programme information: Dengue Virus Inhibitors - CD3 About CD3: The Centre for Drug Design and Discovery (CD3) is an investment fund and drug discovery center created by KU Leuven to drive the translation of innovative research into clinical applications. It provides expert drug discovery capabilities and financial support to academic research groups and small companies to help develop groundbreaking medicines. CD3 has established numerous collaborations with academic institutions, leading to successful partnerships with pharmaceutical companies and has co-created several early-stage biotech companies. www.cd3.be News On Campus Research News Policy News Public Debate Media Resources Staff Resources EN Nederlands English To homepage kuleuven.be

OK Video Video Photo Bangladesh Dengue outbreak Dengue spreads along coast, but no special prevention plan in place Despite the rising dengue burden in this environmentally vulnerable region over the past several years, the government has no special plan targeting the coastal belt. Nor has there been a concerted effort to prevent the deaths occurring there. ADVERTISEMENTContinue to video Powered by VidCrunch Next Stay Playback speed 1x Normal Quality Auto Back 360p 240p 144p Auto Back 0.25x 0.5x 1x Normal 1.5x 2x / Partha Shankar Saha Published: 20 Oct 2026, 06: 17 Three-year-old Fatiha, a dengue patient, receives care from a family member at Mugda Medical College Hospital, DhakaSuvra Kanti Das The Mongla Upazila Health Complex in Bagerhat has 50 beds. On 18 October, 31 dengue patients were being treated there. So far this year, 532 dengue patients have been admitted to the facility. Md Shaheen, the upazila health and family planning officer in Mongla, said the hospital never had so many dengue patients admitted before. He added that the number of hospital admissions did not fully reflect the severity of the outbreak. The situation was even worse, he said. The situation in Mongla reflects the reality across the country’s coastal belt. Dengue was once largely confined to the capital, but it has now spread nationwide. However, the disease has spread more extensively in coastal areas. Nearly 40 per cnet of all dengue patients admitted to hospitals across Bangladesh this year have been in 19 coastal districts. Since dengue re-emerged in the country in 2000, no other period has seen such a high proportion of hospital admissions in coastal districts. The government has not provided any specific explanation for the high incidence of dengue in coastal areas. Researchers, entomologists, physicians and public health experts have offered several possible explanations. Some of the factors, according to them, are coastal areas are relatively new transmission zones for dengue, known in epidemiology as “virgin areas”; water stored because of shortages of safe drinking water; poor sanitation and waterlogging in the absence of elected local government representatives; and natural breeding grounds in agricultural settings. 40pc of dengue patients in coastal districts The spread of dengue beyond Dhaka and other major cities has been a subject of discussion for several years. District-level data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) also show a rising number of cases in coastal districts. The 19 coastal districts are Cox’s Bazar, Bagerhat, Barguna, Barishal, Bhola, Chandpur, Chattogram, Feni, Gopalganj, Jashore, Jhalakathi, Khulna, Lakshmipur, Narail, Noakhali, Pirojpur, Satkhira, Shariatpur and Patuakhali. The survey noted that shortages of safe drinking water and limited access to deep groundwater had led local residents to store rainwater in drums. Stagnant water around homes and a lack of awareness about Aedes breeding sites could also be contributing to mosquito proliferation. According to DGHS data, as many as 43,148 dengue patients had been admitted to hospitals in these 19 districts up to 17 October this year, accounting for 39.6 per cent of all hospitalised cases. During the same period, hospitals across the country saw an admission of a total of 110,312 dengue patients. In 2023, hospitals in coastal areas admitted 97,552 dengue patients out of 321,179 cases nationwide, which was 30.4 per cent of the total. In 2025, coastal districts recorded 35,511 hospital admissions, while the nationwide total was 102,358. The coastal share stood at around 34.7 per cent. However, the 2025 figures cover the entire year, whereas this year’s figures extend only to mid-October. Dengue situation in the coastal districts Prothom Alo infographic Public health expert Mushtuq Husain told Prothom Alo, “The figures we have for coastal areas are based on the locations of hospitals. They do not always tell us where patients live or where they contracted the infection. In reality, the number of cases in coastal areas is likely to be much higher.” Why is dengue spreading so widely along the coast? An analysis of data from Mongla Upazila Health Complex found that more than 55 per cent of its dengue patients came from Mongla municipality. Upazila health officer Md Shaheen said coastal communities faced severe shortages of safe drinking water. Many people stored rainwater or other available water for later use. Since Aedes mosquitoes breed in clean water, he believed this was a major factor behind the outbreak in Mongla. Waterlogging is also common in Mongla pourashava (municipality) and several union parishad headquarters because of inadequate drainage systems. Shaheen said the pourashavas and union parishads currently had no elected representatives to oversee these issues. As a result, little was being done to address water that remained stagnant for long periods. Dengue first emerged in Dhaka and gradually spread elsewhere. When transmission becomes widespread in one area, the virus finds new areas to spread to. Coastal regions offered favourable conditions for Aedes mosquitoes, which may explain the spread there, said entomologist Professor Kabirul Bashar. The information we have about the relative contribution of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus to dengue transmission comes from experience in other countries. The situation in Bangladesh may be different. It is possible that Aedes albopictus has become a more significant carrier of the virus here. This requires detailed research. Entomologist Kabirul Bashar In August this year, the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), under the DGHS, conducted a survey of Aedes mosquitoes in Barguna. Researchers examined 134 containers holding stagnant water at homes and other premises and found Aedes larvae in 26 of them. The Breteau Index, which measures the number of containers containing Aedes larvae per 100 houses inspected, is an important indicator of mosquito infestation. A value above 20 is generally considered a sign of a serious situation. According to the survey, Barguna’s Breteau Index was 53.06. The survey noted that shortages of safe drinking water and limited access to deep groundwater had led local residents to store rainwater in drums. Stagnant water around homes and a lack of awareness about Aedes breeding sites could also be contributing to mosquito proliferation. Jannatul Ferdous, a senior scientific officer at IEDCR, told Prothom Alo that surveys had been conducted in Pirojpur as well as Barguna. Water shortages were a major factor, she said. However, Aedes mosquitoes were also found in large numbers in areca palm trunks and flower nurseries. Unusually high presence of Aedes albopictus There are two main types of Aedes mosquitoes that transmit dengue: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. The former is responsible for most dengue transmission. Yet despite the high number of dengue cases along the coast, surveys have found a significant presence of Aedes albopictus in the region. Work to prevent dengue is being carried out across the country. However, it is true that there is no special programme targeting coastal areas. Professor Halimur Rashid, director of the disease control branch of the DGHS For instance, the IEDCR survey in Barguna in August found that nearly 58 per cent of the Aedes mosquitoes identified were Aedes albopictus, while 42 per cent were Aedes aegypti. Globally, Aedes aegypti is estimated to account for around 95 per cent of dengue transmission by these two species, compared with just 5 per cent for Aedes albopictus. Why, then, is dengue spreading so extensively along the coast? Responding to the question, entomologist Kabirul Bashar said, “The information we have about the relative contribution of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus to dengue transmission comes from experience in other countries. The situation in Bangladesh may be different. It is possible that Aedes albopictus has become a more significant carrier of the virus here. This requires detailed research.” Dengue deaths also higher in coastal areas this year So far this year, dengue has claimed 342 lives across Bangladesh. Of these, 117 deaths were recorded in hospitals in the 19 coastal districts. The actual number could be higher, as not everyone who dies in a Dhaka hospital is a resident of the capital; some may come from coastal areas. Even based on the 117 recorded deaths alone, the 19 coastal districts account for around 34 per cent of the national total. Despite the rising dengue burden in this environmentally vulnerable region over the past several years, the government has no special plan targeting the coastal belt. Nor has there been a concerted effort to prevent the deaths occurring there. Professor Halimur Rashid, director of the disease control branch of the DGHS, told Prothom Alo, “Work to prevent dengue is being carried out across the country. However, it is true that there is no special programme targeting coastal areas.” Public health expert Mushtuq Hossain said, “Unfortunately, coastal areas have become major zones of infection over the past several years, yet I have not seen any specific plan for the region. The people of the coast are silent victims of the government’s overall indifference.” Follow the Google news channel to get Prothom Alo's latest news Read more from Bangladesh DGHS Government IEDCR Coastal Districts Public Health Exclusive Aedes Mosquito Bagerhat Dengue More on Aedes Mosquito Daughter’s dengue deteriorated rapidly without warning signs, physician parents realise too late 04 Oct 2026 100 “hotspots” in North, 29 wards at high risk in South 20 Sep 2026 Dengue: Highest single-day infections this year, 8 deaths 14 Sep 2026 Dengue spreads across country, October poses high risk 12 Sep 2026 More on Aedes Mosquito Dengue: Highest single-day deaths and hospitalisations 08 Sep 2026 World Mosquito Day 5 of 6 insecticides used to kill Aedes mosquitoes no longer effective 20 Aug 2026 Health officials report 546 fresh cases of dengue inflection, 1 death overnight 27 Jul 2026 Interview: Kabirul Bashar Dengue could take a severe turn in August-September 15 Jul 2026

Health Minister Víctor Atallah emphasized the need for continued prevention at homes and in communities, despite favorable national indicators, as weather conditions could increase the risk of dengue transmission. As of epidemiological week 39 of 2026, the Dominican Republic had recorded 396 confirmed dengue cases, including about 15 reported during the week. Authorities said cases remain within the favorable zone of the endemic corridor and below the expected threshold based on the 2019–2025 historical pattern. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Wednesday: IRS Forgives Millions In Tax Debt Before October 31stThousands of Americans are rushing to resolve their tax debts. Although the national trend remains favorable, localized increases could occur. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has reported nearly 1.7 million suspected dengue cases in the Americas through epidemiological week 36. Authorities warned that weather conditions associated with El Niño could favor the reproduction of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, making continued surveillance and prevention essential. Families are advised to keep tanks, cisterns and other water containers tightly covered; empty, scrub and clean containers weekly; remove standing water from tires, bottles, cans and flowerpots; and inspect patios, roofs and gutters after rainfall. supplementary_news.content: ST Pete's Business Daily (and a whole lot more) sign up for a free lifetime subscription And take your seat at the table Name Email Subscribe News Know Innovate Thrive Create Place Impact Venture Arts Content Community Voices Partner Stories Independents The Shuffle Influencers Podcasts Connect Support the Catalyst Contribute Content Promote Your Business Meet the Team Events Connect with us Type a text St Pete Catalyst News Know Innovate Thrive Create Place Impact Venture Arts Content Community Voices Partner Stories Independents The Shuffle Influencers Podcasts Connect Support the Catalyst Contribute Content Promote Your Business Meet the Team Events Know Pinellas combats dengue using Lee County helicopters The dengue virus has reached 351 reported cases in the Tampa Bay region. Published 3 hours ago on October 21, 2026 By Aaron Styza Pinellas County helicopters are not equipped to conduct this type of treatment, prompting the partnership with Lee County. Photo: Pinellas County Mosquito Control. Pinellas County is taking its fight against dengue to the skies, partnering with Lee County Mosquito Control to conduct aerial treatments in parts of St. Petersburg and Clearwater as cases of the mosquito-borne virus continue to rise across Tampa Bay. The treatments could begin as early as Friday, according to Pinellas County Public Information Manager Tony Fabrizio, who said Lee County could deploy up to four helicopters to spray a fine mist of Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti), a naturally occurring bacterium that kills mosquito larvae. “The treatment is very expensive,” said Fabrizio. “They will be using up to four helicopters.”: Official will continue doing rotational treatments each Wednesday. The helicopters will fly at low altitudes between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., allowing the Bti to reach standing water in tight spaces where mosquito larvae breed. Though the low-flying aircraft will be noisy, the bacterium is not harmful to humans, pets or pollinators. Pinellas County’s own helicopters are not equipped to conduct this type of treatment, prompting the partnership with Lee County. As of the Florida Department of Health’s Oct. 15 report, Pinellas County had recorded 37 confirmed dengue cases since August, while the Tampa Bay region had seen 351 cases across Pinellas, Hillsborough and Pasco counties. The numbers are updated weekly on Thursdays. “It’s a regional problem,” Fabrizio said, noting that mosquitoes generally don’t travel far, but infected people can carry the virus into other communities. Dengue isn’t transmitted directly from person to person. Instead, a mosquito that bites an infected individual can acquire the virus and, after an incubation period, transmit it to another person through a subsequent bite. As for where the helicopters will fly, the exact treatment boundaries remain up in the air. “Department of Health (DOH) doesn’t release specific areas,” Fabrizio said, citing HIPAA concerns. “They will draw polygon boundaries and treat within those boundaries. It will include downtown St. Pete. But the polygons have not been finalized.” Preliminary treatment areas in both St. Petersburg and Clearwater are still being determined. Unlike traditional truck-based treatments, which struggle to reach certain breeding grounds, aerial applications can cover larger areas in less time. The county will monitor reported dengue cases to help evaluate whether the expanded treatments are working. Pinellas County has remained under a local state of emergency since September, allowing officials to expedite mosquito control expenditures and potentially seek reimbursement if state funding becomes available. Alongside the aerial operation, mosquito control crews continue daily truck treatments, weather permitting, while additional trucks contracted through Clarke Mosquito Services assist with overnight spraying. County workers are also going door to door in at-risk neighborhoods to help residents identify and eliminate standing water where mosquitoes breed. “In terms of the numbers, we can’t get into the public health part of it, but we’ve had a strong response to dengue,” Fabrizio said, pointing to the county’s outreach efforts and dedicated information website. Residents can register for neighborhood treatment notifications through Alert Pinellas, while additional information about dengue prevention and mosquito control operations is available at Pinellas.gov/dengue. supplementary_news.content: CITRUS COUNTY, Fla. — The Florida Department of Health in Citrus County reported Monday two confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue fever. DOH-Citrus and Citrus County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts. Dengue can present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash. Usually, there are no respiratory symptoms. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 15 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue fever is not contagious, but is transmitted by the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. DOH-Citrus reminds residents of ways to avoid mosquito bites. They include: - Wear protective clothing to prevent mosquito bites. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants. - Apply insect repellents that are registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to exposed skin and clothing. When used as directed, EPA-registered insect repellents are proven safe and effective, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. - Control mosquitoes inside and outside. Repair damaged screening on windows, doors, porches, and patios. Drain water from garbage cans, buckets, pool covers, coolers, toys, flowerpots, or any other containers where sprinkler or rainwater has collected

supplementary_news.content_title: Florida Sees Increase in Locally Acquired Dengue Fever Cases
supplementary_news.content: Gabriela Arevalo Fri, October 16, 2026 at 3:45 PM UTC 0 (bymuratdeniz / Getty Images) Florida is in the middle of a tropical disease outbreak that has surpassed both recent and historical records due to its severity, with one part of the Sunshine State being particularly hit by dengue fever. Related: Recall Expanded for Berries Sold at Walmart, Trader Joe’s, Publix Due to E. Coli Risk As of the latest report issued by state health officials, Florida saw an additional 72 cases of locally acquired dengue fever during the week of October 4 through 10 . “In 2026, 368 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from eight counties,” reads the report, noting that 26 cases of international travel-associated dengue were reported during the same time frame, bringing the year’s total of international travel-associated dengue to 288 cases. Most international travel-associated cases involved travel to Cuba (240), followed by eight cases linked to travel to Colombia, seven cases connected to travel to Nicaragua, and six cases related to travel to India. “In 2026, 368 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported in Broward, Hillsborough (310), Miami-Dade (9), Orange (5), Palm Beach, Pasco (4), Pinellas (37), and Polk [counties] with onset in July (21), August (159), and September (188),” says the report. Related: Meat Recall Issued for Beef, Pork, and More Nationwide: ‘Unsafe to Eat’ Per the Associated Press , this year’s outbreak is the highest for any state “since at least the 1940s,” based on medical journals and historical state health department information. According to Coral Springs News , an 80-year-old person died of “dengue infection” accompanied by multi-organ failure and septic shock in Hillsborough County, where Tampa is located. Workers in the region are spraying to diminish the mosquito population. Related: FDA Issues Nationwide Recall of Millions of Eye Drops–Find Out if You’re Affected Dengue fever is spread through mosquitoes in warm-weather regions like Florida, though historically most cases in the United States originate from international travel. Symptoms of dengue are similar to the flu, including high fever, headache, vomiting, and swollen glands, according to the Mayo Clinic . It’s also called breakbone fever due to the muscle, bone, or joint pain it can cause. Most people recover from dengue in one to two weeks, but may feel tired for several weeks after the illness. supplementary_news.content_title: Dengue fever: why symptoms can worsen even after the fever subsides
supplementary_news.content: Dengue fever: why symptoms can worsen even after the fever subsides Dengue often begins with fever, headache and body pain, but warning signs of severe infection can emerge as the temperature drops. A falling fever is usually seen as a sign of recovery, but in dengue patients, it can sometimes mark the beginning of a more dangerous phase of the illness. Health experts warn that severe dengue may develop as the fever subsides, making it important to monitor symptoms even when body temperature starts returning to normal. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. It is common in tropical and subtropical regions, including India, and mosquito activity often increases during and after rainy periods when stagnant water creates breeding sites. What Are the Early Symptoms of Dengue? Symptoms usually appear four to 10 days after an infected mosquito bite. Common signs include sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, and skin rash. Some infected people may experience mild symptoms or no symptoms at all. Because dengue symptoms can resemble those of other infections, medical evaluation and appropriate testing are important. A fever alone cannot confirm whether someone has dengue. Why Can Dengue Become Dangerous After the Fever Drops? The critical phase of dengue can occur around three to seven days after symptoms begin, often when the fever starts to subside. During this period, some patients can develop complications involving fluid leakage from blood vessels, severe bleeding or organ damage. A reduction in temperature does not necessarily mean the infection is resolving safely. Warning signs that require immediate medical attention include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, rapid breathing, unusual restlessness, and extreme weakness. Pale or cold skin can also signal a serious complication. How Is Dengue Treated? There is no specific antiviral medicine that cures dengue. Treatment generally focuses on managing symptoms, maintaining adequate fluid intake and monitoring the patient for complications. People who suspect they have dengue should seek medical advice rather than self-medicate. Paracetamol may be used for fever or pain when appropriate, but aspirin and ibuprofen should be avoided in suspected dengue because they can increase the risk of bleeding. Antibiotics do not treat dengue because it is caused by a virus. Simple Steps to Prevent Dengue Preventing mosquito bites and eliminating breeding sites are central to dengue control. Health authorities recommend the following measures: - Empty and clean water containers, coolers, and flowerpot trays regularly. - Cover water-storage tanks and discard objects that collect rainwater. - Use mosquito repellents according to label instructions. - Wear clothing that covers the arms and legs. - Install window screens and use mosquito nets when needed. The mosquitoes that transmit dengue are active during the day, so protection should not be limited to nighttime. Community participation in removing stagnant water can also reduce mosquito breeding around homes and workplaces
